div.head: "OUR CHRISTMAS CORNER."
div.p: "OUR CHRISTMAS CORNER."

DREAMING AND WORKING. Cheistmes Eve, and calmly I sat dreaming, Brien fancies entered my rejoicing soul! I thought I saw a second Eden gleaming From torrid woodlands to the frozen pole. The spirit of the Christ had seized the nations, Peace and goodwill had overflown all lands; The skies were thrilling with the exultations Of God•like men, in number as the sands That gird the billows of the awful ocean— No longer slaying each his fellow-man; Rut Raked by love, unstirred by war's commotion, Strong earth to till, free the blue heaven to scan. Hashed was the wail of slavery's bemoaning, Silent the sob of bitter poverty, And stilled the anguish of the captive's groaning, And dumb the voice of human misery. Disease had vanished like a hideous vision, And crime had crept into his den and died, And wrong was palsied and an age Elysian, Soft as the sunrise, o'er earth seemed to glide. With unknown gladness all the birds were singing, The clouds were gilded with unwonted gold, And brighter fountains in the air were flinging A rain of jewels—from all nature rolled A mighty peen louder than the thunder, Sweet as the song of the far seraphim ! I listened, for my soul was emit with wonder— I started, woke, and lo ! it was a dream. And round the house a mournful wind was roaming And ceaselessly the feathery flakes of snow Fell on a silent form that in the gloaming, Homeless and hopeless, wandered to and fro. , About the icy streets the waifs were straying, In city cellars shivering infants cried, In every alley foodless ones were praying For the dry crust that was to them denied. For me the wintry blast was music-haunted, "Peace and goodwill pe OA from a hundred bells! - No joy to them the mellow chiming granted, It mocked their misery—the notes were knells! Then in the room an angel to my seeming Stool by my side and whispered in mine ear : " Dog thou desire fulfilment of thy dreaming ? And would'st thou have a paradise appear aln the drear world? Arise, and clothe the naked, Go aid the sufferers who pine for food, And, from thine idle reveries awako, Go boldly forth, intent on doing good. "'Tis not by picturing the distant morning And musing o'er the glory yet to be That man shall gain it ; but by boldly scorning The thought of self and struggling manfully "To leseen all the weight of human anguish, To dry the weeping eyes, the sick to soothe, "To offer solace to the souls that languish, And show the ignorant the paths of truth. "And while from every steeple bells are ringing Of 'peace on earth' and of 'goodwill to men,' , And joyously the choristers are singing The angel-song, be up and doing; then "The dream will glow with purpose and ahall heighten The hope that makes the humblest toil a joy, And in thy path a golden age shall brighten, And earth claim kinship with the starry sky." Warrington. ARTIMI BENNETT.

[We have substituted 'll3-o'th'-Yatea Audit," given below. in place of 'A Christmas Pic-nic" as previously ancouneed, believing that it will prove to be of greater interest to our read ,rs.—En Ex

AB-O'Tfr-YATE'S AUDIT. BY An EfIFSEL. ',There's a good deeal o' bother i'th' country o' one sort ranother," I said to our Sal one mornin' when th' news- pepper had missed, an' I felt as if th' wond had stopt. "What about?" th' owd rib said, quite unconsarned. Hoo'd just cleared th' table. "Ahout folk no' bein' what they pretend to be,' I said. "Is that summat new; or thou's nobbnt just found it out P an' boo looked at me w'sich a sly look that I suspected hoo'd an idea o' what Pre droivin' at. "I dunno' think it is now," I said; "but they'n getten a way o' findin"em out ut they hadno' used to have. I con Temember a time when th' peeace o' Haziewo'th wur kept by th' baave of a constable; an' he'd nowt to do. Now we'n six policemen; an' it take 'em o their time to look after us." "What rlost' meean by a hauve a constable ?" th' owd ticket said, as if hoo're wonderin' how a mon could live if he're cut i' two. "Well, he ha Ito wayve to fill up his time," I said. "Some times he varied it by gooin' on th' fuddle for a week when ther no signs o' any law bein' wanted. That would be after a pastime, when th' brass wur done, an' they hadno' time to feight." "What has made thee t' begin a-thinkin' about that this =rain'?" boo wanted to know. "It isno' becose thou's seen owt i'th' popper." "Nawe, but th' air seems full of it." "Fall o' what ?" "Well, I conno' co it dishonesty but they're fast cousins to one another." " Thou'rt talkin' strange talk, Ab." "Ay, these are strange times when one doesno' know whoa to trust, nor how soon they're gooin' to be takken in." " HAS thou bin t Ikken in ?" "Well, Pre 'cornered' yesterday." "What's bein' cornered ?" "Thou'd know it if thou wore breeches. I're passin' through th' Market Place i' Manchester; an' when I geet to th" Sponges' corner' Pre tapped on th' shoother. 'Hello, old fellow,' a mon said, are you in form this morning?' Well,' I said, Pm o reet, if that's what yes' meean." Can you do with your throat washing to the extent of two- pennoth ?' he said. 'I could struggle with it, if it wouldno' go down without!' I said. Sc we went Into Fat Jack's, i'th' corner; an' he co'ed for two twopenno'ths wi' as mich swagger as if he're gooih' to get change for a suvverin. When th' glasses wur browt in he began o famblin' in his pockets as if he didno' know they're nowt in; an' when he'd gone throuoh 'em three or four times wi' th' same result,— balance nowt,—he said—' I changed trousers this morning and forgot to take nay money out. Can you put down a shilling for me, and I'll give you an 1.0.TJ ?" I'll do that,' I said; 'l've made th' same mistake mysel. But I'd moore than one pair at th' time. Never mind th' 1.0. U.; it'll nob. but be so mich lumber i' my pocket, for I know it'll never be redeemed." Oh' things are lookin' up,' he said, as he pocketed th' change. Uy,' I thowt, they're lookin' up wi' thee ; if thou con get on to another too' or two; but they'n be lookin' down wi' me if I meet wi' a lot moore friends at wanton their throats weshin! I know what tlaou'rt thinkin' now, owd crayther !" 'Ut foos an' their money are soon parted." " That's just it. I didno' like th' looks o'th' mon. If their short collar's frayed, an' their hat blackleeaded, they're signs 1:1t titer no assets. I've seen him i'th' same trousers till they're welly ready for droppin' off, poor fellow! I darsay he'd like to change 'ern." "Bat thou's a farr rneeanin' P what thou's last said," th' owd stocktnmender hinted. "What is it ?" "Well, now I'll come to it," I said. "For a start we're lain' too fast. Folk man be big chits what else. We dunno' seem to care now whoa's monev it is we spend. It mutt goo f we haa it. I believe some 'folk dunno know th' differ- ence. Look what a row there is gooin' on i' Manchester; an' how they're becoin' one another i'th' newspappers. Not becose some han done owt wrong, but hewn they'n bin fend cut. Thooe ut ha' no' bin rand out are crowin like a cock wi' it's Sunday clooas on, o'er th' tothers. Happen these are nobbut wa.itin' their turns. I feel mysel sometimes as if I'd done summat dishonest; an' if anybody wur to meet me, an awe at me, as if they knew summat, an' say 'Ab, thou's made a bonny mess cn't,' I should feel guilty. I sometimes think I want a saroguard t' prevent me gooin' into some- body's pochets. I thick a pair o' boxin' glooves would be as good as owt, if they didno' look clumsy." "Thou's no' said out thou meeans yet." Th' °wet gel has a deep inseet i' human nature, speshly a mon's. Hoo con read thowts, I believe, as weel as a mountebank, an' could dad a pia if it war hid i'th' hesshole. "4 Well, hardly," I said; "but I' comin' to it. Thou sees dcesuo' matter what position a moans in if he has to hondle

brass he's sure to have some on't. His honesty's i' dange, th' fast minit,—in as great danger as if he'd a lot o' mora` leutenin' flyin' about his yead. He sees th' brass layin' theere, an begins a gooin' round it like a buzze tat a candle. till he's drawn into th' blaze. Then it's w up wi' him. He think, as he's tasted blood, he mit as weel have a sheep as a 13mb ; so th' next thing we yer on him he's missin'. It does seem strange ut better eddicated they are an' wan they are to find out. I should be nobbled af ere I'd pocketed sixpence." I "Ay, it's a good job thou's no larnin', Ab," th' owd I ticket said. "There's no tellin' what sort of a hobble 1 thou'd ha' gotten thysel into if t' had lamed to cypher like 11 owd Judaic. As it is now I con trust thee for bein' owt be. side a foo." ' " Thank thee," I said; "but I'm noane fiehin' for compli- j manta. There's too mony con be had sjrahout—o'th' sort. l But look at our club clack at th' Gerd WM. I've thowt it i etrange a good while at he could do as he does—flyin' about, ' an' driakia'. No wayver con do it. Well, he's bin rand out ; at last. We'a had a moo lookin' through th' books; an' he's I dropt onto him. He's bin dooin' a bit i'th' undertakin' line, I I —quite of a new sort." 1 " What, baryin' folk l' second-hand coffins, an' chargin' I 'em for new uns, like that undertaker at buried owd Schmidt I up at th' Knowe ?" l "No' quite; he's bin baryin em afore they're dead," I 1 ' said, "We didno' know bat what Shoiny Jim war nicely ' beddid i' gravel, till one day he turned up at th' Gerd Bell, an' swore he wurao' deead, an' would prove it if anybody would goo rth' fowt wi' him. That war th' cause co" these ' things bein' fund tawt." , "Well, but he hasno' bin put l' prison for it," th' owd un said. "sow's that bike ?" "It's th' queerness o'th' law," I said. "They conldno' find him guilty a' roguery. He're howdin th' money i' trust till Shoiny Jinr war deead. So he're nobbat guilty o' thingamy. If it could he proved ut he didno' know but what Jim war deead it would ha' bin hanky-panky: and his character would ha' bin clear. As things are there's a blot on it; but that'll wash eawt i' time." "Eh, yo men do mak some strange laws." "Well, if they'n made plain an' straight forrad, we should I ha' no caeion for lawyers. They'd be thrown on th' parish; I so we should ha to keep 'em some road." "If women had th' makkin 01l laws "—an' here th' owd rib looked like owd Moses—" they'd mak 'em so as folk 1 woaldno' want trvin. If they'rn guilty they'd ha' to be ' I punished. They'd ha' no holes to creep out on. No hanky- ' panky nor thingamy. But yo men never do nowt gradely. But what's this bother abeawt i' Manchester?" "Well, there's a lot o' men bin fund eawt to be guilty o' summat. They connot co it dishonesty; but whether it's thingamy or hanky-panky, or legally takkin things as their own, hasno bin proved yet. But I dunno think anybody 'll get i' orison through it.' "Then it seems they con do a great deeal o' wrong ut's rest i' law." "But these chaps ha' no' bin dooM so vary mich wrong o' theirsele. It's nobbut their stomach ut ham bin puttin things oat o'th' sect they shouldno' ha' done; atin, and drinkin, an' smokin. at th' expense o'th' ratepayers. That's what they'n bin dooin." "What, an' getten two pound for everytime meeten ? Ailse o' Jackey's says they'n sometimes as mony as forty meetins in a week. Look at that now. Connot afford 'lowance Out o' that." " They'n nowt e'th' sort as two pound a meetin. They ha' not a penny fro' year's end to year's end." , "Han they nowt nobbut what they con ate an' drink ? " "Nawe ; an' some are so thin they could goo up a stove- pipe." "Well, they shouldao' begrudge 'em o' that. What is twopenn'oth a bread an' cheese an' a pint o' ale? Cr for th' matter o' that, what would a blow out o' potato-pie be? It wouldno' mak O.' rates mich bigger." " Thotert reet, it wouldno'—not above a farthin i'th' pound. But when twenty-one dinners costs above fifty pounds thoose ut conno be in at sich like feedin find taut beco3e they ha' no' their share." "Twenty-one dinners costin' above fifty pound? Wheay, that would be above two pound a dinner." "Ay, if it wur wed l reckoned up." "An' what could they ate to cost that? Gowd?" "It isno' th' atin exactly; it's th' weshin down." 'Well, an' whatever sort o' tubs con they have for howd o that? If they had it i sixpenny it would fill a rain tub. There's nob'deccould get up a stove-pipe wi' o that under their senglets., , "Nawe, nor th' chimbly of a steeam ship." "Well, now, let's see what it would cost twenty-one o' sich like as thee an' me for a dinner, an' thoa's a good twist, Abram. Let it be a good dinner. Th' best ut con be made. Or Fstead o' twenty-one let's say thee an' me an' our lads— five, an' they con side a lot. Two pound o' neck o' mutton at eightpence, that's sixteenpence. Four pound o' potatoes, threehaupence, that's seventeen-pence-haupenny. Two pound o' flour, say fourpence ; tho' it would hardly come to that."

"Co it thrippence-haapenny, then." "Well, we'n say thrippence-hanpenny. That brings it op to one-an'-ninepence. That's th' whal cost of as good a dinner as need be set afore a king." "Thou hasno' reckoned th' fire.' 'Nam), becose we should have a fire if that no cookin." "Nor th' wash-down." " Well, a quart o' thrippeny would just bring it up to two snillin'; an' thou woaldno want nowt better than that. 0 th' what lot thou sees doesno' amount to finnence a yead." This statement caused me to put my stadyin' cap on; an' I began a wotiderin' how it war that wi' atin staff so chep as it war never known to be afore th' same income wouldno' do. Everybody war cryin' out at things war never SO bad. flow is it? I put tlf question to th' owd chancellor olh' exchequer, an' geet this onswer. "Folk wanten moors now-a-days than they'rn used to do. They ha' bin content at one time wi' a walk through the fields ov a summer fleet. Now they mon have a droive somewheere, an' co at a public house. Women con droive now, an' they're gooin to droive as to—" "I know wheere thou meeans, but I thowt some things women could do better than m-n." "Not i' everythin'. I like a woman havin her own place —looking after her husband's brass, an' keepin' him straight, an' goodness knows they wanten lookin after." "That may be; but thou beano' answert my queition. How is it that wi' mayte chepper, it costa us moore to live?" 'l're comm n t 3 that, if thou hadno' stopt me, wer'n satis- fied at one time wi' ale. Now it's gin or whisky, or brandy, an' they keppen it i'th' house too. lack o' Flunter's wif an' me used to have a gill o' fonrpenny between us ; an' that war of a weshin day. Now go to th' Ovvd Bell of a Monday, an' thou'd think there warn° a clock ith' neighbour- hood." _

Why " Ther so mony women come a-seeing what time it IS." "An' what by that ?" "They didno' think it wur so late. They'd left th' dinner part cooked; an' they'd get turned out o'th' dur if it wanto' ready at th' time. But they'n time to hey their three or four two pennoths an' getten as noisy as a skoo." "But it doesno' o goo i' drink," I said. "Then it does house things, an' clooas. Wheere could thou ha' yerd a payanno forty years sin? "Nowheere." "Now they're i' every house. Wheere could thou ha' seen a lad wi' a watch? Nowheere. Wheere could thou ha' seen a wench wi' a bonnet on ov a Sunday? Nowheere. Prin- ted napkins o' their yead, an bedgeawns e' their backs, an' about hanye clemmed to deeath wi' thoose. Now thou couldno' tell 'ern fro ladies, unless it wur by their tongues." "But we'n noather wenches nor lads awhoam," I said. "An' when we'rn bringin' a family up, we could save sum- mat. Now we'n moors cousin' in, an' con save nowt. How is it? "

.—. • "Bost' want to know?" "Ay, an' I meean to know. I'll audit thee. If a Town Council con do wrong, other folk con do wrong. It's nobbut a question of a bigger family. They'n bin overhauled i' Manchester, an' now I'm gooin' to overhaul thee. I want to know th' particulars o' what thou spends ; an' if they are no' satisfactory out thou goes." "Will thou tote me out, Abram ?"; "Nawe, but—" MEP "Ay, wilta ? Thou's forgotten I've bowt a new rollin% pia. Sing smo', my lad, an' I'll show thee how th' money goes. Fotch th' buttery dur." " Wot mon I fotch th' buttery din' for?' "Everything's chalked on theere, even to a pennorth o' sond. Fotch it." Wi' that I went an' lifted th' owd splicin o' booards off th' angles; an' found it war chalked o'er wi' a lot o' things I could mak nowt on—like shopkeepers used to do shop scores afore figures coome i'th' fashin. I reared it up again th' table, an' we proceeded wi' th' AUDIT. Ire never better puzzled my life than when I looked o'er this wooden shopbeok, an' tried to mak out th' meeanin' o' th' figures ut wur on it. I knew that a o meant a shillin', an' a hauve-moon sixpence. I knew, too, that a long chalk stood for a penny, an' a short an a haimenny ; an' that an x war a farthin'. I could add up th' whul lot, an' know how mich it coome to. But what had th' brass bin spoil on? Theere wur th' rub. I should ha' to co in my client to explain. "What does this fast row o' figures meean ?" I ant oar Sal as hoo stood griffin' at me. "Thou man find it out, Abram' hoo said. "But how con I find it out ?" I said. "I mit meean one thing, an' it mit meean another. Th' figures 'll stoud as wed l for atin's as drinkin' stuff." "Ay, it seems thou knows they're a bit mixed up," th' owd ticket said. "There's booath sorts theere. But now I see thou'rt fast, I'll just loosen thee. Thoose fast lot are for flour, an' sugar, an' butter. But whether part on't is for soap, or candles, lam no' sure. It's th' one or th' tother. Thou'll find there's two-an'-thriroence for beef, an' a bit o' suet as thou goes on." "Au' what's this farthin' fore" - A knot o' worsted for t' mend thy stockins wi'. Oh, an' there's sixpence for tae theere. I couldno' mek it out till now. An' there's two three-an'-sixpences for whisky ut thee an' Jack o' Flunter, an' Billy Softly had that fleet at Billy tumbled into th' mophole." "Let's see—when war that?" I said. "Wheay, has thou forgotten, when it's nobbut a week sin ? It shows how thou wur. Billy's had a sore throat ever sin." Seven-an'-sixpence for a fleet's fuddle ! I felt in a good mind to give th' job up. This made me sweeat when I thowt about it. We'd drunken what would ha' bowt three-an'-a- heave dozen o' flour i' one neet. A gradely bakin'—sich a one as forty years sia would ha' caused th' childer to ha' fits. A big mug full o' mowffins an' loaves; o gone down our throttles i' one sittin'-down ! "I'll ha' a pipe o"bacco, I think, afore I goo any said. "I'm getten rayther muddled i' my totals."

" What, has that whisky choked thee?" th' owd nn said. "Well, I man say I'm a little bit flummoxed," I said. "I didno' think we'd had so mich."
CONINDRUMS FOR CHRISTMAS

" Nawe, yo' conno' measure -yor throats when yo' ha' no' fort' keep throwin' brass on th' table. If Billy Softly must ha' paid for his own he wouldno' ha' tumbled into th' mop- hole. His wife sticks to it that some on yo' pushed him in. But I know he went out by hissel. Seven-an'-sixpence, what would ha' bowt me a new pair o' boots for th' winter, gone down yor throats i' one spree. I'll leeave thee t' think about it a bit, an' see if it'll taich thee ony sense." An' th' owd rib dashed iato th' loomhouse, wheere hoo made a cat jump through the window, while I had my pipe. Another eighteenpence gone, I thowt ; but I dustno' say nowt. When I'd getters my pipe fairly lit, an' one leg thrown o'er th' totlaer, I began o' philosophiain'. Th' buttery-dur, as seen through th' reach ut curled about it, took a shape I hadno' calkilated on. Th' figures on it seemed to multiply I to an extent that soon covered th' dur o'er wi' shop scores; 1 and' when they'd filled it, th' dor began o' multiply in' like a pack o' cards, till they seemed as if they'rn showin' me th' I shop-scores of a life-time; an' i' everyone o' these seven-an'- sixpences kept bein' repeated till—l went o'er to sleep uif it had bin fleet-time.

A very little sends me to sleep now. I con goo o'er any- time if th' owd rib's ticklin' my ear wi' one of her sarmons. A nod's very convenient betimes. I' this short sleep I reviewed th' world as it is, or as it's made to be. I seed a grand procession passin' before me; an' everyone i that procession carried a lot o' books that had to be audited; an' ther handret watchin' wi' faces white tinged wi' blue. These war feart o' bein' fund out, I reckon. I'th' front o' me war a grand place about twenty times bigger than th' Manchester Town Hall; an' th' procession wur movin' toard It. I'th' fast rank wur carried a nation's books; an' these had to be overhauled for ages back. Kings, an' shadows o' kings; statesmen, an' shadows o' statesmen, stood by, tremblin' wi' fear. They'd never bin audited before; so never had bin fund out. Mixed among these war a lot o' women; some on their knees, prayin' that certain items wouldno' be seen, or ut th' leeaves wheere they'rn entered mit be torn out. They'd bags o' gewd i' their hoods, for a purpose that'll be seen afore long. These year feart o' bein' fund Out. After these coome corporations wi' their books; an' they'rn fratchin', an' becoin' one another o'th' time they'rn on th' road. They'd everyone bin angels up to this day o' audit; an' they'rn feart they'd ha' to lose their wings. They'd noane on 'em ever had owt, but they kept sayin'—" Thou's had moors than me." ha it war a general case o' pon an' kettle.

Th' next nt coom past war a smart lot. Their books wur o gilt-edged, an' as straight, they wur, as if they'd never bin touched. Nob'dy had ever audited these; an' th' idea that sich a thing ud ever entered anybody's yead war past belief. Everyone o' these wore a white choker, an' looked far, far above suspicion. But a cloud crept o'er the sun Aile they'rn gooin' past, an' some o'th' by-stonders seemed to think it would go hard wi' 'em. These wur followed by a more turbulent gang. These had no books. They'd no occasion for any. 0 th' brass they collected went to one mon ; an' he spent it as he liked. They'rn led up by a band ut made as mich noise as fifty gradely players would ha' done, tho' they'rn nobbut five. But ther lamborines, an' cordions, an' tin whistles to help. A lot beheend wur singin' "Wait till the clouds rolls by," an' just then th' owd sun showed hissel. But he looked as if he're blushin' for summat. Ther a long pause after these had gone ut made a big gap. But de outsiders didno' close in, so there must be someb'dy else cumin'. A shout coome ripplin' up, un geet into a roar at last; 'an' I begun o' wonderin' what wur cousin' next. I didno' wonder long, for, roarchin' as if th' road belonged to her, wur our sal, wi' th' buttery dar. Just then ther a bang as loud as if th' oon had tumbled on th' fender, an' I started wakken. Th' owd rib had knocked th' buttery-dur down, an' hoo wanted to know if I knew which end o'th day it wur. "It looks like mornin', but it feels like neet," I said, hardly knowin' what it war, as I felt a bit dazed. "Art for havin' thy dinner now, or thou'rt for finishin' th' auditin' th' fast?" hoo wanted to know. " Wheay, is it dinner-time ?" I said. An' 1 felt at my I waistcoat. "It doesno' feel above eleven o'clock wi me I yet." An' it didno', noather. "If it taks thee hauve a day to go through a quarter of a dur eson.l be clemmed to deeath afore thou's th' job finished. So thou'd better get thy dinner whether thou'rt

hungry or not." Th' owd crayther war rest. ‘• Well, I picked up this wooden shopbook, an' reared it at yead o'th' house, wishite at th' same time I'd never tackled it, an' sit down to my dinner. I felt a little bit shawmed at what I'd done; an' could hardly look our Sal i'th' face. It war a very quiet dinner-time. Not a word wor spokken o' noather side; an' I felt fain when it war o'er, not feecose I wanted to get to my jeb again, but o' somehow I couldno' help feelin' as if tie' owd rib war auditin' me. How would it be if I gan it up? I'd see what tie' owd lass said. •

" I think I'd better do same as they are at our club, after th' lowance o' whisky has bin drunken," I said. "How's that?" "Write across th' bottom,---' audited, and found correct,' when they ha' no' gone th' hanve way through." "Nay, thou started it, an' thou'll ha' to finish it, if it taks thee o day. So get agate." _

Moore like eightpence. I'll kill it if it comes again. It took a nice bit o' steak last week ut I'd intended for a puddin' ; an' mony a thing it's ta'en afore. Now as thou's finished thy auditin' put th' dur in its place, an' then—" "Then what ?" "I'll audit thee." I hung th' wooden ledger on its angles again; an' prepared my books for examination. "Now, wheere wrir thou o' Monday fleet ?" th' owd ticket begun, as soon as I'd getten i' my cheear. "At th' owd Bell,' I said. _.

"I reckon thou'd nobblit a pint o' fourpenny." Yigh, two." "An' thou sit wi' two pints fro' seven o'clock till eleven, didta ? Had no' thou three glasses o' whisky beside ?" " Whoa's towd thee ?" "1 yerd thee co for 'em." " Wheay, war thou theere ?" "Nawe; but I reckon they set thee agate o' dreeamin' when thou coome whoam; an' thou said just another,' three times o'er. Th' last thou'd have warm, thou said. Abram, if ever thou commits murder thou'll tell P thy sleep." " Well, thou sees I cenno' chet thee." "I dunno' know that. Thou'd moors than three glasses." "How dost' know ?" "Well, thou'd eighteenpence when thou went Out; an' o' Tuesday mornin' thou couldno' pay th' chip lad for a pen- ne'th o' chips." That war auditin' wl' a vengeance, I thowt. "Thou went a-bearin'-whoam o' Wednesday. How mony places didt' co at comin' back ?" th' owd calkilater went on. "1 coome on th' tram back," I said. "What, to th' fowt gate? I didno' know ut th' rails wur laid to our dur."

" Becose it just comes to a shillin. That's a hanve a crown lup to Wednesday—an' sober, too. What would it cost thee o' Setturday neat, when thou're feelin o'th' wrong side o'tle gate for th' latch ?" I couldno' say nowt to that; an' when boo seed I're fast, hoo began her lecture. "Abram, thy drink costs thee as much as would keep th' house on. That's th' reeason ut livin! costa moors now than it did when we'd our lads awhoam. A pint o' fonrpenny ov a fleet would ha' satisfied thee then, a bit of a break-out at a wakes. An' thou'd used to walk to th' town an' back. Now its tram theere, an' tram back; an' stain' like a lord at th' Owd Bell, wi' a cigar i' thy mouth, if anybody's one to gie thee—an' a glass o' whisky under thy nose. Eh, I wish thou could see thy picture when thou's had about three thou'd—." Th' next minit I're i'th' fowt. I couldno' stond bein' audited no longer.—From Ben Bricrley's ,Journal.

It is said that a baby can wear out a pair of kid shoes in twenty-four hours. This is pretty fast work, but an ordinary baby can do much better. It can wear out the patience of an average bachelor in about seven minutes.

CUTTINGS FROM THE ANNUALS. CUTTINGS FROM THE ANNUALS. A BETRAYED WOMAN'S REVENGE. Suddenly, close at hand, I heard a wild peal —a scream of laughter—which made my blood run cold. Swift from the whirling, tossing, drifting snow, emerged a tall, grey figure. It swept past me like the wind; but as it passed me I knew that my quest was ended—that Philippa was found! She vanished in a second, before the terror whicla rooted me to the spot had passed away. Then I turned, and, fast as I could run, followed her, crying as I went, "Philippa I Philippa I " I soon overtook her; but so dark was the night that I was almost touching her before I saw her shadowy, ghost-like form. I threw my arms round her, and held her. She struggled violently in my grasp. Philippa, dearest! It is I, Basil," I said, bend- close to her ear. The sound of my voice ,seemed to calm her, or I should rather say she eased to struggle. "Thank heaven, I have found " I said. "Let us get back as soon as " Back! No! Go on! go on! "she exclaimed. "On, on, on, up the road yet awhile—on through the storm, through the snow—on till you see what I have left behind me! On till you see the wages of sin—the wages of death l" Her words came like bullets from a mitrailleuse. Through the night I could see her face gleaming whiter than the snow on her hood. I could see her great fixed dark eyes full of nameless horror." Dearest, be calm," I said, and strove to take her hands in mine. As I tried to gain possession of her right hand, something fell from it; and although the road was now coated with snow, a metallic sound rang out as it touched the ground. Mechani- cally I stooped and picked up the fallen object. As I did so, Philippa, with a wild cry, wrested herself from the one hand whose numbed grasp still sought to retain her, and, with a frenzied reitera- tion of the words, "The wages of sin 1 "fled from " me, and was lost in the night. • . . I shuddered as the sense of feeling told me what thing, it was I had picked up from the snowy ground. It was a small pistol! Cold as the touch of the metal must have been, it seemed to burn me like a coal of fire. Impulsively, thoughtlessly, as I ran I hurled the weapon from me—far, far away. Why should it have been in Philippa's hand this night / . . . I ran madly on, flashing my lantern as I went on the centre and on each side of the road. I went some distance pastthat spot where I judged that Philippa had swert by me. Then' suddenly, with a cry of horror, I stopped short. At my very feet, in the middle of the highway, illuminated by the disc of light cast by my lantern, lay a whitened mass, and as my eye fell upon it I knew only too well the meaning of Philippa's wild exclamation, "The wages of sin! The wages of sin I". . . Dead! Before I knelt beside him, and, after unbuttoning his coat, laid my he'd on his breast,l knew the man was dead. Before I turned the lantern on his white face, I knew who the man was. Sir Mervyn Ferrand had paid for his sin with his life! It needed little professional skill to determine the cause of his death. A bullet fired, it seemed to me, at close quarters had passed absolutely through the heart. He must have fallen without a moan. Killed, I knew, by the hand of the woman he had wronged.—Dark Days. By Hugh Conmay (Arrom. smith's Christmas Animal).

TO TIIE "BOYS" HERE'S a health to the humorists everywhere, Who help to free life from it cambering care! Who show poor humanity how to unload Their cares by a process of fun a la mode I Whether story with plot so intense, Or a joke with a climax immense, Or a pun with no glimmer of sense, Or an anecdote getting quite old, So often it now has been told, Though the crowd will greet Old frien's whom they meet With a rollicking shout They'd never let out For the newest pun Under the sun! Then strong And long Prolong Song And. toast! Our boast! Laugh! Quail To the funny men, Who, with tongue and pen, "Come up all smiling" again and again —Free Press Flasher.
SARAH WALKER'S COCKTAIL.

"Whin I saw that angel lyin' there," said Sarah Walker's nurse, "as white, if .ye plaze, as if the whole blessed blood of her body had gone to make up the beautiful glory of her hair; speechless as she was, Ithought I saw a sort of longin' in her eyes. Is it anythin' you'll be wantin', Sarah darlint,' sez her mother with a thremblin' voice, afore its lavin' us ye are? Is it the ministher yer askin' for, love ? ' sez she. And Sarah looked at me, and if it was the last words I spake, her lips moved, suld she whispered, 'Scotty.' Wirra 1 wirra 1 ' sez the mother, it's wanderin' she is, the darlin' ; for Scotty, don't ye see, was the grand bar-keeper of the hotel. Savin' yer presence, ma'am,' sez I, and the child's here, ez is half a saint already, it's truth she's spakin'—it's Scotty she wants.' And with that my angel blinks wid her black eyes, yes." Bring him,' sez the docthor, 'at once.' And they bring him in wid all the mustachios and moighty fine curls of him, and his diamonds, rings, and pins all a- glistening just like his eyes when he set 'em on that suffering saint. 'ls it anythin' you're wantin', Sarah dear,' sez he, thryin' to spake firm. And Sarah looks at hitn,and then looks at a tumbler on the table. Is it a bit of a cocktail, the likes of the one I made for ye last Sunday unbeknownst,' sez he, lookin' round mortal afraid of the parents. And Sarah Walker's eyes said, 'lt is.' Then the ministher groaned, but the doothor jumps to his feet. 'Bring it,' sez he, and howld your jaw, an' ye's a Christian sow]: And he brought it. And either the first sip, the child lifts herself up on one arm, and sez, with a swate smile and a toss of the glass: I looks towards you, Scotty,' sez she. '1 observes you, and bows, miss,' sez he, makin' as if he was dhrinkin' wid her. Here's another nail in yer coffin, old man,' sea she,winkin'. 'And here's the hair all off your head, miss,' sez he, quite aisily, tossin' back the joke betwixt 'sm. And with that she dhrinks it off, and lies down and goes to sleep like a lamb, and wakes up wid de rosy dawn in her cheeks, and the morthal seekness gone for ever."— Bret Harte, in Longman's Magazine, Christmas Number.

FARMERS' RENT AGITATION. REPLIES FROM LANDLORDS. On Monday evening an adjourned meeting of the farmers in the fee of Makerfield and the surrounding districts was held at the Gerard Arms Hotel, Ashton, to hear from the committee the replies received tram the landlords and agents to the petitions recently forwaried to them, asking for a re- duction of rent. Mr. Thomas Stone, of Leigh, occupied the chair, and there was a large attendance, at least seventy representatives being present.—The Chairman said the peti- tions had been sent to the landlords in the terms previously agreed upon by the meeting. Those petitions had been couched in the most respectful language, and no complaint could be made against them on that ground.—The Secree tary said petitions had been sent to Lord Gerard, Mr. Short. cede, as representing the executors of the late Mr. Meyrick Bankes, and Mr. Beazer, the representative of Mr. Roger Leigh, M.P. The letter accompanying the netition to Lord Gerard stated: "The tenant farmers on your lordship's and other estates have ventured to join in petitioning your lord- ship and other landowners praying that you will kindly consider their present distressed condition. . . . I desire again, as stated in the petition to assure your lordehip of their loyalty, and that it is dire necessity, and that alone, which has compelled the farmers to appeal to year lordship for help. The committee would be pleased to appoint a small deputation out of their number to wait upon you, in order to place the matter more fullY before your lordship or to render any assistance they Pos- sibly can." The letter sent to Mr. Beazer and Mr. Shortrede were similar in substance, and set out the same facts. The first reply he received was from Mr. Fhorttede, who wrote acknowledging its receipt and stated that it should have early attention.—The Pemberton Representative said, at the dinner following the rent audit of the Winstanley estates, after the health of Mrs. Bankes had been proposed and received in the usual manner, Mr. Shortrede stated, ha reply, that he intended to take the trustees of the estate into consultation with regard to the matter, and he should be glad to do whatever he Paa- sibly could under the existing circumstances in the interests of the tenants on the estate he represented. —The Secretary said the next letter he received was from Mr. Beazer, the agent of Mr. Roger Leigh's estate; and, after some conservation, the Chairman said those gentlemen who had received their petitions courteously at least deserved their thanks.—lt was carried unanimously " That the best thanks of this meeting be tendered to Mr. Shortrede and Mr. Beazer for their kind and considerate replies to the petition."—The Secretary said the reply from Lord Gerard was as follows :—" Garsword, Newton-le-Willows, Lance.' shire.—Sir,---I am directed by Lord Gerard to return to yea the farmers' petition for a reduction of rent, as he has de- cided to receive neither a deputation nor petition on such a subject, as was made known to the tenants on Monday and Tuesday last. Lord Gerard, however, expresses his perfect willingness to fully consider any individual cause of com- plaint, if made known at the estate office, as his inteetion iS far from desiring to countenance any injunctice whatever. —I am sir, your obedient servant, A. B. MOIIBERT." The secretary added that no man who had read the petition as well as the letter sent along with it would scarcely hoe expected to receive a reply of that sort. It was not courteous, and he trusted his lordship Was not serious in directing that the petition should be re- turned.—Several persons present spoke to the same effect. -- The Ashton representative said, although Lord Gerard 's re- ply was not satisfactory, they must not be discouraged; The replies from the other landlords were encouraging, an when Lord Gerard saw those be might be disposed to change his opinions.—A representative said Mr. Hugh Ainecough had given his tenants, or was about to give them, a ten Per cent. reduction.—The Shavington representative said tlezi petitions had been sent to their landlords by the farmers la his neighbourhood, and some replies had already been re' ceived. one unfavourable, and others favourable.7' The Westhoughton Representative said nine or ten landlord! had replied up to the present, and be warp 'lorry te pay 99; of the whole of them not one was considered entirely eatirl: factory. Some promised to consider the application, sac; some made various excuses and various objections. general discussion ensued amongst those present as to what steps should be taken with respect to the refusal of Leta. Gerard to receive the petition. It was decided to respect, fully ask his lordship to reconsider his decision.—A vote et. thanks was passed to the chairman, and the meeting was aa journed.

div.head: SPLIT ON A PUDDING.
div.p: SPLIT ON A PUDDING.

Mrs. Mangles' first pudding was a flaccid failure. Bad enough, but not the worst of it, for Mrs Mangles took the thing In an airy, flippant manner that was almost insulting to a man who had a theory about puddings. Just a "So sorry, 'dear," and a light little laugh, and nothing more. Mangles sighed, but hoped again, and was happy for another year. This time the pudding was a soup, and he had to apologise abjectly to a dozen guests, while Dolly laughed merrily and suggested serving it in a tureen. Then began a long martyrdom for Mangles, and in ten years of married life he had carved puddings that crumbled like sandstone, puddings that melted into black fat when you touched them, that resisted the knife like a cricket ball, that came up without any sugar in them, or were sent down because they contained not one raisin—every kind of pud- ding save a Christmas pudding that was simply eatable. The unhappy husband essayed reprimand, persuasion, education, caresses,arguments—nothing availed. Dolly was still amiable all the year round, and regularly, when the Christmas catastrophe came, said, " It didn't matter this once, dear; and, oh, wasn't it too funny? " Next year the pudding came, it was seen, it conquered. It might have been the pearl of its species,it might have been beyond Soyer and Francatelli—only Dolly had forgotten to have it boiled, and it came up raw, with a sprig of holly collapsing in the middle. Mangles rose sternly and took his hat. "Madam," he said, " during eleven years of married life I have endured puddings like mutton broth,puddings with no suet, and puddings like balls of extinct lava—this is too much. You see me no more." And he went away and was heard of no more—for a year. Three months af that year Dolly spent in exciting but futile hysterics. After- wards she bought nine cookery books, and learnt one a month by heart. Mangles returned on Christmas Day. He said he couldn't live without her, and she might do as she liked, and she was is own popsy-wopsy, and ever so many other pretty things; and he sat down without giving a single thought to the pudding. Not so Dolly. She was intensely anxious about something; her brmer light-heartedness and nave indifference to all things pudding-wise had fled. At last the servant entered, bearing the pudding triumphantly: there never had been such a masterpieee since puddings were invented. He tasted it—stared—then sorrow- fully rose again. "This time it is adieu for ever. You accustom me for years to puddings nobody could eat out of the Chamber of Horrors; I became used to an abomination on my table every Christmas Day; and now when I come back to you, hungry for the dear familiar failure, and your pretty innocent way of laughing at your failure, you serve up something delicious' and are as pleasant a companion as a wet blanket. Good-bye; you are not the Dolly I knew." Dolly's cheeks became white for an instant, and then were dyed with a rich scarlet. She threw herself at Mangles' knees, and seized his hand. "You dear old goose," she exclaimed, in a choking voice, "forgive the deception—the first and last—your Dolly has practised upon you. I've tried all I could, but it's no use, I can't make a Christmas pudding. I wanted to please you, and so .1 bought this pudding at the partrycook's round the corner, and made it hot. I was so afraid Sarah Ann would let the water boil away, or upset it, or muddle it in turning it out, that it's quite spoilt my Christmas dinner." Words cannot describe the rapture, the ecstatic happiness of Mangles. "Darling,' he whis- pered, smoothing her hair as she nestled to his manly bosom, "there is only one thing necessary to complete my bliss. Oh, if only one of your dear old failures-- "She laughed—a low,rippling, ,nusical laugh. " I did make one, before I went to M‘Duff's in despair. It—it stuck to the bottom of the copper, and got burnt ; but if you'd like to see it—" The remainder of the sentence was smothered in the kisses which Mangles showered upon her. The burnt pudding was produced, tasted and unanimously pronounced the most unmitigated failure which even Dolly had perpetrated. They were now happy. Both suffered severely from in- digestion, but for all that there was not a pair of lighter hearts in the whole world that Christmas than Mangles and his wife Dolly.—Funny Folhs Annual.

"No, indeed, ma'am," she replied, tartly, „" I was just as wide awake as I am this minute." During the late American presidential election there have been awful rhetorical efforts. div.head: SHOOTING A MAD SAILOL
div.p: SHOOTING A MAD SAILOL

After very few words, the major agreed to do his best, and, glancing up at the maintop, asked, "Where's the best place to hit him ? " "In the head, if I had my way," growled the old bo'sun. "Ala, well," said the major, a fine, soldierly-looking man, in the prune of life, "I'll try and cripple him somehow." The excitement was now great. Officers, sailors, and passengers all seemed to hold their breaths as the rifle was levelled at the fierce. looking, seemingly unconscious figure, whose eyes were staring fixedly at the steamer, which had now edged in almost too close for safety, and whose rigging and yards were crowded with anxious spectators. It seemed to me that the major aimed straight at Hans' right leg. A good time appar- ently had been chosen, for the vessel was steady as a re& ; but almost simultaneously with thia eport, she gave one of those quick, treacher- bus lurches, and I saw the muzzle of the rifle fly upwards, as, in common with the rest of us, the major lost his footing and slid leeward. Before the Princess rolled back again the smoke cleared away, and we saw our unfortunate shipmate lyirlg &Cross the mizen stay, bent nearly double, and his blood dropping and plashing down on the white lifeboat immediately beneath him, and running down her sides in ghastly crimson streaks on deck. There he hung whilst you might count five, and then dropped wi th an awful thud between boat and spars on to the quarter-deck. The noise of his fall seemed to break the spell of dismay which had come over us, and all hands rushed down the poop ladders on to the deck, where lay poor Hans on his face, quite dead, the bullet having entered just over the right hip. The major stood leaning against the capstan, looking steadily at the corpse, till the "man in blue " clapped him on the shoulder, with "Now, major, the boat ! " Then said he, suddenly, "I feel almost like a murderer."— Graphic Christmas Number.

div.head: SPECTRE'S BRIDE.
div.p: THE SPECTRE'S BRIDE.

Janie was lying there, pale, with her big eyes looking beseechingly at Lady Ossory, as if mutely asking, praying, for the impossible. The half- opened lips quivered now and then, and the cam- bric moved under the deep, long-drawn breath; but these were the only outward signs of life in her. Thus she had been lying there all the after- noon. At last Lady Ossory felt a slight pressure of Janie's hand on her own, the head moved wearily, with the eyes still fixed on her as before, the lips opened and muttered, "The very, very next day i The very, very next day ! " Then, with a small cry, Janie started up and looked around, clutch- ing convulsively Lady Ossory's hand. "Be still, be calm, my child," whispered the old lady. "I am his mother, I know your secret, and I love you as my daughter for his sake." "But—but--where, —and you." "I am his mother—your Jack's mother, and you must be quiet and not excite yourself." "The very, very next day! The very, very next day I " muttered Janie with a slight shiver, nestling closer to Lady Ossory." And this is the day when we were to be married: Married And Jack never broke his promises, you know. He always kept them truly truly -- truly "—" You really must try to sleep! Do not think of it, at least, not just now. There now— that's a good girl." "But he said so, you know, and he always kept his word; he will not break it now, I know. Re will come. He will come and fetch me and then; and then we will be married— married this very day 1 " My child, my dear child, you must not think of this. You must "-- "Not think of it? Not think of hem? Not think of him, when he is coming to me; coming to me to fetch me," and Janie's eyes, which had been wandering about the room before, were fixed on a corner where a:deep-green velvet curtain covered a door leading to the dressing-room. "My child, my darling; what, what is the matter? Look at me," "Look Do you not see him?" " Him ? Whom ? " "Why, him, my Jack; my Jack!" "I see nothing, my dearest. Oh, calm yourself. This excitement will kill you; what can I do?" "But do you not see him There, he holds out his 'arms to me. I am coming, Jack. Oh, look there, look." Lady Ossory's glance again wandered to the velvet curtains, and with a cry, in which terror and joy intermingled, she nearly jumped from her chair. For there stood her son, smiling, and holding out his arms. "My boy; my boy!" she exclaimed. The vision had vanished as quickly as it had appeared. Lady Ossory staggered to the spot, and lifted the curtain, but there was nothing. Then she returned to the bed where Janie was lying, her face beaming with supreme joy, happiness glowing in every feature. Janie was dead.—Henry Herman, in Society. Christmas Number.

Ere Advent dawns with lessening days, s' While earth awaits the angels' hymn, I When bare as branching coral sways _ In whistling winds each leafless limb, - When Spring is but a spendthrift's dream, And Summer's wealth a wasted dower Not dews nor sunshine may redeem, Then Autumn coins his Golden Flower.

div.head: MAYOR OF WARRINGTON ON
div.p: THE MAYOR OF WARRINGTON ON
BAZAAR LOTTERIES.

A bazaar in aid of the school building fund of St. Barna• _ has Church, Warrington, was opened in the Drill Hall, 00 Wednesday afternoon, in the presence of a fair number of visitors. The Mayor of Warrington (Alderman Harriscr, J.P.,) in declaring the bazaar open, after referring to its Oh' jects and congratulating the Vicar, Mr. Allton, on his un• selfish conduct in taking charge of a new parish in a work' log pepulation,Tproceeded to speak on the question of lot' teries at bazaars. He said : I cannot resist the present opportunity of saying something with reference to a discus' sion which has taken place in the papers. You will hay! observed that the Watch Committee of the Town Council of Birmingham, in a sort of pious horror, ill may use such a term, at raffles and drawings which go on at bazaara. have instructed the police of that town to prosecute everr one taking part in them, although they may be got up for religious or educational purposes ; to prosecute everyOn! taking part in them as gamblers. It is contended the' this drawing for prizes is gambling, and that there is no dif- ference between a raffle at the " Pig and Whistle" fel money, or a fat pig, and a drawing for prizes al' a bazaar. If it is illegal it would not be !noun' log in me to counsel anyone to break the law: nor yet to breae it myself, but I do not believe ths" the gaming laws were ever intended to apply to an innocent drawing for small prizes contributed by the benevolent for charitable and religions purposes. (Applause.) To eel that there can be any analogy between public-house raffles and those in connection with bazaars of this kind is sirrilqt in my opinion, preposterous. A publican breaks the law i° permitting them, from the fact that he is prohibited by the 'conditions of his license from allowing anything in the shape of raffling or gambling in his house; therefore if be does permit such a thing in contravention of the law, be can have no cause to complain if he suffers for his infra! , tion of that law ; and I think myself it was a wise problh," tion that a publican should not allow these things to tee° / place, because where men indiscriminately meet together I° ' considerable numbers, and are more or less perhaps under the influence of drink, it would almost be sure to lead to cheat' : jog and trickery, and probably to breaches of the peace. (AP' ' planse.) Therefore I think it judicious that when s publican obtains his license he should be prohibited.' from allowing things of that kind to take Place' But how widely different are all the circumstances and EV" roandings of a raffling at a bazaar, presided over by a ladY' as a means of disposing of her expensive and unsaleable articles for the benefit of a bazaar in which neither she not anyone else has the least pecuniary interest in the worle; (Hear, hear.) Can such a harmless proceeding be comPa!!'„, for one moment to card playing, card sharping, or shaking-, with the dice in a public-house, or to horse racing for stakes, with all its unwholesome and scrofulous surroundings, where cheating of almost every kind is practiced with iril" punity ? Drawing for the unsold goods at these bazaars, may fairly be compared to drawing for prizes at our ar' unions for pictures and articles of virtu, which is just as much gambling as drawing at a bazaar. If one is suppressed, so ought the other to be; and so, presumably, must the athletic sports, to which the public so - generouell subscribe. I am exceedingly sorry such a ritr tion should have been, in my opinion, so unnecessarill raised, because the suppression of bazaar drawings means a loss of thousands a year to all kinds of charitable and religious objects, throughout the kingdom we may sal' and simply for what purpose—to gratify a few crotchet./ individuals who see evil in almost everything. Dr. Job°' son defines a gambler to be a knave whose practice it is to invite the unwary to game for the purpose of cheating than- Bailey, in his time, defined a gambler to be a sharper? 3 cheat, and a guinea dropper: hence we have the explatt.a. tion why any person charged with gambling, as Mr. White says in his letter, will be liable to be convicted as "a reign° and a vagabond." If a man is a rogue or a vagabond, or it a woman is a rogue and a vagabono, it is very proper that he ehould be prosecuted, and I dare say in the majority cl instances he would richly deserve three months' imprison' msnt with hard labour, but what a monstrous farce it is to bring before a magistrate a respectable person of character, whether a lady or gentleman, and because he or she bapPos to have presided over a drawing for religious or charitable purposes to attempt to brand them with the ignominiouS name of a rogue and a vagabond. It is too preposterous to engage anyone's serious attention for one =men!' This interpretation of the law by Dr. Johnson clearly indi- cates to whom the law was intended to apply, and the eta!: acter of the offence it was intended to suppress. FancYr I' you can, some of the leading ladies in London Society, frona the Princess of Wales downwards, and even estimal?le ladies whom we are in the habit of seeing at bazaars—ladlo. of culture, position, and refinement—in our own neigh; bourhood, being brought before a magistrate and committed as rogues and vagabonds for three months hard labour! lt is ridiculously absurd. The art unions at this country are conducted upon the very same principles. They are Per; mitted to have drawings, and I never heard or knew tbs" any bad conseuuences arose frem it. But to go and brand 3 person with the opprobrious names of rogues and vagabOnfls' and threaten them with three months' imprisonment with hard labour for doing a work of charity, why, can Y°° believe that there is a magistrate living who would so Per' yert his common-sense and judgment as to do such a morli strous thing. We must look at the motives which prOWF, people to do an act in order to measure the degree of well& or culpability. The motive that prompts the ladies wh° preside over bazaar stalls and the drawing of prizes is noble! pure, and patriotic. It is to be hoped that we shall noi follow the example, at all events, of Birmingha!!' in their endeavour—a very silly endeavour it is—to revr‘e, a law which had grown almost obsolete by its Own inherenbt impracticability of application to such cases as drawings 3 a bazaar. I can only say that I would not wish my bitterest enemy to undergo a more severe punishment than to be the prosecutor in such a case as those to which I have allude?: I hope we shall hear no more about it. I hope that maglso trates when called upon—if they are ever called upon—'.r exercise their functions in this respect, will allow t_be,..' common sense to triumph over bigotry and prejudice. %to° sale was then proceeded with.

FOREIGN lEWS
t&ist—kKlD THE SOUDAN. SEWS FROM UENERAL GORDON.-THE REBEL;

FORTS BLOWN UP. Kortn, Idee.znay.—A messenger arrived here to-day from Khartoum, faaving accomplished the journey in elevenelays. He brings news that General Gordon is well, and has in- flicted a severe reverse on the rebels by means of his mines. Their forts at °alderman were blown up, and many of the rebels, killed. DEBBED, SATURD&Y. The Mounted Infan'vy and the Guards' Camel Corps arrived here to-day from Ha idak on their way to Korti. The trove are to assemtle at Korti, which is healthier than Ambukol. The telegl aria office has been moved from that place to Korti. DEBBER, Sum:Nev.—Many of the whalers have b len found to be badly injured after their perilous ex, er;ences, and several will probably be unequal to the passage of the upper cataracts unless they are thoroughly repaired at Ambukol. Some of the stores which are being saved for use up coun- try have been damaged by water. Sir C. Wilson expresses himself satisfied with the demeanour of the tribes between this place and Merawi. DEBBEII, MOND&Y.—Lord Wolseley arrived here to-day, and was received by a guard of honour of 300 Bashi- Bazoaks and 100 men of the Sussex Regiment. H after- wards inspected the fort, and received from the command- ant an account of the two unsuccessful attempts made on that place by the Matull's forces. After inspecting the fort, the Stores, and the military hospital, Lord Wokeley pro- ceeded for Korti. Five hundred rebels are still re- ported to occupy an entrenched position, two days' jour- ney beyond Merawi. KORTI, MONDAY.—Sir Herbert Stewart and Staff, with the Mounted Infantry and Guards' Camel Corps, arrived to- day, and will encamp on the west bank of the river, about a mile from Korti. The route from Dangola to Korti is easy for marching, and the line on both banks of the Nile is rich and fertile. The gradual advance of the British is enabling the tribes to cultivate their lands without fear of the troops, whom the natives now approach fearlessly. There is an abundance of cattle and produce in this neighbourhood. Seventeen of the whalers with troops have arrived. The latest reports sate that the Mandi's health is declining, aud that he is losing his influence over his followers. THE FIGHTING AT SUAKIM. Scamer, SllNDAY.—Yesterday a large force of rebels was prevented from attacking the railway by the fire from the water fort. Two of the rebels were killed and several wounded. Spies report that 49 of the rebels were killed and more than 100 wounded in last Monday's attack.—Daily News. SUAYIXE, MONDAY.—It is reported here that Osman Digma has received a letter from the Mandi appealing urgently for reinforcements, to which Osman replied that it was impossible for him to comply, as he expected to be attacked himself. STUMM, WEDNESDAY.-Major Chermside has arrived here. Intelligence has been received from Kassawa that the gar- rison there has made a successfal sortie, and captured a quantity of cattle. TELEGRAM FROM LORD_ WOLSELEY.—BRITISH

div.head: ADVANCE.
div.p: ADVANCE.
The following has been despatched from the War Office:— " Telegram from General Lord Wolseley to Secretary of State for War.

" KORTI, DECEMBER. .—Brigadier General Stewart, with troops from Handak, arrived yesterday. The English boats have up to this point fulfilled all my expectations. The men are in excellent health, fit for any trial of strength as the result of constant manual labour. The work in the boats against the current is very hard, but is borne most cheerfully, without a grumble. All thoughts bend on the relief of Khartouin, and of the gallant comrade besieged there." [VIM/UGH NEUTER'S AGENCY.] KORTI, WEDNespes.—Whalers are leaving here to bring the Sussex Regiment and stores from Debbeb. The last -company of the south Staffordshire Regiment is expected here at the end of the week. A redoubt is being erected to protect the hospital after the departure of the troops. The climate here is very good. The natives are bringing in pro- duce freely from both sides of the Nile. THE BERLIN CONFERENCE. BERLIN, SATURDAY.—The sub-committee held a final sit- ting this morning. The committee met afterwards at half- past three, and concluded the discussion of the Ade de Navigation for the Niger. The report of the committee regarding the navigation statutes for the Niger and Congo has been handed to each of the plenipotentiaries attending the Conference. The committee has still to settle the neutrality question. It is understood here that the English Government propose to appoint six additional Con- Buis on the West coast of Africa without delay, and that these appointments will be followed by further ones as occa- sion may require. This resolution is believed to be due to the representations made by Liverpool and Minchester mer- chants who were in Berlin during the early stages of the proceedings of the Conference. GERMANY.—DEFEAT OF PRINCE BISMARCK.—A

div.head: SCENE-IN THE REICHSTAG.
div.p: SCENE-IN THE REICHSTAG.

13Entaw, MONDAY.—The Reichstag to-day sanctioned the Government proposal, which had been referred to a com- mittee, for increasing the salaries of two officials in the Imperial Chancellery. The Centre supported the proposal. The House next proceeded to discuss the vote demanded for the creating a second directorship in the Ministry for Foreign affairs. In the course of the debate Prince Bis- marck rose to justify the measure. He reminded the House that in 1877 he was compelled, through overwork and fail- ing strength. to ask to be relieved of his functions, and was only enabled to remain in office by a law providing him with a substitute. The Imperial Chancellor continued, *lf the House 'refuses to grant me the means of remunerating a representative, I must decline all responsibility for the further conduct of German foreign policy. When I assure you to-day, on my oath of office, that the post is necessary, and you say 'No,' then you declare me to be either ignorant or incapable. I have sacrificed my strength and health to the service of the Empire and the Fatherland. Do not re- fuse me what is most necessary for the service."—After Herr Haenel had spoken against the vote, Prince Bismarck again spoke. Herr Vollrnar, the Socialist Deputy, remarked that some people had a bad experience of official oaths in the courts of law. The President interrupted the speaker, and requested him to abstain from such observations. Herr Vollmar thereupon added that he was referring to proofs ad- duced in the courts that the official oath had been abused. This rejoinder occasioned great uproar, and evoked tum- ultuous protests and calls to order. Prince Bismarck claimed to be treated with the decency prevailing in educa- ted society. "If," he claimed, "I do not reply in the way the occasion deserves, it is on account of my training and education. I did not stake my oath of office on the ques- tion. I said I considered the grant necessary, and in saying co lam expressing my absolute conviction." The vote was shortly afterwards taken, and resulted in the refusal to grant 20,000 marks, the figures being 110 for and 141 against the grant. THE CHOLERA.

MADRID, SATURDAY.—One death from cholera occurred at Vergel to.day. There was one death and ome fresh case at Toleda. GIBRALTAR, SATURDAY.--Tha Malteo BrUZZO, an Italian •emigrant ship, has arrived here from South America, on her return to Italy. She requires coals and provisions. Twenty deaths from cholera occarred on board the vessel since her departure from Geno I, for South America, two months since. She was refused admittance in any South American port. THE FRENCH NAVY.

PARIS, SATIIRDAY.—The Naval Estimates came on for de- bate in the Chunber of Deputies to-day. Vice-Admiral Peyron. Minister of Marine, explained to the house the pro• gram effected in th 3 construction of war vessels and in naval material. The operations of Commander Riviera had proved that the material and personnel of the French navy were equal to the work before them. Replying to criticisms upon the building of the ironclads. the Minister declared that It was not correct that they would be at the mercy of torpedo boats, and pointed out that Englandcoatinuod building iron. dads. Nevertheless, the naval department would be satis- fied with the ironciads actually laid down, and direct its chief efforts to the building of swift cruisers and torpedo vessels. ANARCHIST TRIAL. Lmassic, MONDAY.—The trial commenced to-day of Reinsdorf and seven others for being concerned in various projected dynamite outrages, including the attempt to blow up the Niecierwald monument, on the occasion of the unveil- ing by the Emperor in September, 1883. Fifty-four per- sons, including six experts, were called to give evidence. After the indictment had been read charging the prisoners with high treason, attempted murder, and incendiarism, the 0183 of the prisoner Buchnan was proceeded with. He ad- mitted having caused the dynamite explosion at Elberfeld, and made various damaging disclosures against Reinsdorf. The latter, on being questioned, declared himself not guilty with regard to the Elberfeld explosion, but described himself as an Anarchist' LENZ, Mosines.—Four Anarchists were arrested yesterday at Urfahr by the police, who at the same time seized the material of a printing press and a number of seditious pam- phlets. AUSTRIA-HUNGARY.—THE COLLIERY EXPLOSION

AT ANINA. PESTS, Mom:AL—ln to-day's sitting of the Lower House in answer to Count Appenze, the Minister of Commerce stated that the mining authorities had instituted an inquiry into the causes of the disaster, adding that the fire was still burning. As regarded compensation no anxiety need be felt, as the comp tny possessed a relief fund of two million florins. It is stated that the explosion was caused through some coal dust becoming ignited. Twenty-three dead bodies have been recovered, and 47 are still missing. This afternoon the pit WU still burning.

div.head: PORTUGAL.
div.p: PORTUGAL.

Motiosr.—ThesPo-rt-ta-liu-ess Cortes were opened t3-day. The Speech from the Throne announces that the relations of Portugal with Foreign Powers are friendly. During the comiog session Parliament would be invited tO deliberate upon the revision of some articles of the Consti- lotion and the reform of the House of Peers. LORD DUFFERIN AND LORD RIPON.

CALCurre, SATIIILDAY.—Lord Dufferin arrived here to-.day, an met with a reception from all classes as enthusiastic as that given to the Duke of Connaught. Troops lined the streets, and the houses were gaily decorated. His Excellency has assumed office as the Viceroy of India. The Marquis of Ripon will start for England on Monday next. CALcurra., NIONDAY.—Lord Ripon has left for Bombay. Bombay is pupating a magnificent farewell. It iq stated that as many as sixty deputations will present addresmes to the Marquis there. Aft-r a stay of three days in EOM- bay, Lord Ripon will embark on Saturday in one of the

Indian government steamers and proceed home, calling at Goa tnd Aden on the way. Eromnev, WEDNESDAY. Lord Ripon has arrived here, itad will make his public entry into the city to-morrow. ' The native population are calking preparations on a very large scale for according the Marquis a magnitic,mt fare- well. LORD RIPON AT BOMBAY. BOMBAY, THURSDAY—Lord Ripon made his state entry into Bombay to-day. From the entrance to the city to the Town Hall, a distance of six miles, the streets were decora- ted with banners, and bands of music were stationed at frequent intervals along the line of route. Thirty thousand cotton operatives in procession accompanied Lord Ripon, and the streets were thronged with an immense concourse of spectators. FRANCE AND CHINA.-200 KILLED. Penis, TUESDAY.—AO official telegrain from Eelung, dated the 13th, says Commander Is Crolx has dislodged the Chinese from threatening positions, inflicting a loss of over 200, French loss, one killed and seven wounded. The Times Hong Kong correspondent says the Fghthouse tender Feichoo is still detained by Admiral Courbet, which renders the maintenance of four lights iropossil,lo and eleven others improbable. This is important to naviga- tion. PARIS, TUESDAY NIGHT.—SDRie of this evening's papers state that several ironciads will be equipped next January and sent, together with three torpedo boats, to reinlorce Admiral Courbet's squadron. PARIS, WEDNESDAY.—According to a telegram of Wed- nesday's date, from General Briers de Lime to Admiral Peyron, a Chinese force of from 2,000 to 3,000 men came down from the mountain to attack a village situated eight kilometres to the north-east of Chu. A portion of the gar- neon of that place, composed of the Foreig,n Legion and Tonquinese sharp-shooters, went in the direction of the village and dispersed the enemy, inflicting upon them very considerable loss. The French loss amounted to 24 in killed and wounded. SPAIN AND WEST AFRICA. MADRID, TUESDAY.—AR official telegram states that 63 miles of the West African coast line, between cape Blanco ' and Bojador, has been put under Spanish sovereignty, besides the trading stations already established in that dis- trict. _ .

CAPE lowx. Nov. 2d -(V-1:PIY-M-0-11T11).—MeSSrS Uping- ton and Sprigg reached Kunana, Moshette's village, on the 15th inst. They could not gain much information from the chief, who, however, expressed himself as the friend of everyone, including Mr. Mackenzie. All they could gather from him was that he hated war and wanted peace. The Ministers then proceeded to Rooi Grond, which they reached on the 17th. BANK FRAUDS IN VIENNA.

--- VIENNA, THURSDAY, 9-40 risr.—The evening 13.mrse w is considerably shaken by the reported disappearance of Herr Jauner, director of the securities department of the Lower Austrian Discount Company. It was evell said that he had committed suicide, but this rumour remains uncontirtneci. THE REVOLUTION IN COREA.—MASSACRE OF

div.head: MINISTERS.
div.p: MINISTERS.

The Shanghai correspondent of Standard, telegraph- ing on Thursday, reports that the discontent with the fresh order of things established in Cores has culminated in a re- volution, accompanied by massacres which for barbarity have scarcely been equalled by any of those characteristic exploits in butchery which from time to time influence political changes in the far Erst. The first outbreak was directed against the Cabinet, which has been accused of un- due preference for the interests of China. The partisans of the Japanese suzerainty massacred seven of the Ministers and compelled thee King to appoint a Cabinet of Japanese nominees. But the Chinese party, recovering themselves, seieed the new Ministers and butchered them in turn. During the conflict it is reported that Prince Ming, the Queen's uncle, was mortally wounded. After the massacre of two sets of ministers the King man- aged to escape from the capital, which was thereupon given over to carnage. A series of sanguinary struggles have taken place in and around the city between the Chinese and Japanese troops, who jointly garrisoned the country on be. half of the suzerains. The Corean troops on their part at- tacked both parties indifferently. The Governments of China and Japan have both despatched troops for the pur- pose of restoring order, but whether they will not aggravate the anarchy and bloodshed which prevail retrains to be seen.

div.head: FRIGHTFUL DYNAMITE OUTRAGE IN
div.p: FRIGHTFUL DYNAMITE OUTRAGE IN
LONDON.

Shortly before six o'clock on Saturday evening, the 17th anniversary of the attempt to blow down the wall of the House of Detention at Clerkenwell, an explosion, which was heard several miles away, took place at the west side of the southern end of London Bridge. There is an entire absence of injury to the stonework of the structure, but there has been a great destruction of property, more especially on the wharves on the northern bank of the river. As in the ex- plosions at the Local Government Board, on the Under- ground Railway, the Victoria Station, and in Pall-mall and Scotland-yard, dynamite is believed to have been the agency employed in the commission of the outrage. When the explosion occurred there were, it is believed, about 500 people on the bridge, and a considerable number of vehicles. A few persons were knocked down by the concussion and some horses alarmed, but no personal injury resulted. No clue has been obtained as to the perpetrators of the outrage. A scientific examination by Captain Cundill, Her Majesty's inspector of explosives, has led to the adoption of the theory that the dynamite was thrown over the bridge into the water, and not laid down with any attempt at precision. A member of the Court of Common Council will move on Thursday that a reward of £5,000 shall be offered for the discovery of the offender. A Paris telegram, dated Monday, says it is stated that the London Bridge outrage was or- ganised there. The police are making inquiries, and hope to obtain evidence which will connect the active spirits among the Irish dynamitards with the crime. It has been suggested that the parcel containing the ex- plosive was lowered by string, but, if so, some portion of the string would be expected to have remained, but no string was found. The theory that the explosive was floated to the spot is rejected on the ground that the firing of the charge could not have been accurately fixed by that means, and, further, had the charge been placed on the abutment of the bridge it would have dislodged the masonry, whereas not a stone has been perceptibly injured. Two shreds of canvas, picked up near the scene of the explosion, have been care- fully examined, and it is believed that they formed part of a piece of sacking, in which the supposed infernal machine was packed. In addition to being badly charred, both rags are impregnated with the gases which are given off in explo- sions of dynamite. Beyond this the police have no clue to the origin of the outrage. Numerous persons have come forward with information which they have considered rele- vant to the outrage, but nothing of any value has been elicited in this manner. The watchman on duty at the hall of the Fishmongers' Company, which has an extensive river frontage immedi- ately adjoiraing the western side of London Bridge, has made the following statement to a correspondent:—" About 5.401 was standing on the wharf. It was quite dark, and, as it was low water, there was very little traffic on the , river. Suddenly I heard a most tremendous explosion, which nearly took me off my feet. At the same instant I saw a very vivid flash, very red in colour, and with a light kind of smoke. There was a gentle breeze b'owing down the stream, and consquently what smoke there was went quickly towards Billingsgate. Simultaneously with the re- port I heard a fearful noise as of smashing glass, and turn- ing round I found that the windows of the warehouses in Swan lane abutting on the river were nearly all smashed. At the time of the explosion I was watching a very ragged- looking man who was standing on the steps leading down to the river on the western aide of the bridge. The man's movements were somewhat peculiar, and as I thought he was a "sneak," having some designs on the adjoining ware- houses, I followed his movements closely. As I was watch- ing him, which would be perhaps about a few minutes 'before the actual explosion, my attention was further at- tracted to a man whom I saw climbing the railings dividing the stairs from the wharf. Not liking the look of this man I either, I made a move towards him, and as I was nearing I the railings the explosion occurred. Thinking that the man whom I had been watching must have something to do with the explosion, I rushed as fast as my legs would carry me towards the bridge. By the time I reached the steps the , second man had disappeared, but the ragged-looking man WS9 still there, fend I at once recognised him as a rag- picker. Thinking he could have nothing to do with the explosion I let him go." 1 Colonel Majendie and Mr. Dupre inspected the buttresses 1 of London Bridge on Tuesday morning with Captain Cund- , hill. The weather was hazy, and although the tide was out , the water was not so low as the inspectors had hoped, and ! another examination will be made at low water, when the 1 river's bed will be searched by drags. Further portions of the woollen material have been discovered, and have been taken charge of by the autholities with a view to analysis. The fragments correspond to the previous portions found. Near where the explosion occurred there is a deep hole in the bed of the river. It is surmised that the miscreants were aware of this, and thosight te shatter the foundations of the bridge by selecting this point for the explosion. The police have received information that about half an hour before the explosion on Saturday night three men hired a boat from the wharf at Quemahithe from the boat- keeper, named Carter. They left 43 on the boat. One of the men carried a parcel 'wrapped in coarse . sacking, which he placed carefully in the stern of the boat. They rowed into midstream, and then let the boat drift. Carter has not since seen either the men or the boat, and, his suspicions being aroused, he on Tuesday communicated with the police. Two empty boats were picked up on Sunday morning. Whether either is the missing boat has not yet transpired. Further examination of the piers and buttresses of Lon- don bridge on Wednesday morning led to the discovery of traces which serve to show that Saturday's explosion was the outcome of a deliberate and carefully planned attempt to destroy the structure. It appears to be beyond doubt that the explosive substance was not thrown over the bridge, but was placed in position from a boat under one I , of the arches, the dynamite having been affixed to the iron , ;grating of an aperture near the bass of one of the piers. In , the light of this discovery the suspicious circumstances ' connected with the hiring of the boat at Queenhithe Wharf lacquire additional importance. No clue has yet been ob- tained as to the wberabouts of the missing boat, though a careful search has been made, and it is presumed that it has I drifted out to sea. GREAT DISCOVERY OF DYNAMITE AT DOVER. i A discovery of dynamite was made on Thursday morning

among the goods landed from the London and Chatham Company's c,rgo boat. Among the goods was a large box labelled "tin." This was opened, and a layer of the metal was found on the top, but on some of it being moved it was discovered that the remaining space was filled with dynamite to the amount of nearly two hundredweight. The matter is in the hands of the Scotland Yard authorities, who were at once communicated with. The case would in the ordi- nary course have been forwarded to London.
