div.head: REDISTRIBUTION BILL.
div.p: THE REDISTRIBUTION BILL.
SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE.

Southport.—At a meeting of the Executive Committee of the Southport Radical Association, held on Friday evening, Mr. William Warburton, the chairman of the association, presiding, the following resolution was passed :—" That this committee having reason to believe that the people of this locality have not been consulted respecting the intended division of South-West Lancashire, so far as it affects South- port and Bii kaiak, would respectf ally submit that it would be more just and more in accordance with public feeling here, that Southport, Blikdale, and the immediate locality shall be constituted a borough and uota county constituency for the following and other reasons, viz. :—ln 1881 the popu- lation of Southport was 32,191, and the population of Birk- ' dale 8,705, making together 40,896, to which it bad risen Ifrom a total of 21,461 in 1871. The population is still rapidly increasing, being fat the present time not less in Birklale and Southport combined than 45,000—having thus more than doubled itself in fourteen years, and at the seine rate it is morally certain that long before the close of the present decade it will exceed 50,000. The committee would, therefore, earnestly press upon the Gaverninent that they shall consider, or. if necessary, re-consider, the claims of Southport and Birkdale, an I deal with them according to the demands of justice, believing that the Government has no other desire."

div.head: NORTH. LANCASIIIRE.
div.p: NORTH. LANCASIIIRE.

.rnackpod.—At a preliminary meeting of party leaders, held at.the Lane Ends Hotel, Blackpool, on Friday, the following resolution was passed unanimously :—" That this meetiug, is of opinion that In the apportioning of a Parlia- mentary representative to this part of North Lancashire, the Fylde poor-law and petty sessional divisions should be the basis of the Blackpool district, with such additions of ad- joining townships as will make up the required population." It was further resolved to cmsalt the people of the country districts, and to lay the proposal b!foro the Corporation without delay.

div.head: NORTH-EAST LINO ASHIRE.
div.p: NORTH-EAST LINO ASHIRE.

Accrington.—The interests of Accrington in reference to the redistribution of seats are not being neglected. A special I meeting of the General Purposes Committee is to be held t) consider the Redistribution Bill and its bearing upon this I district, and steps have been taken by the Liberal party to watch the interests of the town. The Conservatives will I probably be asked to take action, and, if necessary, the two 1 political pirties will co-operate with the Town Council in a I representation before the Boundary Ccmamission. Damen and Bacup.—An "informal meeting" of gentle- men representing the Town Councils of Darwen and Bacup I was held at the Mitre Hotel, Manchester, on Monday, for the " discussion" of the Redistribution Bill in its relation to North-East Lancashire. Rossendale.—The Rawtenstall Local Board, at a meeting held in private, have decided to form themselves into 1 a committee with a view to taking all necessary steps towards souring a member of Parliament for Rossendale— that is, a district—comprising Bacup, Rawtenstall, and Has- lingden. Bu;nley Union —Representations will be made to the Boundary Commissioners, urging upon them the desire; bility of making the Burnley Union, exclusive of the borough of Burnley, 3 constituency of North-East Lanca- shire. Liverpool.—The Liverpool Nine Hundred, at an adjourned meeting on Tuesday night, declared by an overwhelming majority in favour of dividing the city into single member constituencies. An amendment in favour of voting for the nine members en bloc was negatived. The Liverpool Con- servative party leaders had also tinder consideration the boundaries of the nine divisions intu which the town will be cutup, but so far have not adopted a definite scheme.

Mr. J. T. Hibbert, M.P., Financial Secretary to the Treasury, opened a Reform Club at Delph, near Oldham, on Saturday. He saw no objection to the one-member system lof divisions in the larger towns, and did not believe its appli- cation would degrade Parliament by enabling men of "a Ivestry mired" to secare seats. I Mr. W. E. Forster paid a visit to Bradford Central Liberal Club on Monday, and, in the course of a conversa- tion with several leading members of the local Liberal party, expressed his hearty approval of the Government plan of single member constituencies, which he was de- lighted to find also received the approval of the Bradford Liberal Association. Mr. W. S. Caine, in opening a Liberal club at Brixton on Monday evening, spoke strongly in favour of the single- member principle of the Redistribution Bill. Instead of being afraid of introducing parochialism into Parliament, Mr. Caine points to Mr Sclater-Booth, Mr. Pell, Mr. Clare- Read on the Tory, and to Sir. Charles Bilks and Mr. Chamberlain on the Liberal side of the House, as ex- amples of men who have occupied local positions, and says that what he fears is not the parochial element, but the money bag. At a meeting of the Birmingham Liberal Eight Hundred on Monday night, Mr. Powell William said the statement had been made that Mr. Bright was opposed to Aston being included in Birmingham. In reply to a letter' Mr. Bright had written to him that" the opposition to its being added to Birmingham arum from the desire not to increase the con- stituency of Birmingham without increasing the number of Its members, and not to remove the urban population of the county; and unless the urban population should have a re- presentation of its own, or in conjunction with Birmingham, I should think, for many reasons, it would be better to make Aston a part of the Parliamentary Birmingham, as it is now a part of the great industrial centre of the Midland district. ' Why Aston should form a separate borough I cannot imagine. Birmingham is great. Let Aston partake of its greatness and dignity." The Liverpoo/ Post publishes from a speceial correspon- dent an estimate as to the results of the operation of the Redistribution Bill at the next general election. According to this calculation, Preston is again to return two Conserva- tives, Blackburn to divide its representation, Birmingham to -send six Liberals and one Conservative, and Sheffield (which never yet returned a Conservative, though it has now a " Liberal-Conservative" member) three Conserva- tives and one Liberal. Liverpool is expected to send six Conservatives and three Liberals, and Manchester four Liberals and two Conservatives. Three or four Home Rulers, it is anticipated, will displace Liberals in English constituencies. The following is a summary of the complete results predicted : Liberal. Tory. H.R. *lLiroughs 9l ffew B iraughs Counties, ae. Foot land Ol Ireland Total Showing a Liberal maj nay of 84 over Tories and Home Rulers combined. A table of all the constituencies is given. This allots all doubtful seats to Tories, and assumes only a very small Liberal advantage from the lowering of the county franchise, the chief Liberal gain being assumed in counties already Liberal having increased representation. It is con- fidently believed that it gives the maximum the Tories can return. Sir William Harcourt is reported to have given as the result of his calculation that only 150 Tories would be returned to the next Parliament. The above estimate allows 213 ; probably the figures will be between the two, and the Liberal working majority may fairly be taken at 100. - -
*rhe boroughs at present return 184 Llberals and 83 Tories ; the counties 61 Liberals and 121 Tories.

A table has been issued showing the changes in each county of the United Kingdom which will be effected if the Redistribution Bill be passed in its present form, and illus- trating farther how, owing to the extension of the single- member system, the scheme will very largely affect the number of separate elections to be held. For example, the metropolis now returns 22 members, with 10 polls; in future there will be GO members, with 59 polls. Lancashire now sends 33 representatives, with 19 polls ; in future it will have 53 members, with 54 polls. In England there are now 275 polls; at the next general election there will be 440.

Sir Herbert Maxwell, M.P.. issued an address on Friday to the electors of Wigtownshire, in which he says the Re- distribution scheme appears on the whole to be deserving of their favourable onsideration. TEIE BOUNDARY COMMISSION.

- . The Boundary Commission had a long sitting on Monday, at 8, Richmond-terrace, London. Present:—Sir J. Lam- bert (chairman), the Hon. T. Pelham, Mr. Henley, Lieu- tenant-Colonel Jones, Sir Francis Sandford, and Mr. Howell Thomas (secretary). It is stated that the results of meetings held last week at Bedford, Dorset, Notts, Bucks, Derby, Somerset, Berks, and Northampton were dis- cussed.

Major Hector Tulloch, RE., held an inquiry at Cambridge on Monday into the proposed division of the county into three districts under the Seats Bill. A proposal was made to give Ely separate representation, but the Commissioner pointed out that the proposal was contrary to the instruc- tions of the Commissioners, and would create a disparity in the population. The population of Ely was 62,000, of West Cambridge 44,000, and of East Cambridge 42,000. Other suggestions as to naming the divisions were made, and the inquiry concluded. The Boundary Commissioners held several inquiries on • Saturday. Sir Francis Sandford presided at Reading. It was arranged that the three county divisions should be New. bury, eateucling worth to Reading; Abingdon, the rural j north-western portion of the county; and Wokingham, the eastern division. Major Hector Tulloch, RE., presided. at Northampton. The Liberals and Conservatives approved generally of the principal features of a plan by which the county will be divided into four divisions. Mr. Henley, one of the Boundary Commissioners, held an inquiry at Huntingdon on Tuesday into the proposed divi- sion of the county ander the redistribution scheme. There was a small attendance, and no opposition was manifested to the Government proposals, which were to divide the county Into two divisions—Huntington with a population of 27,412, and St. Iva with 29,809. I Mr. Pelham held an inquiry at Oxford on Tuesday' into 'the boundaries of the county Parliamentary division as pro- posed in the Seats Bill. It was proposed in the Government scheme to call the three divisions of the county Chipping Norton, Woodstock, and Watlington, and some discussion took plate on this point.

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

Mr. Adams writes to contradict the statement that he has married Miss Coleridge. An extensive fire occurred on Tuesday at Jones's timber wharves, Haggerstones, London; damage about £12,000. Two men employed on the South-Western Railway, be- tween Lyndhurst and Brockenhurst,were run over and killed on Tuesday by a ballast train. THE CATTLE Suow.—Friday was the closing day of the Cattle Show. The total number of visitors who passed the turnstiles was upwards of 12,000, making a total for the week of upwards of 100,000. Speaking at Dublin, on Tuesday, Mr. O'Brien, M.P., said the Irish Parliamentary party vrould next year meet the de- mand for a renewal of the Coercion Act, with the demand for the impeachment of Earl Spencer. THE DIIMISESS OF SOMERSET died suddenly on Sunday. Her Grace, then Lady Seymour, was thja "Queen of Beauty" at the memorable tournament given by the late Earl of Egiinton at Eglinton Castle, Ayrshire, in August, 1830, Disemincom or RAILWAY WORKMEN.—In consequence of depression in trade, the London and North-Western Railway Company on Monday gave notice to about 50 men to leave work at Crewe. The worka will be closed seven days at Christmas. _

FEMILE SUFFRAGE —Mr. Theodore Frv,MP., has re- ceived the fcllowing letter from the Premier's secretary : " Mr. Gladstone desires me to acknowledge the receipt of resolution which you sent him from Darlington in favour of women's suffrage, and to say that individually he will be g‘ad if this subject receives a full and dispassionate con- sideration."

VISIT OP THE ARCHBISHOP OP YORK TO LANCASHIRE.— The Archbishop of York will pay a three-days' visit to Liverpool towards the end of January. On the 29th he will distribute the prizes in connection with the Liverpool Coun- cil of Education, and on the following day he has promised to take part in a great meeting of the Diocesan Temperance Society in the Philharmonic Hall. THE MIGNONETTE CASE : SENTENCE OF IMPRISON- - Captain Dudley and the mate, Stephens, of the yacht Mignonette, who were sentenced to death for killing and eating the lad Parker, and whose sentences were afterwards respited during her Majesty's pleasure. have now been sentenced to six months' imprisonment. The men were informed of this in Holloway Gaol on Saturday. REMARKABLE ESCAPE by A CONVICT.—A ticket-of-leave man, named George Crawford, better known as "Cockney Joe," a notorious coiner, on Monday made an extraordinary escape from the lockup near Birmingham. When the officer went in to give him his breakfast Crawford sprang at him, knocked him on the floor, ran out of the cell, and locked the door. The officer was thus Imprisoned himself, and the con- vict escaped. SCIENCE wITH PnacTinet—At the annual distribution of prizes at the Bradford Technical College, on Monday night, Mr. Mundella said what they wanted and what that insti- tution was trying to do was to unite is one person a man with a practical knowltdge of the workshop and a scientifie man who brought intelligence and knowledge to bear upon the industries in which he was engaged. Mr. Forster also spoke and referred to the services Mr. Mundell& had ren- dered to education. _

MANOLAIIGHTINI IN IBELAND.—AI Minder Assizes, on Tuesday, Philip Guron was tried for the murder of Hannah Walsh, in Cork city. An illfeeling had existed for some time between the parties, who were of the labouring class. Prisoner was found guilty of manslaughter, and sentenced to five years' penal servitude.—Thomas McNamara, mason, was found guilty of the manslaughter of an old woman named Johanna Barry, in Limerick city, and was sentenced to five years' penal servitude. Wzron VERSUS Exousu.—An amusing incident has arisen at the Holyhead Board of Guardians in consequence of the Welsh members being unable to understand English and the English to comprehend Welsh. The Welsh wished to have the proceedings conducted in their native tongue, and the English-speaking members protested. After pro- tracted discussions, it has been decided to allow each member to speak as he pleases, and his observations will have to be translated for the benefit of those who do not understand. _

IGIFT OF i HOSPITAL TO LIVERPOOL.—Mr. Henry Tate, sugar refiner, of Liverpool, and Streatham, Surrey, has an- nounced his intention to erect in Liverpool, and furnish at his own expense, a building to be used as a hommeathic hospital for the free use of the public. A site has been secured in Hope-street, and the arrangements for c irrying out Mr. Tate's intentions have been given into the hands of the Committee of the Homcepathic Dispensary, who are now considering the details. It is understood that Mr. Tate's gift represents a money value of £lO,OOO. A WINDFALL FOR PAUPERS —Two workhouses were each deprived of an inmate last week. Jane Handyn, widow, 70 years of age, and her brothers and sister have received a legacy of £2,500. Jane has been in Devonshire Workhouse 14 years; her brother, John Balsdon, is believed to be in Liverpool, and another is in Torpoint Workhouse. Their brother Richard went to Bermuda 67 years ago. It has been ascertained that he died leaving a fortune t lii relatives. I The husband of another sister, by whose inquiries the be- quest was discovered, is a widower, and therefore receives no share. ISERIouS CHARGE AGAINST A BUTLER AND HousE- HEEPEß.—Joseph Johnson and Ella Smith, who were until ; recently butler and housekeeper respectively at Gledstone ! Hall, near Skipton, have been committed for trial on char- ges of stealing paintings, engravings, water-colour sketches, Oriental plate, and other articles to the value of nearly a , thousand pounds, the property of Mrs. Roundel!, widow of a late High Sheriff of Yorkshire. The valuables were re- moved from the hall by degrees, and were not missed until a few days ago. A great portion of the goods have been , recovered. WHOLESALE SWINDLING OF HOTEL AND SHOPKEEPERS.— Renfree, described as a tutor, of London, was again charged at Leicester, on Saturday, with systematic frauds upon tradesmen and hotel proprietors. He was remanded last week pending inquiries, and the Chief Constable now stated that the prisoner was connected with a notorious I gang of swindlers in London, and was wanted at Birming• ham, London, Wolverhampton, Portsmouth, and other places, having defrauded tradesmen to an enormous extent ,in all parts of the kingdom. He was again remanded for seven days. THE BILADLAUGH CASE.—In the Court of Appeal, on Monday, in the case of "The Attorney-General v. Brad- laugh, the defendant, in person, applied for a new trial on the ground of improper reception of evidence, that the ver- dict was against the weight of evidence, and that there had been misdirection. Mr. Bradlaugh argued that he had com- plied under the statute when he administered the (nth to himself; that therefore the penalties amounting to £1,500 'were not recoverable, and that he he had in no way contra- vened the Standing Order of the House Of Commons. The Court reserved judgment. SHOCKING. MUTILATIONS ON THE RAILWAY.—About 5-30 ' on Saturday morning a greaser named Jackson was knocked down by an engine at Heaton Mersey, and bad his skull crushed in a frightful mantle,. Jakson was taken to Stock- port Infirmary, but is not expected to survive. He lived in Bamford-street, Heaton Norris. About the same time a pilot guard named John Hopwood was knocked down by an engine at Heaton Norris, one of his legs being completely taken off above the knee. The other leg was broken. He now lies in a very dangerous condition at the Stockport In- firmary. He also lives at Heaton Norris. IN AND OUT OF GAOL—The chaplain of the prison at Chester haa drawn the attention of the Commissioners of Prisons to the serious evil of the frequent recommitment of prisoners for short terms. As an instance of commitments from the city of Chester, he notes that during the past year a brother and two sisters had been received, the man having been iii prison more than 100 times, and the two women twenty and ten times respectively. When not in prison all three were inmates of the workhouse. The chaplain ex- presses an emphatic opinion "that nothing short of legal power to keep such characters for a long period under some sort of reformatory discipline and beyond the reach of temp- tation to drink" will meet cases of this kind. MR. CHAMBERLAIN AND LORD RANDOLPH CHrriCHILL. —The following letter from Mr. Chamberlain in reply to an inquiry, has been received by Mr. F. E. Allen, of Hock- ley-hill, Birmingham :—" 40, Prince's-gardens, W., Dec. 6. —Dear Sir,—l am in receipt of your letter of the sth inst., enclosing an extract from a newspaper in which it is stated that Lord Randolph Churchill's return for one of the Con- servative districts in Birmingham had been secured by negotiation between the noble lord and myself. The statement is, of coarse, absolutely without foundation. I do not know of any Conservative districts in Birmingham, and I have neither authority nor inclination to negotiate with any one for the future representation of the borough. I shall be glad if you will communicate this contradiction to the newspaper in which the statement appears. —I am, yours truly, J. CHAMBERLAIN.—Mr. Frank E. Allen, l Birmingham. THE ROCHDALE EQUITABLE PIONEERS.—On Saturday evening the annual meeting was held at Rochdale, Mr. J. Whitworth in the .chair.—Sir U. Kay-Shuttlewortb, who was the principal speaker, said it was an encouraging and hopeful sign that English workmen could succeed on a large scale in the co-operative movement, which inculcated economy, self-elevation, and advancement in education. He advised them to read an interesting volume which was in their library—the report of the commission on foreign in- dustries and technical education,—for it gave the effect of various movements in different countries. There was one subject which it was scarcely necessary to allude to in Rochdale, for there was no likelihood of them going wrong on the subject of Free Trade.—A report of the year's wprk was read, in which it was stated that the tall number of members on the books on September 9 was 11,033 e with a share capital of £328,476 ; cash received for goods sold amounted to £268,846, or an average of £5,072 per week; the total profit for the year, excluding interest, amounted to £37,599, of which £34,000 had been absorbed in the pay- ment of dividend to members. div.head: LIBERAL WARD MEETING.
div.p: LIBERAL WARD MEETING.
-SPEECHES -841--IIL4Lc3INNIE3, M.P., AND MR.
W. CROSFIELD.

On Tuesday evening a meeting of the Liberals of North- West Ward was held in Wycliffe Hall, Bewsey-striet, when addresses were given by Mr. J.G.Mcßlinnies, M.P., and Mr. W.Crosfield, J.P. The chair was occupied by Mr. F. Monks, IP., and there was a large attendance, amongst those pre- sent being the Rev. R. Filcher, 8.A., the Rev. G. E. Cut- ting, Dr. Gornall, Councillors Broadbent, JP., Barker, and Roberts; and Messrs G. Wallington, jour., F. R. Roberts, J. W. Hall, James Evans, (kc. The business of appointing ward cauncil and committee for the ensuing yoar (Mr. Monks being re-appointed chairman) having been gone through, The CHAIRMAN, in the course of a few introductory re- marks, said that he thought the scheme of redistribution which had been submitted by the Government and which was the work of both the political parties, was at any rate a very fair attempt at representation of the whole country, and what they wanted was a fair representation. There seemed to be a great deal of doubt as to the single-member principle of representation, which formed a very prominent feature of the new measure, but he did not know that they should be afraid of it. If he himself bad had the choice he:would rather have had two-member districts, but at the I same time he was not afraid of the constituents not choos- ing very suitable men. (Hear, hear.) He thought that in the framing of this measure both sides had risen above mere party considerations and had fairly considered what was beat in the interests of the country. (Hear, hear, and

• Mr. W. CnitagmEan, who was received with loud applause, said that he should like to draw their attention that night to a comparison between the state of matters before what they spoke of as the original Reform Bill that was in 1831, and the position in which they now found themselves on the verge of this greatest of reform bills that had been passed in this country. He spoke of comparison, but where things were s) different it would be more suitable to use the word contrast, for he thought that before be had gone far they would see that contrast was a more suitable desig- nation than comparison. He would allude to the political influences which reigned in the year 1831. Tney found that the landlord interest was then preponderant. It has been said by an observer that in those days members of Parliament sat in the seats they had bought avaiting for the highest bidder to take the votes which they were empowered to give. (Hear, hear.) That was not a flattering descrip- tion of the position of a member of Parliament, and they now knew something better than the condition of affairs which that described. (Applause.) The power was in the hands of the landlords, and even the middle classes whom we now look upon as so powerful were practically ignored in politics. It is recorded that the calico printers of. Manchester having a special grievance, their trade being specially depressed in conse- quence of oppressive taxation, determined that their voice should be heard in Parliament. The way in which they set about this great undertaking was to raise a fund of £4,000 lin order to buy a seat in which they might place some one of their number to state their case in Parliament. (Hear, I hear, and laughter.) The working classes—he used this phrase because it was the common one, not because he thought any on 3 of them could claim a patent right to the title of working-man ; he thought they all did their best at working hard, and he hoped, succeeded. (Hear, hear.) He used the phrase then because it came readiest to one's tongue. Working-men were absolutely ignored. They were voiceless. They found, however, that though their political voices were inaudible the grievances under which they suffered did find expression in the record of crime. They found that in that day even in England there were crimes which were now unknown, and which were unfortu- nately identified with the sister isle. Crimes which they now classed as agrarian crimes were then rife in England. They read in the history of that time of such incidents in country life as rick-burning, and other dangers of the like kind to which the farming interest was specially subject. They read again of bread riots being the expression of the starving population against the excessive prices of the most necessary article of food. It was a state of affairs that still existed in some of their neighbouring countries. No doubt some of them would have read in the last few days of threatened riots in Paris, where there was a working popula- tion pressed down by the difficulty of purchasing bread, and insisting upon the Government lowering the price and fixing it at a low and reasonable figure in order that they might be relieved from this pressure. (Applause.) He might just allude in passing to another incident in France. Whilst the working classes were feeling this pressure, the governing classes had taken a somewhat curious way of remedying the evil by putting a tax upon imported grain, a remety one was inclined to think it would not prove to be. (Hear, hear.) This system of dutiee reminded one of the grotesque way in which trade used to be fostered in Eng- land—he was now alluding to a period further back than 1832. When the woollen trade was in special depression an Act of Parliament was passed to foster the woollen trade, land it was fostered in this way: it was enacted that all bodies should be buried in woollen shroudg. (Laughter.) They found that that system of fiscal policy was imitated in Scotland at a time when Scotland had only one industry to rely upon—that of linen. They enacted that all Scotch bodies should be buried in linen shrouds. (Laughter.) They, however, knew better than that now. Since the Reform Bill they had been gradsally arriving at an almost entirely free state of trade. Just before the frce , trade agitation came into operation their customs tariff con- 1 ' tained no less than 1,200 articles' and there were now only I six articles which stood between them and that free break- fast table of which John Bright frequently spoke. (Ap- I please.) He made a slight mistake in saying that, for one of these articles was tobacco, and that was hardly an article which they saw on the breakfast table. (Laughter.) They no doubt had felt that the prosperity which had flowed over their country through the adoption of free trade principles ' had been a general one. He would show to them that the advantage which had been gained had been to a great ex- tent gained by the artisan classes which dwelt in their large towns, and that the unrepresented field labouring class has not reaped the same benefit, thus showing that it was political influences of each class that brought to it an ame- liorated condition of life. In the year 1839, when Cobden and Bright were beginning to think about agitating the country for cheap bread, he found in the "Life of Cobden"' that a Somerset labourer with a wife,, and five children 1 under ten years of age, only earned a weekly wage of 7s , 1 while the price of commodities was as fellows : They re- quired half a bushel of wheat which cost 4s. out of the 75., bacon, balm, ate., cost 6d., and rent monopolised is. 61 making 61 61,and leaving that family of 7 persons ad per week with which to provide themselves with clothes. (Hear, hear.) It was an interesting matter to look at the amount of crime which existed in the early days before the Reform Bill was made into law, and they foudd that the committal of pri- soners throughout the country in 1830 amounted to 55,000 in the one year. Last year, with a vastly increased popula- tion, the committals for crime only amounted to 20,000, thus showing how much better was the general condition of the population throughout the country. (applause.) Mr. Crosfield then quoted statistics, which went to show the ine- provemests which had taken place during the last fifty years in the condition of artisans, both with respect to the increase of wages and the decrease in the price of tta , greater number of articles in COMEttOtl tall. There were those, he went Ala to Say, who saw danger in the extrsardi- hary prosperity which was indicated by these statements he had jest been making, and there was a feeling that the mass of the voters who had been enabled to im- prove their position so much might go on im- proving their position to such an extent that the prosperous classes might some time become the dangerous classes, and 1 that democracy would bye and bye become "king in the land." (Hear, hear.) He for one had no fear of this. lie believed that concurrently with all these improvements there were other improv-naents going on which gave them very material guarantees for the safety of their loved land. (Hear, hear.) They had a greeeer amount of intelligence and education amongst them, and tbe classes who had re- cently got votes had secured good schools for their children, and had provided for the future voters of a class more inlet- ligent than they had had in the past. He found from edu- cational returns which went back as far as 1851 that where- as then the Government inspection only covered a quarter of it million scholars, while the last examination embraced four millions of scholars. (Applause.) There was another material guarantee that was likely to have some weight amongst the working classes, and that was the money argu- ment. The working classes were rapidly becoming monied classes. He found that in 1831 the number of depositors in savings banks only amounted to under hilt a million, and that in 1881 the number of depositors were four millions. (Hear, hear.) Their deposits in 1831 only amounted to £14,000,000 sterline' whereas in 1883 they amounted to £88,000,000. (Applause.) Some information was given by the figures concerning to-operative societies, for whilst in 1862 the capital of the co-operative societies was 8.483,000, again under half a million, in 1881 they had a capital to the extent of £7,000,000. (Applause.) There were other figures which he coul go into, showing how rapidly the working climes were t cumulating money, and giving hos- tage for their good be 'vim he was going to say, and for their stability. (App. ase.) There was the department of building societies, and Although he had not the figures with him they would find that the amount of money which build- ing societies held,and which was entirely invested in land, represented as great an increase and was as great a security as the figures which he had already quoted. (Loud applause. Mr. MCMINNIES, M.P., who was received with loud ap- plause said: I beg to move "That we, the Liberals of the North:West Ward, heartily approve of the candidature of William Crosfield, Esq., J.P , and pledge ourselves to use every possible lawful effort to secure his triumphant elec- tion at the next Parliamentary contest." (Loud applause.) I suppose, Mr. McMinnies went on to say, that our business to-night is an entirely local business, and that we have to do particularly with local politics. But I daresay those of you who have read what appears in the public papers as the speeches of public men will have eeen that they appe.,- not to be able to keep Out of their view what has pie I in London very I recently. The Franchise Bill, or Act, as may now call it —(applause)—and the Redistribution Bill have been like Charles the First's head in Mr. Dick's memorial—it seemed to be quite impossible to keep them out of the public speeches. In order, therefore, to gee quit of this inevitable digression 1 tieg as briefly as possible to congratulate you upon what has occurred in London during the last few • weeks. (Hear, hear.) We have got the Franchise Act, and that is a matter which is entirely for the congratulation of

1 the Liberal party, inasmuch as it has realised all theirhepeS and efforts. (Hear, hear.) We have got in additioa a prospect of the Redistribution Bill —of a Redisiriba. tion Bill better, I should think, than most of us ever ex- . pected to see, one which at any rate entirely satisfies ate, and I believe entirely satisfies the great bulk of the ad- vanced Liberal party. (Applause.) That is what we have got; I am not careful to go into the question at to which party comes off with flying colours. It does not matter to me very much. We have got the Franchise Bill and a good RadistrEution Bill, and I for oae am—and I hope you are—satisfied. (Applause.) Gentle- men, we have got the oyster, and if anybody is anxious about the shells they are welcome to them. (Laughter and applause.) As far as I know the only objection of any great moment that is entertained 1 towards the Redistribution Bill is the division of great cities and boroughs into districts. That is no objection to my mind. I have been of opinion'that that is the best and fairest way of getting an equitable representation of the opinion of each community that coald possibly be devised, and I have had this opinion ever since it was promulgated by my friend, Riahard Cobden. (Hear, hear.) I believe Mr.Cobthn was a man of the most sagacious and thoughtful mind that ever characterised a public statesman in our day, and I should say that that man is a very rash man wee would place any living statesman on a higher level for the possession of those qualities than ha would place the late Richard Cobden. (itear,hear.) You may depend upon it that scheme which was promulgated :tad advocated for years by that man is note scheme that advanced Liberals

need be afraid of. (Hear, hear.) Having got quit of Charles the First's head, I come to my own resolution. You have all heard many addresses from Mr. Crosfield—l sup- pose he must have delivered about a dozen. some of them I have, the rest I have read, and I think I may say that it is your opinion that for breadth of view, for thoughtful- ness, for sagacity for intelligent knowledge, he pm- ' sesses everything that you need desire as a Liberal representative. (Applause.) In addition to these he has the gift of tongues ; he has the facility of expressing his views in a clear and lucid way so that they may be "nu- .

. derstanded of the people." (Applause.) I do not know speeches that read so well, I do not know at any rate speeches that read better than do the speeches of my friend Mr. Crosfield. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Crosfield is a man of approved Liberalism ; he has been for years endeavouring to promote Liberal opinion in the neighbouring town of Liverpool, and he has succeeded, and his efforts in teat tcwn are valued. (Herr, hear.) This reminds me of whet 1 hive seen stated somewhere, tbat Mr. Croefied is a strang,r— (laughter)—and that be dots not five near us. Well, I don't know about that. Liverpool is only 20 minutes ride from • Warrington at any rata and I should not be at all serialised, if, after the next election, many of the people in We, ring- ton should find Liverpool nearer than Weton. ( Land cheers, and laughter.) But, at any rate, lam reminded of whet wee once said in my presence by a Mayor of Warr:nee ton. Somebody from Liverpool was disparaging Warriega ton as a small and insignificant town, and the Mayor of Warrington at that time, with a great deal of local p attot- ism that did Lien much credit, said, " Why, I knew :nen who have lived in the time of other men when letters for Liverpool were directed to 'Liverpool, near Warrington.'" (Laughter and cheers.) We are a good deal nearer Liver. pool now than we a ere in those days, and I daresay we shall be nearer still. Mr. Crosfield is a man of mature age. He his lived long enough to have a great experience and great poiltical know- ledge, and be has not lived long enough to forget it. (Loud laughter and cheers.) I daresay there are serae of us who aredisposed to envy him in this respect, and I must say that in enterprise, energy, endurance, and power of labour, time beats us. I have heard of peeple, who, in- stead of growing old, grow younger, and it is a very happy thing if they do. But it is not my experience. At the same time, if it is so—if there are old men who grow younger, it is a very good thing for them. At the same time it does appear to me, from my experience of mattere, and from what is around me, that it comes very much to the same thing whether old men grow older or whether old men grow younger, for I think they arrive about the same time at second childhood. It would not be at all proper to recent- mend Mr. Crosfield to you as a person who is likely' to stand up sturdily for his own epinione. Those who have heard. him and those who have seen him are very likely to form their own opinion about that. I have known Mr. Cresfieldes family for four generations, and lam quite in a position-to . assure you that if he has not the courage of his opinions, he - is the first Crosfield that had not. (Laughter and cheers.) I daresay you will agree with me when I say, very briefly, that I believe he is his cousin John's frost cousin. (Laugh- ter and cheers) Then there is the question of Mr. Crote. field's prospect of success at the next election. What we - have to do is to carry our candidate. (Cheers.) But we have something more to do in 1886 then we had in 1880. In 1880, after a very gallant battle, creditable,. I must say, both to the leader and to the followers, although, perhaps, I ought not to say it, but in 1880 what we had to do was to break a yoke which had been resting upon us for 33 years, with an exceptional interregnum of, perhaps, some four or five years. We had to break that yoke, and we did it. What we have to do in 1886 is—(A. Voice : "Keep it") —yes, but not only to keep it, we must strengthen it, and make that which was a breach in the Tory party in 1880 an entire smashing of it in 1886. We are going to win, that we know—ilaughter)—and our opponents know it. (elp. plame ) The venerable chief of the Tory party, about whom, I hope, none of us will ever speak except with the respect which is due to his advancing youth—(loud laugh- ter)—he knows it. And the young men who are muttering about future membership in terms which it takes hal a zen letters in the newspapers to explain afterwards, they know it also. (Laughter.) The old men see vision; and the young men dream dreams —(load laughter)— bat they are the phantasms of the imagination, all dreams of the night. We are going to win, but we are going to win more than before. I hope we shall so win that we shall never have to fight another battle. The figures " 529 "—(applause)—have become familiar to us . . .

let us raise them; let us go in for a thousand, and depend upon it if we get a thousand in IMO your dilliculty will be imnaeasureably less at every future election, and perhaps we should never have a contest afterwards. (Applause.) This is what you have to do. You have a good candidate, von have a good cause. (Hear, hear.) You have a united party, and in all these opportunities you be.Ve the advantage of your opponents. Let us take the advantage of what is before us, let us be determined to win, and win well; and, gentlemen, if we de this you may depend upon it we shall succeed, and make Warrington what such places as Wolver- hampton Walsall, and Birmingham are, and the great centres of population In the Midland counties; the district to which We beleng, to which the great majority of the people of this ward belong; you will make Warrington what those places are—a firm and impregnable position, an inviOlate stronghold of Liberalism. (Loud cheers.) The Rev. R. Putman, in seconding the resolution, said he was one of those who thought that on the whole there was come danger that an inferior class 0 men might reach the honours of members of Parliament, anti therefore he had taken particular care to watch th."., Clhaidate that had come before them, and in orde: that he might have a fair and proper standard by •flich to judge him he (Mr. Filcher) - had selected e speech of a superior being of the member of rar.lit"Lent order for his guidance—a gentleman who had been. on Parliament 33 years with a short interregnum t'aird who therefore was an authority on that subject. He like the rest of them had a strong—a sentimental objection 'to the splitting up of constituenees, and if it could have - been managed that they should have had a member for 'Warrington and a Member for Walton it would have been a nice arrangement. (Laughter.) Well though their friend was a stranger, he supposed they should do thelr beet to take him in. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) On looking at this speech, which he took for an authority, he found there ;vas a great absence of compliment. (Laughter.) Mr. Fierpoint was unfortunately not able to be there that night. Ho (Mr. Filcher) was sorry for him, because that might account for the fact that Mr. Crosfield did not say "We thisk ourselves fortunate, and we think you, Mr. Plerpoint, also fortunate—we think it no small advantage to Mr. Pier- point that he lives so near to us as to be able to enter this spacious and good building, and to soy that be, eith you and me, rejoices to come here." (Loud, laughter.) Well as Mr. Pierpoint was not there Mr. Crosfield could net say that, _ bat Mr. Roberts gas, and Mr. Crosfield might certainly have said "Mr. Roberts has always been right, and wheel he speaks favourably of me I am almost disposed to think better of myself than I should have done if I had not had Mr. Roberts'a good opinion and good word." (Laughter.) So he (Mr. Pilcher) thought their candidate had still some little to learn from the superior being he had to replace. (Renewed laughter.) In concluding, Mr. Filcher said that although their friend Mr. Crosfield had bees strangely de- fective in the question of complimen.s, and though he did not repeat what a superior 'beirg said the other night, he was just the man they wanted. (Loud ap- plause.) The Rev. G. E. Cu ITING, in supporting the resolution, said he should support Mr. Crosfield because helves a tem; perance reformer and because the Liberal party would give them mori of that legislation which the temperance party w„.ntad. (Applause.). _ _
" Mr. T. Maillse and M. JAMES Evan also supportedthe resolution, which was carried by acclamati.m,

_ Mr. G. WeLmucerou, jun., then moved the following resolution— That this meeting, being of opinion that the House of Lords is a great obstruction to all necessary and progressive legislation, and a serious danger to the welfare of the State, demands such a reform thereof as will bring it more into harmony with the spirit anO rqulre t the age." menta of Mr. .1. &taw GREEN seconded the resolution, which was also carried by acclamation. div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, DECEMBER 20, 1884.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, DECEMBER 20, 1884.

THE members of the Proportional Repre- sentation Society have entered upon an edu- cational campaign ; they have been twitted with advocating something that is not wholly intelligible, and they are determined that at any rate they will make themselves under- stood. If they are to perish, they are re- solved that it shall not be said of them that they died and made no sign. A public meet- ing was held in London on Monday, and another in Manchester on Wednesday. Each meeting was addressed by Tories as well as Liberals—the platform being one upon which politicians so widely divergent as Mr. EDWARD CLARKE and. Mr. BRADLAuGH can take a common stand. Sir Joliri LUBBOCK, who occupied the chair, was disposed to be rather severe upon those who have urged that the method of voting under a system of Pro- portional Representation was beyond the comprehension of the ordinary elector. It was equivalent, he said, to suggesting that the people who had so lately been spoken of as "capable citizens" were " really born idiots after all." " All the electors would have to do would be to place i and z against the names of the candidates they preferred." This, is, no doubt, simple enough; and yet it is an explanation that wants explaining. The fact of the matter is the advocates of Proportional Representation, while agreed as to the object aimed at—that of aetting full value for every vote, and thus securing a true reflex 9f the opinion of the nation—have been at odds with each other, until lately, as to the best method of attaining this end. Is iL to be wondered at that, whilst the thinkers in this matter were still feeling their way, every-day sort of people should be disposed to refer to them as the political visionaries? They have not so long been out of the wood, if they are yet out, that they need to shout. They are, however, now agreed amongst them- selves that .Proportional Representation can best be attained by what is known as Mr. HARE'S system of the single transferable vote. This does not permit of town or coun- try being parcelled. out into single-member constituencies ; quite the reverse, and hence the resignation of Mr. COURTNEY as a mem- ber of the Government, on single-member constituencies being made a feature of the Seats Bill. But let us give an illustration by way of making the matter plain. Take Liver- pool, with nine members under the Reform Bill, and assume that the candidates—a score of them it may be—are before the whole of the electors. Each elector has one vote only, and in marking his voting paper he puts the figure 1 opposite the name of the candidate of his choice, and the figure 2 opposite the .name of the person who stands second in his affections and to whom in certain contingencies he would wish his vote to be transferred. Let it be supposed that the voter is a Home Ruler and a Liberal, and that s,OOO votes will secure the return of any one candidate. He has voted, say, " " for Dr.

Commixs as the Home Rule candidate, and put the figure " " opposite the name of Mr. SAMUEL SMITH. The votes are counted, and as it is found that Dr. COMMINS is " in " with s,OO r. The one vote which is thus to spare is carried to the credit of Mr. SMITH, and thus helps to secure his return, and, so on, if there should be one thousand instead of one to spare. This process would, of course, operate vice versa—that is to say, when Liberals who were Liberals first had voted for Mr. SMITIII they could help Dr. COMMINS, who might otherwise be low down on the list. But it will be said, what is to be gained by this, see- ing that the opposite party would work in the same way? Would it not come to the same thing in the end? The contention is that it would not—that it would give a section a chance of obtaining a representative of their opinions which they could not otherwise obtain. To keep to the case of the Home Rulers—though the reasoning holds good as to Tichbornites and Bradlaughites, and other " ites "as well as .Parnellites—it is possible to conceive of their being strong enough in Liverpool to return one representative with ease under HARE'S plan of Proportional Re- presentation ; whilst under the new Seats Bill, through being in a minority in every single constituency, they would have no chance at all. The question is— Is it advisable to risk leaving a body of electors—large when looked at in the aggregate—wholly without direct representation in such large centres of population as Liverpool, Manchester, Bir- mingham, and Glasgow? Sir JoHN LUB- noc and Mr. COURTNEY are ready with an emphatic " No "; but those on the other hand who do not take to the new-fangled scheme urge that majorities ought to rule, and that it is unwise to trouble about the representation of minorities. But this latter is a statement which requires to be examined. The majority ought certainly to rule; but what majority? It would be possible to deal with the United Kingdom as one great constituency, leaving the party that obtained the largest number of votes in the possession of power, with the Opposition snuffed out. That, of course, would never do—though it would still be the rule of the majority. Division of some kind is seen to be necessary ; but what division ? "Ay, there's the rub." There are difficulties, as Mr. GLADSTONE said, whichever way we turn. The Proportionalists have h strong desire to preserve the unity of towns and cities, and are thus diametrically opposed to ward representation ; but even they do not propose to apply their system, pure and simple, to the metropolis. Yet, to be con- sistent, they ought to do; but they, doubtless, think that London in this, as in many other respects, must be regarded as an exception It will thus be seen that no scheme which has yet been proposed can be regarded as theoretically perfect ; but we are disposed to conclude that Mr. HARE'S plan more nearly merits that description than any that has yet been proposed. It is pointed out that under the defective system of representation which Parliament is seeking to remedy, it was a misnomer in 1874 to talk of the majority ruling, the fact being that, although the Tories at the General Election obtained a majority of representatives, the Liberals had 240,000 of a majority of votes. If, as the members of the Proportional Representation Society urge, such an anomaly would be im- possible under the system they advocate, it is not to be denied that that system has a strong claim at the present moment to the considera- tion of the electors of the United Kingdom.

THE Mayor of Warrington has entered the lists as champion of Lotteries at Bazaars; and , having on our side taken a stand on this question, it shall not be said that we shrink from breaking a lance with him. He is aware, he says, that it would ill become him to counsel anyone to break the law, or to break the law himself; but he does "not be- lieve that the gaming laws were ever intended to apply to an innocent drawing for small prizes contributed by the benevolent for charitable and religious purposes." This, however, does not amount to much ; the "I do-not-believe " of Alderman HARRISON would scarcely be accepted as a legal author- ity in a court of law. It would be found, we are afraid, that those who depended upon it would be leaning on a broken reed It would be interesting to observe what his Worship would do if a summons were taken out against a clerical offender for "keeping open a lottery." Would he take the law into his own hands, if he were sitting on the bench as chief magistrate, or would he, as is usually the case, seek advice as to the law of the magistrates' clerk ? He would "cut a funny figure " if he acted contrary 'to the advice given him by the legal adviser of the Bench, and Mr. WHITE, as he has publicly explained, has no sort of doubt , that those. who take part in Raffling at Bazaars are liable to a heavy fine, or three. months' imprisonment with hard labour. It 'would be small consolation to the offender who was caught tripping to find that the I MAYOR had been caught napping, and com- pelled by a mandamus to reverse his decision. IThe fact is the MAYOR is "not in it" as to the law on this question, and if he would keep ' himself and his friends out of trouble, he had better abstain from setting up in opposition to the regular authorities. Mr. WHITE knows what he is about, and the MAYOR and Cor- poration of Birmingham know what they are about. But for those who want something more, let us ref -r to the law itself:— "Every person playing or betting by way of wagering or gaming in any street, road, highway, or other open and public place, or in any open place to which the public hare or are permitted to have access, at 1 or with any table or instrument of gaming, or any I coin, card, token, or other article used as an instrument or means of such wagering or gaming at any game or 'pretended game* of chance, shall be deemed a rogue and vagabond, and as such may be convicted and punished tinder 5. Geo,_, 4, c., 83.' (The Vagrant Act) [36 & 37 Via, c., 38, S. 3.] *" Any game, the result of which depends on the drawing or colour of a card, the throw of dice or coin, the revolution of a ball or teetotum, or other purely accidental circumstance will be within the meaning of these words and the mischief intended to be remedied." (Stone's Justices Manual.) It is no use the MAYOR suggesting to his brother magistrates that the law has grown "almost obsolete," and that if a case came before them they must "allow their common sense to triumph over bigotry and prejudice." He knows, or ought to know, that it is the primal duty of magistrates to administer the law as they find it; and we do not hesitate to say that magistrates who took upon themselves to deride by over-riding the law, whatever their "common sense" might be, would soon find that their names had been removed from the Commission of the Peace. As to the law being " almost obsolete," that is a question of facts,and the facts are against the Mayor of Warrington. If his Worship had not been so absorbed in the duties of his office, he might have heard that within the past few weeks several persons have been fined from L to to L I 5 and costs for selling lottery tickets

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, DECEMBER 20, 1884.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, DECEMBER 20, 1884.

at St. Helens. Publicans, the Mayor may say, who "raffle at the Pig and Whistle for money or a fat pig." And what then? Is it very much worse than raffling for a five pound note at a Bazaar ? As for the "fat pig," for ourselves we should much prefer it to some of the "lean kine " that are frequently raffled for when the bazaar of a Church is on its last legs. We are not, let it be understood, defending raffling in any form ; all we ask is that I if the law is brought into operation I against publicans, it shall be put in force against parsons. • But publicans, we are told, know that it is a breach of their license to keep open lotteries. Of course ! they know it, if they know the law; and 1 in that respect they can rub shoulders with ! clergymen, churchwardens, and deacons. Alderman HARRISON is surely aware that it is an old legal maxim that the plea of I " ignorance of the law is no defence " for I wrong doing; and if it were it would scarcely avail in this part of the country, after the ! "awful warning" which wa3 given last ' week by the magistrates' clerk. But, , to carry the matter a step further, it should ' be pointed out that some of the offenders fined at St. Helens were not even of the Pig ' and Whistle order; they were shopkeepers of the ordinary class. Again, we have in ' mind the case of a poor Irish girl who was brought before the magistrates and com- mitted to Preston Sessions, because she had I ventured to try to raise a little money, by ! means of a raffle, to support a sick mother. Talk about the " noble and pure" motives of "the ladies who preside at bazaar stalls and , the drawing of prizes," will the MAYOR ven- ture to say that their motives were nobler or ! purer than those of this down-trodden Irish I girl who was committed for trial, because she !! had, in a small way, and from a feeling of !' filial affection, kept open a lottery ? Or are we to abase ourselves before purple and fine !! linen, and "with bated breath and whispered humbleness" say : Through tattered clothes small vices do appear ; Robes and fur'd gowns hide all. We must defer for the present what we had ! intended to urge on some of the moral aspects of this question of Lotteries at Bazaars. Meanwhile we lay before our readers the following powerful passage from a recent sermon by the Rev. R. J. WARD, Congregational minister at St. Helens. He says:— It makes one bang down one's head in shame, that, in the name of our common Christianity, people should be asked to take part ir religious sweepstakes; that the youths of our town should learn their first lesson in gambling in connection with religion, that while publicans who sell lottery tickets are fined and imprisoned occupants of the very Bench which passed sentence upon them shortly being found in another part of the same building, dabbling in lot- teries themselves. There; we think it will be admitted that that lance has struck home.

VISIT OF THE REV. PETER MCKENZIE TO RUNCORN.— The Rey. Peter McKenzle will lecture at Runcorn on the 12th January next, on "Simon, the Galilean fisherman." The lecture is in aid of a local Wesleyan movement. RATEPAYERS' ASSOCIATION.—A meeting ef the members of this society was called to take place on Tuesday evening for the transaction of annual business, but as there was not an attendance large enough to form a quorum, it was ad- journed sine die. HALTON MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.-411 connection with this society, on Tuesday evening, the Rev. Thomas Hackett delivered a lecture in the Trinity Weelevan School- ' room. Subject : "The use and abuse of the sense of humour." Mr. Hugh Rowe, sen., presided. I RUNCORN Y.M.C.A. HISTORICAL SOCIETY.—Dr. Bagnaa.,, on Thursday evening lectured before the members of this society on " Cheshire Border Castles," displaying an inti- mate acquaintance with the interesting subject. There was a good attendance and Mr. S, C. Beckett presided. RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH DIVIDING CLUB —The ac- counts of this society for the past year have just been closed, and on Monday next a dividend of £l. 2s per member will be paid. The income has amounted to £l9B 17s sd, and the sum of £55 17s 3d has been paid in sick and burial claims. LEorrne AT RUNCORN. On Wednesday evening the Rev. Robert Morton, of Liverpool, lectured in Brunswick schoolroom, on "Untitled Noblemen," under the auspices of the Young Men's Mutual Improvement Society, The lecture, which was delivered in an eloquent manner, was much enjoyed by a large audience. Mr. r. Norman presided. FIRE AT HALE Featee.—About eleven o'clock on Wednes- day night the joiner's shop at the Hale Hall Farm was dis- covered tube on fire by Edward Peedlingtm and William Leadbetter. Through the energetic measures adopted by the bailiff, Mr. Winskill and P.C. Clarke, the flsmes were extinguished in a quarter of an hour after the discovery of the outbreak. The roof of the building was considerably damaged, and a quantity of wood was destroyed. SMITH'S RUNCORN Amdeerac.—eMessrs. Smith and Co., druggists, of Runcorn, announce the early publication of their almanac for 1885. Although the book has always been a capital production, this year the publishers have surpassed all their previous enterprises, and the public will be able to obtain a most interesting volume for the small sum of a penny. Besides a mass of useful local and general information on a variety of subjects, there is a short but attractive historical sketch of Runcorn from the tenth cen- tury to the present time. SUDDEN DEATH AT WIDNES.—On Thursday, Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, held an inquest on the body of Matthew Butler, ages 62 years. Butler, it appeared, lived with his son at 14, Princess-street, Widnes, and also worked for him at the Widnes Alkali Works. It was his boast that his constitution was unimpaired, and that his health bad always been good, but on Monday night previous to retiring to rest he complained of flatulency. Next morning at six o'clock the son went to awaken him, and found him lying in bed dead. There was no suspicion of foul play, and the jury retarded a verdict of natural causes. PRIMITIVE METHODIST BAND OF HOPE RUNCORN. The members of this society gave an entertainment in Re- gent-street schoolroom, on Thursday evening, to a fair audience. The Rev. J. Pickwell presided and delivered an addreSs on the temperance question. An attractive pro- gramme of songs, recitations, dialogues, ikc., was gone through by H. W. Pickayell, Arthur Stubbs, Fanny Shine ler, Annie Tomlinson, James Shingler, Charles Davies, Elizabeth Davies, and E. M. &Angler. Under the leader- ship of Mr. James Stubbs, the choir sang several temper- ance glees. Miss Midwood presided at the harmonium. ZION UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH, WIDNES.— The members of the band of hope in connection with this chapel gave their monthly entertainment on Monday even- ing to a good audience. Mr. E. Gandy, of Runcorn, pre- sided, and delivered an appropriate address. Concerted music was sung by the children in good style. Recitations were given by Nellie Farber, Lilian Wate, Jane Summer- bell, Mary Wilcock, Bertha Woodward, Sarah Grey, Cl ar- Woodward, Timothy Wilcock, Harry Wilcock, and Archi- bald Gray. A dialogue was taken part in by Jessie Betnev, Eliza Jane Betney, and Mr. A. Greig ; and another by Jessie Hughes and Lily Bradburn. Mr. D. Price contribu- ted the song" Hurrah friends, hurrah 1" The usual votes of thanks brought a pleasant entertainment to a close. Lecnossm.—Rock Ferry v. Widnes. This match was played on the ground of the former. Play was commenced at 3-30, and although the home team were without Paton, G. Davies, W. H. Stott, and A. Morecrofr, they were never- theless victors by one goal to nil •, the visitors on the , other hand were short of a man for their right attack, but as the ball was kept well in play it could be seen the teams were equally matched. Though seveal good attempts were made on the visitors' uprights by Harding and Broad, they were ably guarded against by White and Gossage, who played a very good game. Up to half-time nothing was scored, but shortly afterwards Rock Ferry scored a goal by Harding, who after numerous attempts succeeded in beating the visitors' guardian. Afterwards the light became bad, and as there were ten minutes longer to play, it was agreed to bring the game to a close, leaving Rock Ferry victorious by one goal to nil. S. ; Swale, were theuked for their past services and re-elected. I I TEMPERANCE MISSION AT WIDNES.—Each evening during I the past week Mr. Thomas Rosbottom, of Wigan, has con- iducted temperance mission services in Mali's Temperance Hall, Slintll'al Cross. There have been large audiences, and many persons have taken the pledge. THE UNEMPLOYED AT WIDNES.—DGITiDg the past week the Widnes Local Board have employed about 30 men, who I have been thrown out of work by the depression of trade, in preparing materials with whieh to repair the roads. A further number will shortly be engaged. I ORANGE CELEBRATION AT WIDNES.—The members of the Widnes "Beaconsfield " and "Invincible " Orange Lodges commemorated the anniversary of closing of the gates of Derry by a meeting at Unsworth's dining rooms, , Victoria-road. Bro. Rankin, G.M., presided. I A "DOLLS'" BAZAAR AT WIDNES.—Mies Polly Edward- son on Thursday held a bazaar in a large room on her father's works, Ilibbert-street, in aid of St. Paul's Church, !Widnes. There was a stall containing dressed dolls and ' various articles of apparel, and also a well-stocked refresh- ment stall. The bazeer was well patronised. RENT REDUCTION IN CHESHIRE.—MT. R. C. Naylor, of Hooton Hall, has remitted to the whole of his tenantry on 1 the Hooter' estate in Cheshire 10 per cent. on their rentals, and also intimated that he will do everything in his power Ito assist them to improve their lands and homesteads. Mr. I Naylor has made a substantall reduction of rents now for several years in succession. FORTHCOMING BAZAAR AT WIDNES —ln our advertising columns will be found the announcement of a beater to be held in L icey-street School-room, Widnes, on Tuesday the 130th inst. and two following days. The committee having charge of the arrangements are sparing DO effort to make the affair attractive and successful, and the object will commend itself not only to the Wesleyans but to the public at large. THE DISAPPEARANCE OF AN OLD MAN AT RUNCORN.— Up to last evening no tidings had been received of Mr. Jonathan Rushton, 80 veers of age, who has been missing from his home in Halton-road since Wednesday the 10th inst. He was last seen near to the Bridgewater Coma and the water has been dragg-d, with the result that a hat identified as belonging to the missing man has been found. It is fearcd that he has been drowned. IMPROVED STREET LIGHTING AT WIDNES.—For a con- s'ilereble period there have been complaints of the insuffi- cient lighting of various parts of Widnes, and on Thursel.), night are:sire. Midwood, Sadler, and Johnson,of the Highway , Committee, mode a tour of a portion of the town. They have in consequence, we understand, decided to recommend the Board to erect a lamp to be erected on the footpath. leading from Moss Bank to Newtown, one in Waterloo-road, one in Moorfield-lane, and one on the Marsh Hall foot- path. HALTON WORKING MEN'S MUTUAL BENEFIT SOCIETY.— The annual meeting of this society took place on last even- ing week, in the Wesleyan School-room. There was a large attendance of members. The treasurer's account showed that the total receipts for the year were £1.4 18s 7d, and the expenditure, including funeral money, sick pay, secretary's salary, and rent of room, £25 OS 6.1, leaving a balance to be divided of 40 IS3 ld, or 133 8d to each member. The fol- lowing officers were re-appointed :—J. H. Gamon, treasurer; , Robert Hughes, secretary. The following were appointed as the committee for the ensuing year: Messrs. Cooke, Wil- I liamson, Richardson, Heleby, Walker, Leech, and Bosworth. President: Hugh Rowe, junior THE NAVIGATION OF THE IRWELL LED THE MERSEY.— A special meeting of the Bridgewater Navigation Company was held on Wednesday, at Manchester, to consider a scheme ' for the Improvement of the navigation of the Irwell and Mersey by deepening, widening, and straightening the rivers, and constructing new locks, weirs, and other works. The estimeted cost of the improvement is £324,000. It pro- vides for reducing the number of locks from eleven to six, shortening the r• ute by several miles, and making the rivers navigable for boats of several times the tonnage of those which can now use them. The chairman denied that the scheme arose altogether out of what had been done by the promoters of the Ship Canal, and said the company had the necessary parliamentary power to carry out the work. The scheme was approved by the shareholders. PATENTS.—List of applications for patents filed from December sth to December 11th, 1884, selected by Messrs. !
