ROBBED BY A SHIPMATE AT WIDNES —At Runcorn Police Court. on Thursday, before Mr. C. Reynolds and Captain C. W. Haz'ehursr, Winkel Frederick Spiller, a sailor on board the schooner Janie, of Runcorn, was charged with stealing a purse containing 10s. from the per- son of William White, a sailor on board the same vessel. It appeared the the two men visited a house of Wayne in the town on Tuesday night. About eleven o'clock W bite was lying asleep on the ofa, when another sailor named Stroyan observed the prisoner E.B to the sleeping sailor and abstract a purse from his pocket, aed take some money from it. Nest morning information was given to the police, and Police-clerk Wallace apprehended the prisoner on board the schooner.--Mary Wilson deposed that when the prisoner entered her house he hod no purse nor money upon him, but next morning he gave her two half-crowns.—The prisoner, who said he did not remember anything about the matter, was sentenced to 21 deys' hard labour. THE PARTIAL DISFRANCHISEMENT OF WIGIN.—The Mayor of Preston has reeeived a letter from Mr. Henry Park, Mayor of Wigan, referring to the proposed partial disfranchisement of Wigan. He says :—" You will pro- bebly hare noticed that the Redistribution Bill now before Perlin-rant proposes the partial disfranchisement of the very ancient borough of Wigan, incorporated in 1245. The case is a very bard one, as Wigan—though at the census of 1831 it was returned at leas than 49,000—has, as you are pro bably aware, populous out-townships immediately adjoin jog it, and forming one continuous town with a population of over 90,000. And yet it is by some means or other not in- cluded in the schedule of boroughs which are to have their boundaries enlarged. As chief magistrate of a con- stituency consisting almost entirely of working-class people, who have thrice done me the homer of electing me to be their mayor, I would most earnestly ask you to give us any assistance—much as influencing your M.P.'s in our favour —which may be in your power." MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL—The weekly meeting of the Provisional Committee was held in the Board Room. 70e, Market-street, Manchester, yesterday afternoon, Mr Henry Boddington, junior, presiding, in the absence of the chair- man, Mr Adamson. Amongst the contributions towards the Parliamentary expenses from various sources received since the last meeting, a communication was submitted from Messrs P and R Jackson and Co, of the Salford Rolling Mills, announcing that their workmen had stated their willingness to subscribe to the Parliamentary fund to , the extent of about £6O, to be paid in weekly instal- ments. The workmen of a number of other firms are also ' arranging similar contributions. It was reported that the Bill had been duly hedged in the House of Lords, and alsa that the petition for leave to introduce the Bill into the House of Commons had been sealed by the Corporations of Manchester, Salford, and Warrington, and signed by the gentlemen named in the Bill as promoters, and would be lodged in the Pri-ate Bill Office this day. The committee adjourned till after the Christmas holidays. CHILDREN'S PANTOMIME AT RUNCORN.—A number of children in connection with the Pariah Church Sunday school, on Thursday evening, gave a performance of the pantomime entitled " Sleeping Beauty" in the infants' schoolroom. The room was crowded with an appreciative audience. The scenic arrangements were admirable, the children, who had been carefully trained by Miss Bar- clay, acted their parts in a most creditable manner, and the pantomime was altogether a success. The following were the principal characters :—First King of the Golden Isles- Henry Clarke; second ditto, Charles Clarke; Prince Phara- mond, Edward Harrington.; Lord Fandango, Arthur Hough- ton ; The Dragon, William Dudley; Rick (the sprite), Thomas Williamson; Gentleman of the Court, John White- head; Messenger, John Hampson •, First Queen of the Golden Isles, Clara Hampson ; second ditto, Bessie Saun- ders • Princess Fair Star, Clara Withington ; Lady Chris- tabal, Elizabeth Coward; Lady in Waiting, Eva Sutton ; Fairies Moonbeam, Bertha Smith and Agnes Hitchrnough ; Sister Fairies, Annie Moss, Jennie Gleave, Fanny Buckley, and Alice Williamson ; Fairy Mildew (the malignant fairy) Miss E. Hampson ; Nurse, Sarah Brierley. The vocalists were Miss A. Howard, Miss E. Hampson, and Masters A. Houghton, C. Clarke, and A. Abel. Miss Barclay officia- ted as accompanist in the various songs and the Misses Crosby played the interludes in capital stile. The perform- ance was repeated last night. The proceeds will be added to the Sunday school funds. WIDNES LIBERAL ASBOCIATION.—A. special meeting of the Executive Committee of the Widnes Liberal Associa- tion was held in Lacey-street school-room on Wednesday evening under the presidency of Mr. H. Brunner. There were present Messrs E. Carey, J. Morrison, D. Wright, T. Handley, W. Whitby, J. Robinson, S. Robinson, T. Cosier, S. Owen, J. Taylor, Fogg, F. Lawrenson, J. W.Cerlile, T. Sadler, Booth. Warne, Hirst, Rae, Hughes, James Har- greaves, and H. B. Shores (secretary).—The Secretary re- ported that the result of the last revision at Widnes was as follows ;—Struck off old register, 3 Liberals, 21 Tories •, property claims allowed, 12 Liberals, 2 Tories; struck off .£l2 list, 22 Tories ; £l2 claims allowed, 10 Liberals and no Tories; making a net gain in Widnes of 60 votes on the last revision. (Applause.) This was the third time in four years that Widnes had occupied the highest place of the different districts of the county as regarded the number of voters placed on the register at the revision court, although it was by no means the largest in population. Last year St. Helens held the premier position, Widnes being second.—A. long discussion took place with reference to the Redistribu- tion Bill and the way in which Widnes would be affected by it. A strong resolution was passed unanimously that Widnes should be the centre of a division, and that the name of the town should be given to the division. The committee in- tended to have an interview with Mr. G. H. Croxden Powell at Widnes, larit night, for the purpose of defining the boundary of the division in which Widnea will be placed. Mr. Powell, however, adopted the views of the committee as expressed in the resolution, and will advoeate the adope ton of their suggeetions,

IPOACHING AT PARWWORTIL—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, William Lofthouse and Joseph Worth were summoned to answer a charge of having, on the 4th last, . been found in pursuit of ganee.—P.C. Almond proved seeing r the defendants pursue game on land at Farnworth belonging to Mrs. Newton, and finding three nets, which they left be. hind them, in order to get away.—Lo thouse pleaded guilty, and was fined 10a and coats, 12a, or 14 days' imprisonment. —Worth did not appear, and the gamekeeper, George Scott, applied for a warrant for his apprehension.—Superintendent Barker said the defendant was a very bad character, and the &Inch issued the warrant.

A VIOLENT WIDNES Womax.—On Wednesday at Widnes Police Court Ann Griffin. a strong-looking female, pleaded guilty to being grunk and. disorderly on the 15th inst. She I was also charged with assaulting P.C. Lamb, and to this ac- cusation she pleaded not guilty. About a quarter to three , on the Monday in question P.C. Lamb took the defendant into custody for being drunk and creating a disturbance in Nelson-street. She threatened to split his head, and kicked him very violently on the legs and various parts of the body. She was brought to the police station with difficulty by Constables Lamb and Evans.—The Superintendent In- formed the Bench that the defendant had previously served a term of 18 months' hard labour for unlawfully wounding her husband, and she was now sentenced to pay a total sum of 15s del, or go to gaol for 28 days. THEFT BY A BOY' AT WIDNES.—At WOrla Police Court on Monday, before Mr. F. H. Gossage and Mr. J. Brock, Edward Chipman, 14 years of age, living with his parents in Frederick-street, , was charged with stealing, a cardigan j ecket, the property of Mary Darken, of the Temperance Hotel, Victoria-road. It appeared that on Friday afternoon Ann Jane Muller, in the employ of the prosecutrix, was riding from Hale to Widnes with the jacket in her care. On the road the prisoner and another boy got upon the vehicle, and when they alighted at Ditton junction the 1 article, which is worth 18s 61, was missed. The same evening PC. Hargreaves found the jacket in the house of the prisoner's parents, and later P.C. Robinson apprehended the prisoner who admitted his gull!. He wai fined £1 or 14 days' im- prisonment. The money was paid. CRUELTY TO A PONY. AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sa- slow, on Wednesday, before Mr. F. IL Gossage and Mr. John Brock, William Hewitt, hawker, Travis-street, was charged with cruelly ill-treating a pony by workirg it whiist in an unfit state.—Mr. Thomas Cooksey, inspector of the S.P.O A., stated that on the 6th inst., he saw the defendant's pony in Widnes. An examination revealed that the animal was suffering from an old suppurating wound, front which matter was oczing on the near eide of the back, and another wound on the off side. Both wounds were in contact with the saddle. The forelegs of the animal were bent, and it was altogether in very poor condition and totally unfit for any kind of work.—Defendant said Mr. Robinson, veterinary surgeon, had seen the animal and given him a certificate. He had not, however, the certificate with hint —The Bench imposed a fine of Ws and coats, 12s, or 14 days' imprison- l ment. _ . . .

TRACKING TRAMPS AT RUNCORN —Before Captain Hazle- burst and Mr. G. L. Davies, at Runcorn Pence Court, on Saturday, James Matthews end Patrick Mather. men of dis- reputable appearance, were chireed with obtaining relief by . false pretences. On Friday night the prisoners applied to • Inspector Roche for a ticket for a night's lodeings. He give them an order far Dutton Workhouse. About an hour sub- sequently they returned to the police office, and stated their feet were sore, and they ceuld not walk to the Workhouse. In consequence of this statement the Inspector give them a ticket to go to Mrs. Higgin'e lodging-house. Next morning P.C. Wallace discovered that the prisoners had on the pre- vious night left Is 01 with a man named Michael Kennedy, , of Water-street, before they applied for relief; that they I were drunk at 11 o'clock; and that they paid 61 Ur their lodgings. He therefore app-ehended the prisoners in Irgh- street—Evidence bearing out this et itement was given, and the Bench sentenced each prisoner to 21 days hard labour. CARD PLATING AT WIDNES.— UNFORTUNATE CONSE- QUENCE.—Btfore Mr. Brock, at Widnes Police Court, on 'Thursday, Joseph Hazlousky, a Pole, was broueht up in custody charged with unlawfully wounding John Butinsky, also a Pole.—lnspector Wood informed his worship that on , Saturday night the two men with two ether Poles were at I the house 40, Barn-street, where they engaged in card play- ' leg. After the game had been proceeding for an hour, a I dispute arose between two of the men, who arose from their • seets and struck Butinsky. The prisoner seized a poker with which he struck Butinsky a 4 heavy blow on the head. ' Batinsky WAS in a very dangerous condition, and unable to appear before the court.—A witness stated that Butinsky I was acting as banker in the game when he was struck.—Dr. I A.B. McLennan deposed that on Tues?.ay uight he was called to Cromwell-street, and saw the prosecutor Butinsky in bed. He was suffering from an incised wound on the back of the head about two inches in length and penetrating to the bone. Be had seen the man that morning, and he would not be fit to leave the house for eight days—The prisoner, through an interpreter, said, he had not beat Butinsky, but that "it was the other fellow."—The pri- soner WAS remanded for eight days. BREACH Ow THE LICENSING Acr AT RUNCORN.—At Run- corn Petty Sessions on Monday, before Captain C. W. liezielinrst and Mr. James Handley, James Wade, landlord of the Mariners' Arms Inn, Percival's-lane, was summoned for sellieg intoxicating liquor to a drunken person Lamed James Johnson.—P.S. Walley stated that on Wednesday, the 10th inst, he was in search of a man upon whom he wished to serve a summons. Shortly after twelve o'clock he entered the Derby Arms and found Johnson there in a very drunken condition. He had not been served with any liqnor and he ordered him to leave. A few minutes later he (witness) went to the Mariners'Arms. Johnson was there with a pint of beer before him. Witness told the landlord he was surprised at him serving a man in such a condition with liquor. Johnson was in a beastly state of drunkenness, and bis clothes were saturated with water —Edward Cook, labourer. Penketh-lane, corroborated.—The defendant was sworn and stated that Johnson was leaning on the counter when he served him with the beer, and he did not perceive his condition —The Chairman said the Bench considered it a serious offence, and defendant was fined 40s and costs, 183 61.--Jamcs Johnson was then charged with being drunk on licensed premises.—He pleaded guilty and was fined lOs and costs. A Row AT THE ''ROCICERY," RUNCORN.—OH Monday, at Runcorn Police Court, Michael O'Hara, Heber Webb, and James Clayey, young men, were charged with being drunk and disorderly in Mersey-street on Saturday night. Clayey , was also charged with assaulting Inspector Roche at the ' same time and place. About 20 minutes pest ten on Satur- day, P.S. McMichael received information that there was a row in the "Rookery," and proceeded there accompanied Iby Constables Bennett and Fryer. The prisoners Webb and { O'Hara were there fighting in the centre of a crowd. The 1 sergeant seized O'Hara, but Webb ran away. Constable Bennett chased and captured him, and the combatants were being brought to the police station when Clavey seized the I sergeant by the leg and slid he should not take his prisoner. At this point Inspector Roche appeared on the scene and , took Clayey into custody for attempting te rescue the pri- soners. Clayey now became most violent, struggling in vain to release himself, and he kicked the inspector several times on the leg. He was with great difficulty taken to the police office, where a crowd of several hundred persons had assembled, and it appeared as though a riot was imminent. All the prisoners were drunk. On the first charge each pri- soner was fined 103 and costs, Os Bd, and for the assault was fined 208 and costs, 75. THE Rrneconer Commie LAerns.—At the beginning of the present month Mr. Brookes, secretary to the Runcorn I Improvement Commissioners, issued a printed circular to the freeholders of the town informing them that the Com- missioners had decided, if they could obtain the necessary sanction of the freeholders, to apply to the Inclosnre Com- missioners for a provisional order empowering them to en- close and regulate the common lands within the township. The circular farther stated that at present there was no body or authority vested with power to protect and regulate the lands ; that the area of the land proposed to be dealt with comprised 75 statute acres, and that if Vie provisional order be obtained the necessary cost of carrying it out would be paid out of the general district rate. But the Board before incurring any expense in preparing a memorial to the Inclosnre Commissioners, wished each freeholder to state on a fly-leaf whether he was willing or not to subscribe his name to the memorial when presented for signature. Ta the 163 circulars sent out there had been 6S replies received from the freeholders up to Friday evening. Of these tZ expressed their willingness to sign the memorial, and three only diseented from the proposed application. There is no doubt that the freeholders will be all but unanimous in sup- , porting the action of the Board in the matter.

div.head: RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS AND THE REDISTRI-
div.p: RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS AND THE REDISTRI-
BUTION BILL.

On Thursday evening a special meeting of the Runcorn Board of Improvement Commissioners was held at the Town Ball, Waterloo-road, with the object of considering the de- sirability of the Commissioners appearing before the Boundary Commissioners with a view to secure Runcorn as a centre of one of the Parliamentary Divisions of Cheshire. Mr. R. Shaw presided, and there were present Messrs. Meadowcroft. Norman, Timmins, Speakman, Dobson, Prit- chard, Williams, Fisher, Harris, Taylor, Briscoe, Lighthurn, W. H. Linaker (law clerk), W. Brookes (secretary), M. Barker (sunveyor)—The Chairman said he should have been neglecting his duty if he had not called the Board together with reference to the Redistribution of Seats Bill, because there was no doubt it wasa question which woralcrafLct the future of Runcorn to a considerable exteot. He thought Runcorn was entitled to be the centre of one of the divisions both by the extent of its population and its being one of the largest centres of trade in Cheshire. and it was important that the Commissioners should see that the town took its proper position. If they did not seize the opportunity they might find one of the smaller towns occupying the position which properly belonged to Runcorn. He suggested the appointment of a small com- mittee to deal with the question.—Mr. Speakman observed that there was nothing political in the matter, as both parties had agreed upon it, and they could all enter heartily into the whale thing. He did not like the idea of being be- hind Widnes. (Laughter.) He understood that Widnes was likely to be the centre of a division, and as these two towns had been closely allied for many years he should not like them to be separated—The Chairman explained that the Boundary Commissioners would receive the sugges- tions of political parties and municipal bodies. The Im- provement Commissioners had nothing to u-ge from a political point of view. The committee would simply have to urge that they were one of the largest towns in popula- tion, one of the most important in point of trade, and that in considering the town to be made the centre of the division the claims of Runcorn ought not to be overlooked.—Mr. Meadowcratt wisbed to know what ad.

, vantages Runcorn was likely to derive from being made the centre of a division. He thought past experience had not been such as to make them very anxious to establish them- selves as a centre where politicill feeling was likely to run very high at election times. If It was considered to be an advantage that they should take the foremost position in a division, by all means let them secure it, and as far as he was individually concerned he should be glad to co-operate as far as he possibly could.—Mr. Norman remarked that un- less they took steps to secure their position Northwich, which was a much smaller town, might step in and be the chief place.—The Chairman, replying to Mr. Meadowcroft, said if the committee were asked to interfere and say where the boundary should be drawn that might cause what Mr. Miiadowcroft feared, but considering that they were not go- ing to touch the boundaries at all, be thought they need have no fear. All they asked was that Runcorn should oc- cupy its proper position, and that its claim should be pro- perly represented to the Boundary Commissioners.—Mr. Lightburn supported the Chairman's suggestion, and moved that a committee consisting of Messrs Shaw, Fisher, Speak- man, Lake, and Norman be appointed to deal with the goes- ' tion. At the request of the meeting, Mr.. Lightburn also included himself a member of the committee—The motion 1 was seconded by Mr. Pritchard and carried unanimously.

Deacon moved the adoption of the report of the District Education Committee, which stated that there had been daring the month of November 104 applications for the payment of fees, and 287 persons appeared before the committee for contravention of the Education Act. Fees were ricommended to be paid in 97 cases. There were 80 prosecutions before the magis- trates, and 78 convictions were obtained. An attendance order was granted in one case, and ons boy was sent to an industrial school.—The report was adopted.

The busines3 concluded by the Chairman wishing the 'members a Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year. Re hoped that they would all meet again in good health and spirits.

WIDNES AND THE REDISTRIBUTION BILL. In a letter addres3ed to the Liverpool Mercury, Mr. G. H. Dresden Powell thus refers to Widnes in reference to the Seats Bill :--" Widnes has the misfortune-important as ills in many ways-to be considerably under the scale to entitle it to one member. Its situation is somewhat dif- ficult. Runcorn looks down upon it across the Mersey, while St. Helens will have no connection with it, having sufficient population to make a borough within its munici- pal boundaries; so that Widnes will form the basis of a district for parliamentary purposes, which will include a rural, a residential, and a .manufacturing population of great importance. An important point will be whether it shall include Wavertree, which ought to go into the borough of Liverpool, as it is sandwiched geographically between West Derby and Toxteth Park. Probably a little demur may be made in some quarters when Haytonians and Gars- tonians find themselves: in the parliamentary district of Widnes ; but such persons must remember that men seldom die there, that its death-rate is lower than elsewhere, and that that they will not have to vote in Widnes, but in their own localities. PENKETH WESLEYAN DAY SCHOOL.—The usual festivities in connection with the above sohool were held on Thursday afternoon, when the school broke up for the Christmas holi- days. There were recitations from "The Merchant of Venice," &c., and singing. All was gone through in a very efficient manner. Drawing prizes were given which were earned by the scholars, and prizes 4 f attendance, &c., offered by Mr. Garnett-, who, in presenting the prizes, gave a prac- tical address on the importance of cultivating drawing. Great praise ie due to Mr. Watson, the head master, for the training the children bad gone through. There was a good attendance of parents and friends. Oranges, &a., were also distributed to the children. Banner Counsirea.—Upwards of 200 persona assembled at the Star Inn Recreation grounds, St. Helens, on Monday, to witness George Shaw's " Hannah " and Joseph Welsby's "Rose," both of Warrington, contest a match at rabbits, 21 courses, for £l5 aside, at catch weight. Both dogs were in excellent condition, " Hannah " having been prepared for its engagement by J. Ashurst, of Wigan. while .1. Porter, of Warricgton, acted as mentor for "Rose." The latter commenced well, winning six causes out of the first eight, when it met with an accident, and" Hanzah," only allowing "Rose "to win another course, ultimately won the match by killing eleven to its opponent seven. Mr. S. Hamons acted as referee and stakeholder. PROPOSED PRESENTATION TO ME, J. C. div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON, THURSDAY.

Very little news comes from the Relief Expedition, still Slowly making its way up the Nile. What there is, is satis- factory. Lord Wolseley and the Advance Guard are already at Korti, the starting point for the dash across the Desert, which has not yet been officially announced, but which is an inevitable portion of the scheme. Lord Wolseley re- ports the men as healthy, strong, and in the highest spirits. They certainly must be in admirable training, rowing every day against the strong current of the Nile. Gordon himself is not inactive. For a beleagured man, on whose behalf between ten and fifteen millions sterling are being spent, he Is singularly active and dominant. His last feat has been to blow up the principal fort of the Mandi's forces. This I was done by mining, and the successful issue is likely to do more for Gordon's prestige than the winning of a pitched battle. If the Soudanese, seated within their own fortifica- tions, at a moderate distance from th terrible besieged, are- suddenly—without a moment's notice—to be inscrutably blown up into the air, the sooner they leave this indom- itable magician alone, the better for their own comfort. One reason for the meagre accounts which reach this country from the front is to be found in the strict censorship which Lord Wolseley holds over the representatives of the Press. This is done with the object of preventing information reaching the enemy, an important precaution, if it be true, as reported, that the Mandi, through a French agent in his camp, is in constant communication with Cairo, and keeps his employer fully informed of all the movements of the British forces.

Nothing is yet settled Wits respect to the British pro- posals dealing with financial affairs in Egypt. There is a general impression, sustained by telegrams from Berlin and Paris, that the renewed effort to grapple with this trouble has failed. But it would be well to await confirmation. The Stock Exchange is ever kept in mind in all that concerns Egypt, and reports are distributed with special view to 'to- day's prices." One thing is certain, there has been no feces. sity, in Mr. Gladstone's view, to call together a Cabinet Council. Earl Granville has been in town one day of the week, and has conduced business at the Foreign Office. But this is the only sign of Ministerial activity in this depart- ment of the State.

It was inevitable that when the new Parliament met the question of a new House for the Commons should c ma permanently to the trout. It did in 1880 under less strong aggravation. That was the year in which Mr. Mitchell Henry addressed the Speaker from one of the side galleries, creating as much sensation as if he had attempted to walk on a tight-rope from one side to the other. In that Session, also, was made the discovery of the duplicity of certain members who kept two hats, one of which came to be known as " the warking hat," and the other kept for the special purpose of being placed upon a seat and so retaining possession. But the time of discussion has been forestalled by a correspondence in the Daily News, and the cry of more room has already commenced. This is very natural. But the new House for the Commons is not planned yet, and it will probably be some years before it is. The inconvenience, as Mr. Glad- stone pointed out in 1880, is, though recurrent, temporary. At the beginning of every new Parliament, curiosity and the virgin interest of new members brings them down to the House in numbers that begin to fall away even after the first two months of a Session For the remainder of the existence of a Parliament there is practically no inconveni- ence in respect of the smallness of the Chamber, whilst the experiment of equalling the acoustical properties and general conveniences of the present Chamber is exceedingly delicate and dangerous. Of course, there will be more pres- sure in the new Parliament, not so much because the number of members is to be increased—a dozen here or there is nothing—but because there will probably be a large propor- tion of members who, not having the social opportunities and attractions of some of their colleagues, will make more extended use of what is not unjustly called the best club in London.

Daring the present dull season various ingenious effarts have been made to start subjects for correspondence in the London newspapers. These have touched the questions of Housemaids, the Ladies' Gallery in the House of Com- mons, the Nuisance of Railway Whistles, and the Oppres- sion of Authors. For this last the Pall Mall Gazdte has found room. One has a more or less remote acquaintance with the men and women who write books. But I never saw in a familiar profession such a remarkable array of no- familiar names as those appended to letters, of complaint 11 about occult influences being at work to prevent the public satisfying its unbounded desire to possess the works of the writers. The complaint made by the originator of the cor- respondence was against publishers, who, be alleged, not only pay very little for manuscript, but indefinitely delay the meagre p tyment promised. Of course, there are some impecunious bangers on the publishing world who print all kinds of rubbish, and can scarcely be complained of if they find it hard to scrape together the money to pay for it. But the charge is ridiculous as applied to the firms usually in the mind when London publishers are alluded to. A. cable message from America announces the pleasing intelligence that Sitting Bull and his companions created some sensation in Philadelphia last Sunday by attending, clad in their Indian costumes, the services of St. John's Rornan Catholic Church. From this it will appear that this wily Indian is again cequetting with the Church. I met at St. Louis last autumn the priest who had been detailed to bring about the convaraion of Sitting Bull, and bad devoted many months and much money to the enterprise. The In- dian regarded as a necessary preliminary to conversion that he should be'carefully tended in the matter of personal comfort. He was regarded as a great prize, and nothing in the way of meat and drink, pipes, and an occasional dram were soared in order to secure him. At length the time came when it was reasonable to suppose that preliminaries might be dispensed with, and Sitting Bull received into the bosom of the Church. Great preparations were made for the event, in which a bishop was to take a leading port. But at the last moment there occurred to Sitting Bull an insu- perable difficnity. He had at least two wives, one more than permitted by the Church. If he had put away one all would haye been well. But so tender were his feelings and so scrupulous his regard for his wives that he posi- tively could not decide which las was to abandon. The end of it was that negotiations were broken off, the bishop and the cathedral service was set aside, and Sitting Bull, greatly cheered and strengthened by the preliminaries," went back to his wives and his wigwam. Now he seems to be again troubled in his soul with far reaching thoughts. I fancy the excitement and sensation created here by the explosion on London Bridge has been a little exaggerated in the newspapers. The fact ie Lendoners are gettine used to these cowardly outrage's, and have learned to dread them less since they generally turn met to be harmless as far as human life is concerned. Not the least rernarkeble thing about _them is the almost absolate immunity from personal risk which accompanies them and the comparatively small damage effected to property. It is said that another "link with the past" is to be snapped. Years ago the penny postmen were conspicuous for their red coats, and on the Queen's birthday were bright indeed. Then came a reform, and the were modest dark blue has since been adopted. But though the letter carriers had sombre uniforms, the guards of Her Majesty's mails remained resplendent in red cloth and gold braid. The dignity of the Post Office was shorn, but it still survived. It will not survive long. The existing red coats will still be worn. They shall be worn until they are worn out. Bat when the time for renewal comes the link with the past will have been snapped and red or scarlet will be confined to the army, so long—that is—as it shall be the good pleasure of ; Lord Wolseley to permit it.

FATHER Tnoste i s.—lt s with regret that we announce the death of the Rev. Father Paulinna Thomas, of Warrington, which took place early on Monday morning. Father Thomas was a member of the Order of St. Benedict and was assistant priest at St. Mary's Catholic Church, Buttermarket-street. He had not been long resi- dent in Warrington, having come to the town about eighteen months age, but daring that short period he won golden opinions among those with whom he was brought into con- tact. He was particularly regarded by the poorer members of his flock, amongst whom be was an assiduous and sympa- thetic visitor, and indeed it is probable that be caught the disease—the measles—from which he died, through his un- selfish ministrations in the lower quarters of the town. His illness was brief and his death at ten minutes past throe o'clock on Monday morning was unexpected. He was °rig 36 years of age. The remains were interred in the Cemetery on Wednesday in the presence of a large concourse of spectators. Previous to the cremony, service was held in St. May's Church, Buttermarket-street, the officiating clergy being the Catholic Bishop of Liverpool, the Very Rev. P. .t.nder- SON and the Very Rev. W. Bede Prest. The heame was followed by the members of the Warrington League of the Cross. Al. the graveside the services were conducted by the Very Rev. W. B. Prest, of Woolton, and the responses were made by about thirty of the Catholic clergy of the district, amongst whom were the Right Rev, Bishop of Liverpool (Dr. O'Reilly), Rev. C. V. div.head: 110 W TO DISCOURAGE A CHOIR.
div.p: 110 W TO DISCOURAGE A CHOIR.

BY OLD Iluxerranx. There are times when the best way to explain how a thing should be done, is to show how not to do it." So much has been written and said regarding the proper treatment of choirs that possibly a brief put- ting "on the negative side" may help to better the condition of affairs in some churches about. If it be 1 desirable to disintegrate and either totally destroy or render useless the choir organisation' a constant observance of the following rules will hardly fail to accomplish the purpose. I speak mainly of Volun- tary Choirs. Ist. Let the leading people of the church and con- gregation hold themselves aloft from the choir, show- ing thereby that they consider themselves too refined to engage in such a menial service. 2nd. Habituatly allude to the choir as if it were a sort of necessary evil which must be endured but not enjoyed. Harp away on the old but false assertion that singers are more quarrelsome than other people. Tell them often that they are too sensitive. Scarifica.- tion and frequent blistering may cure it. 3rd. Never study how their happiness personally or collectively may be promoted. Da not invite them to social gatherings or elsewhere—unless you want to use them. Make them feel that they are looked upon as belonging to the " oommou herd "—whatever they may be; make them feel that they must not intrude into other society, lest they might feel. "stuck up." 4th. Criticise them freely, and pass by no opportu- nity for finding fault. To show a grateful apprecia- tion of the effort to do well might give them too exalted ideas of the importance of their work, and they are " so sensitive" that "praise is not safe." sth. Do not furnish adequate supplies. If they want new books let them pay for them as they alone are to use them. It is effective in such a ease to tell them that the old anthems are much better than the new, and don't forget to taunt them with " everlast- ingly singing the same old things." A careful observance of the above rules would, I venture to predict, bring a choir to the point of dis- solution.

div.head: FARNWORTH GRAMMAR SCHOOL.
div.p: FARNWORTH GRAMMAR SCHOOL.
DISTRIBUTION OF PRIZES.

The first annual aistribution of prizes in connection with the Farnwerth Grammar School, since the old foundation was resuscitated, took place on Tuesday evening in the Lecture Hall. The room was crowded. Major Cross, Chairman of the Board of Governors, presided; and he was accompanied on the platform by Mr and Mrs F U Gossage, the Rev G Bond, Messrs J Brock, J P, T S Timmis, R 11 Davies, E Carey, W A Watts, M A (head master), and S S Adkins, B A (assistant master). Amongst the audience were the Revs S A Spooner and J Holden, Mr and Mrs H Brun- ner, Mr and Mrs R Lewis, Mrs Kershaw. Mrs Pankhurst, Mrs Carey, Mrs Dr Booth, Mr and Mrs Barlow' Miss Downie; Messrs R Kidd, J W Waring, A Kyle, H. W. Deacon, J Morrison, A MacLennan, J Hough, —ln opening the proceedings, the Csairman said they did not wish to make too great a demonstration at this their first prize meeting, but they would be encouraged by that excel- lent meeting to try and make room for a good many more next year. He hoped that full meeting was a good augury of the success of the school, and that all present would do what they could to increase the number of the scholars, not that he complained of the number of scholars at the present time, for considering the short time that the school had been open he thought they had done very well indeed. Still there was room for about as many more as were attending at present. He drew attention to the fact that the school was founded on an entirely unsectarian basis, and said he thought if Widnes would make a long pall and a strong pull, and a pull altogether, they would make the school one of the first grammar schools in the country. (Applause.) Alluding to the examination for the two free scholarshipe offered by the governors, he announced that the two successful scholars were Bate and Sherratt--(applause)—of the Widnes Board Schools. Bate had 781 marks and Sherratt 732 marks out of a possible 1,000; and they were closely followed by Hart from one of the National schools, who received 674 marks. (Applause) Two other scholars, Stringer and Mainwariag, received 671 and 649 marks respectively. (Applause.) The very fact of these scholars receiving something like three-quarters of the marks they could possibly obtain showed that the standard of education at Widnes was rising very fast, and they must keep the standard of the Grammar school up so that they could show an advance on the other schools in the district. He concluded by expressing a hope that the next year would be a very successful one.—Mr. Watts explained the principles upon which the prizes were awarded and read the Hat, as follows :—Latin—Upper form : 1, Smith ; 2, Knowles. Lower form : 1, Mercer; 2, Franklin. Mathe- matics—Upper form: 1, Knowles; 2. Smith. Lower form: 1, Bate; 2. Mercer. English—Upper form : 1, Knowles ; 2, Kyle. Lower form : 1, Mercer, 2, Franklin. French— Upper form: 1, Knowles; 2, Kyle. Lower form: 1, Mer- cer; 2, Barlow. Science—Upper form: 1, Knowles; 2, Linnell. Lower form : 1, Mercer; 2, Franklin. Music: 1, Mercer ; 2, Kyle. Mr. Watts addressed a few encouraging remarks to the unsuccessful scholars.— Mr. F. H. Gossage then distributed the prizes. In a brief speech Mr. T. S. Timmis referred to the deep interest he took in education, and said he believed that Grammar School met the great-felt want of a secondary school, and under the careful guidance of their very able head master, Mr. Watts, would take high rank in the grammar schools of the coun- try. Speaking of the free scholarships, he said that al- I though the schema adopted by the Charity Commissioners did not pros ide for the education of the poor, the governors in offering scholarships to the elementary schools were I carrying out the intention of the founders of the school, and were restoring to the poor what was their due. He expressed hie gratification that the scholarships had been secured by two boys educated in the Board schools. One of the boys had evidenced great ability, and he hoped he had a great future before him. He concluded by moving a vote of thanks to Mrs. Gossage in a few complimentary phrases.— Mr. J. Brock seconded the motion, expressing the hope that they would see Mrs. Gossage amongst them on many future occasions. (Applause.)—The motion was carried by ac- clamation.—Mr. Gossage replied on behalf of his wife.—On the motion of Mr. R. Kidd, seconded by Mr. H. W. Deacon, a vote of thanks was accerded to the chairman.—During the proceedings the music class sang several roundelays under the leadership of Mr. Watts. At the conclusion of the business a number of the scholars gave a dramatic per- formance, entitled "Little Toddlekins."

The Court of Appeal granted Mr. Bradlaugh a rule nisi for a new trial, on Thursday, on the ground of misdirec- tion. WMle-walking near a pan of boiling brine at Messrs. Verdin's Cheshire Salt Works a man named Hunt fell in and was so horridly scalded that he now lies without hope of recovery. A man and a woman stand remanded in Birmingham, charged with coining. A complete set of coining apparatus was seized. AmrsiNG EtoPESIENT FROM GOLBORNE.—The quiet dis- trict of Gotheme has this week been thrown into a state of excitement by the particulars of an elopement having come to light. The forsaken husband is a young man named Goulding, who has lived in Golborne about three years, and is employed at Messrs Smithson lirothers' mill. Some 18 months ago he married a damsel about eight years his junior, and for a time all things went well. Recently, a young bricklayer who has been brought up in the neigh- bourhood, but who of late has been living in lodgings close by, commenced paying visits:to Goulding's. Mrs. Gould- ing was ultimately warned not to encourage the man she bad begun to regard with such favour, and in reply she assured her husband that the visitor was none other than a well-meaning and well-behaved young man. Events tend- ing to confirm suspicion, the husband repeated his protests, but as he was a dwarf in comparison to the bricklayer, he deemed it prudent to confine his remonstrances to his wife, and as a consequence the visits continued. Recently the young man removed to St. Helens, and then the husband began to hope for better times. But he was doomed to disappointment. The wife took sud- denly ill, and like a dutiful husband a doctor was quickly called in. The bricklayer, too, put in an appearance, and began to pay unremitting attention to the sick one. Under the care of her "nurse" the faithless wife seemed to re- cover, but it is said that when the visitor was again:absent her indisposition returned. Matters however, cane to a climax last Sunday night when the visitor again made his appearance. Goulding mustered tip courage to ask his rival if he was going home that night, and the reply came, No ! Seeing that his wife was unwilling to retire to rest, the husband decided to remain down stairs the whole of the night. He awoke about 5-30 on Monday morning, and still found his friend in possession but he was informed that the latter intended leaving Lout half-past six. At six o'clock Goulding, as was his wont, went to his work and re- turned at breakfast time to find that both his wife and the bricklayer had made their departure, and left behind a four year old child, which belongs to the woman. The forsaken husband dressed the child and took it to his wife's mother, where be vows it must remain. On searching the house he discovered that the woman had wisely taken nothing that did not belong to her, a circumstance that has prevented him from setting the police on her track. He states, how- t ever, that she has left Lim in debt. Since Monday morn- I ing nothing that may be added has been heard of the run- aways. No shopkeeper should be without W. P. Hartley's Jams and Marmalade which may be had wholesale from E. H. , Monks, 78, Seholes, Wigan.—Advt.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY. DECEMBER 20, 1884.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. DECEMBER 20, 1884.
TEMPERANCE-JUBILEE- --

On Monday, the fiftieth anniversary of the temperance cause in Warrington was celebrated by a meeting in the Workmen's Club. The chair was occupied in the early part of the meeting by the Rev. W. Mules, and later on by Mr. E. Miss. There were also present Messrs. Thomas Hall, James Gandy, sen., William Mee, Ben., John Green, D. Plinston, G. Ditchfield (High Leigh), William Roberts, and Mr. Sykes (of the British Temperance League). The Rev. W. Mutes, in a few introductory remarks, said they were met together that night to celebrate what was termed the jubilee of the temperance cause in Warrington. The history of the past fifty years bad been a very surprising one, not only in cennection with the 01550 of temperance, but also in cennection • with every other cause that has had for its object the moral uplifting of mankind. (Hear, hear.) It bas seemed to be a period in which social advancement could not be stopped. Arid one of the most remarkable features about that period to his mind had been the rapid development of enthusiasm amongst the masses, the work- ing-men, of our land in the cause of social improvement. For a long time they waited apparently for those who were called their superiors to bring them better things, and they seemed to be content with that position which the upper classes chose to give them. They scarcely dared to assert their own independence, and as far as putting in a claim to be heard on their own behalf was concerned, it seemed to be an idea which never once entered into their heads, and the consequence was that for ages they werelittle totter than slaves of the privileged classes of this land. (Hear, hear.) Bat, thank God, they had to rejoice to-day over the fact that the people of England—lhe workingmen, for they were its backbone—were beginning to think for themselves. (Ap- phuse.) lhey have began to inquire into and to demand the removal of those hindrances to social advancement which they suffered in the past and that which they had waited in vain for others to give Lem they are now claim- ing for themselves, and they say "if you won't give us these things which we rightly ask then we will take them for ourselves." (Applause.) In regard to no phase of this question of social advancement, bad this rapid change been more strikingly developed than in the temperance cause. Fifty years ago the temperance movement was looked upon as a most absurd enterprise, and its objects were regarded as utterly impracticable It was thought to be a hobby only fit for fanatics and certain weak-Minded men to ride. Those who lived in the present day were born with silver spoons in their months iu regard to that great temperance cause, and did not know what it was to endure hardship in that nobli cause each as their forefathers had to endue. Thee its pioneers were subjected to the must unkind treatment and criticism, . . .

and were I:egarded as little batter than idiots and fools. All honour was due to that noble band—some of whom they were privileged to have on that platform that evening—who fifty years ago unfurled the temperance standard that they and their children might share in the reward of their glorious toil. (Applause.) Mr. WILLIAM ROBERTS, in explaining the object of that meet- ing, said those who were in office in connection with the Warrington Temperance Union felt it was their duty to do all that they could to celebrate that occasion in a fitting and suitable manner. He thought they would agree with him that that was a memorable event in tke history of that town, and one which they would ell do well to look back upon with pleasure and gratification. That night fifty years ago—December 15th, 1634—the first public total ab- stinence meeting was held in Warrington, and it was held in the Friars'-green Chapel, and he was glad to tell thorn that there were one or two on the platform that night who were present at that first meeting. kApplause.) Ou looking over the names of a number of those who first signed the temperance pledge in Warrington he found that there were eaveral of them still living. He found that John Monks was the first secretary, and he was still living; then there was John Cassidy, well-known to most of them, and still alive., although more than 90 years of age ; John Broad- hurst and William Mee, John Green, and James Gandy, who were with them that night ; and also William Dutton. He wO3 sure they all felt that it was only rieht and fit that their Meads who had so nobly worked in the past should be recognised and honoured for the work they had done. (Applause.)—Mr. WILLIAM MEE then gave a short account of his early experiences as a total abstainer, and mentioned that for more than forty years he had been assistant secre- tary to the Warrington Temperance Union, and he had also for 46 years been secretary for the Rechabite Society. (Ap- plause.)—Mr. JAMES GANny also gave an interesting ac- count of temperance work in Warrington, as did likewise Mr. T. HALL —Mr. DITCHFIELD having referred to the part he took in instituting temperance socitties in variona places in Cheshire and South Lancashire, Mr. SYKES gave a vigor- one address, which was evidently much appreciated by the audience—The meeting was brought to a close by the sing- ing of the Doxology. Meetings were also held on Tuesday evening, in the Pri- mitive Methodist School-room, Legh-street, and on Wed- nesday evening in Buckley-street School-room, at both of which Mr. Sykes delivered eloquent and effective addresses on temperance. The former meeting was presided ever by Mr. James Dodds, Penketh, and the latter by Mr. N. B. Percival. Entertainments were given by the members of the Band of Hope of each school. The audiences were large.

ECCLES.—PIayed at Runcorn on Saturday, when an interesting and fast game terminated in the home team's favour by one goal, one try, one dead ball, to Eccles nil. Joule kicked off, to which Parker replied, sending the ball into the home half. Following some loose forward play, Speakman ran well, but failed.to pass Bury, who col- lared safely. Andrews subsequenkly gave the latter more work, but giving the ball to Speakman the latter got on a bit further. A forward rush assisted flatland to get within . . . .

an ace of scoring, but Park r transferred the play towards the home half, Hughes sending the bull back into touch. From th 3 line out Hoff:lend ran strongly over the line, Lewis making a good attempt at goal, the ball striking the posts. After the drop into play Johnson returned to centre, and Wright, followed by Andrews, made good progress, but the safe tackling of the visitors' backs stopped their efforts. A dead ball was soon afterwards scored from a drop kick by Speakman. After changing ends Evans kicked off, and no return being effected, play followed in the home quarter, where the Eccles team made strong attempts to score. Fol- lowing some packed scrimmaging, Hugh Hughes ran into the centre, punting towards the Eccles half. The ball was returned. by Holt, the forwards also making headway. Johnson, coming to the rescue, made a splendid dribble through the pack, for which piece of play he gained a merited acknowledgment from the spectators, and Holt saved by kicking in touch. H. Hughes showed up in a run, gain- ing considerable ground. Worthington was next to get away with the ball, and succeeded in getting to W. Hughes, who brought him to grass, Eccles being again close to the home line. Johnson frnstrated an attempt by Bury. Cox however, got the ball out of his 25, and the danger wa again tided over, and centre field being gained, H. Hughe tried again to increase the score, but was well tackled. ' Packed scrimmages were not unfrequrntly seen now, and front one Andrews made another of his dodgy runs over the line close to the posts, Lewis having no difficulty in placing a goal to the score. Nothing further was scored up to call ' of time. Hoffland, Cox, Wright, and Joule headed a good lot of forwards ; Johnson, H. Hughes. and Andrews played hard behind the scrimmage. SPEECH DAY" AT WARRINGTON GRAMMAR SCHOOL. Tuesday being what is knoverCas "Speech Day" in con- nectioo with the Warrington Grammar School, the annual distribution of prizes to the successful scholars took place ia the afternoon. The priz3s were given to the successful scholars by Dr. Greenwood (vice-chancellor of Victoria University and principal of Owen's College, Manchester), in the presence of a large and select audience, amongst wham were the Mayor and Mayoress. The HEAD MASTER (the Rev. E. J. Willcocks) after hav- ing given those present a suitable welcome, said that on an occasion like that they would, of course, be desirous to hear what account they had to give of themselves for the past year, and what was the position of the school at that moment, lie thought he could give them a satisfactory report on both points. The school was examined in July last under the Oxford and Cambridge Schools Examination Boyd, and they received a somewhat lengthy report ex.; pressing general satisfaction with the work and progress of the school ; and when it was laid before the Governors at their last meeting it received their entire approbation. (Ap- plause.) In conjunction with the examination of the whole school, the six form, numbering seven bey, was examined for the " Higher" or "Leaving "certificate, granted by the Oxford and Cambridge Schools Examination Board, and five of their boys were successful. (Applause.) The examiaa- tion for these certificates was of a very high character, and was taken by most of the best public schools in England. Since a list is published giving the names of the successful candidates collectively from the schools, they are able to gauge approximately the position of this school with other institutions of a similar nature to themselves. He had taken some trouble in anelysiug this lift, and he found that 63 schools gained certificates, and that the Warrington Grammar School stood twenty-eighth in regard to the nnm- ber of successful candidates. (Applause.) Of course Eton headed the list, and then followed several of their great public schools, such as Harrow, Rugby, Marlborough, Bsc., but when they descended nearer to themselves theyfound that Malvern College and Uppingham School gained eight; Bath Cellege and Christ's Hospital, seven ; Bromsgrove School, Cheltenham College, Denston, Reading, and Tonkridga Schools, six ; Brighton College, Elizabeth College, Guern- sey, °Ahem' Redley, and Warrington Grammar School, five. As in the previous year, they last Christmas sent in 13 boys for the Cambridge Local Examinations, eleven of these passed, and five of them with distinction in various subjects. Out of the 114 candidates who were examined and obtained certificates at the Manchester centre, they were fortunate enough to secure the first place both among the seniors and juniors. (Applause.) These results had not been obtained without hard work beth on the part of the masters and the boys ' • and he took that opportunity of thanking his able coadjutor—the Rev. IL G. Smith—and the other assistant masters for the energy, zeal, and hearty co-operation which they had at all times displayed in order to ensure the success of that school. (Applause.) The strain that they had felt in preparing for two public examinations in the year, had compelled him to make some alteration in their future arrangements; and he had plea- sure in informing them that that school had been constitu- ted a special local centre under the Oxford Local Examina- tion Board. The advantages they should derive from this change are manifold. They should now combine the school examination with that for the local certificate, and should not be compelled, as before, to send their boys out of the town to be examined: (Applause.) These certificates ex- cuse under certain conditions the preliminary examinations for law and medicine, and also the examinations known as Responsions" at Oxford. He had pleasure in announ- cing to them that he had secured the chemical laboratory which belonged to the late Warrington School of Science. They had given instruction in the school in theoretical chem- istry for the last few years, but now he hoped after Christ- mas to be able to extend their teaching, and give to these • boys who may desire it a thorough course in laboratory ' practice. They had also this year extended the school • buildings, and have erected a commodious class-room' cap- able of containing thirty boys, at the cost of nearly £4OO. (Applause.) Mr. IVitcoons, having thanked Mr. John ' Hesketh ad Mr. J. C. Thompsea for having painted the scenery which was to be used In the play that after- noon, then read the names of the priz3 and certificate takers. The prize list was as follows :—Midsummer term. Classics, sixth form, Hannah, ma; fifth from, Stone; upper fourth form, Scotson ; lower fourth form, Webster ; third form, Rose, mi ; second form' Gorse ; first form, Owen ma. —Mathematics. Sixth set. Curjel; fifth set, Schonberg ; upper fourth set, Thorpe; third and second sets, Wrightson; first set, Mackey, mi.—English history, Tudor period. Fifth form, Haynes, ma; upper and lower fourth forms, Webster; third and second forms, Gorse; upper and lower first forms, Wagstaff.—Science, fifth set, chemistry (Rev. S. Wilkin- son's prize), Schonberg; fourth set, physical geography, Stone.—Scripture knowledge, Lamplagh Memorial, St. Matthew with the Greek, Hannah, ma; fifth form, St. Mate thew with the Greek, Stone; fourth form, Genesis and Exodus (Rev. E. C. E. Carleton's prize), Scotson • Massing. ham Memorial, St. Matthew, Isherwood.—Modern lan- guages, Dr. Gornall's prizes. Sixth set, German, Curjel ; fifth set, German, Thompson, mi • sixth set, French, Hannah, ma; fifth set, French, Jackson, ma ; fourth set, French, Stone; third set, French, Williams.—Michaelmas term. Form prizes. Sixth form, Hannah, ml; fifth form, Stone ; upper fourth form, Webster ; lower fourth form, Wheeler, mi; third form, Thorpe; second form, Haynes, mi; upper first form, Jackson, mi.—Dictation. Fifth and fourth forms, Soottion third, atoond, All IDOL forms, liOrSe.— Writing. Fifth and fourth forms, Wheeler, ma; third, I second, and first forms, Thorpe.—Drawing. Shading, Healey; model, Morley, ml; advanced freehand, William- son, ma; elementary freehand, Haynes, mi.—Latin prose prize, Hannah, nia.—English essay. The struggle between the Crown and Parliament during the Tudor and Stuart periods, Wheeler, ma.—Fitchett Marsh prize, Greek history , 510-404 8.C., Hannah, ma., Ashton Memorial, Kidd.— Oxford and Cambridge Schools examinations for certificates. a, b, c, e, f, Tuckey; a, b, c, e, f, g, Hannah, ma.; a, b, c, d, f, g, Curjel ; b, c, e, f, Kidd; a, b, c. e, f, Brundrett. A Latin; b, Greek; c, French; d, German; e, divinity; f, dee mentary mathematics; g, advanced mathematics.—Cam- bridge Local Examinations, 1883. Senior candidates, class 2, Hannah ma., distinguished in religious knowledge and Latin, prize and certificate; Tuckev, certificate. Junior candidates, class 1; Curie!, distinguished in Latin, Greek, German, and mathematics, prize and certificate; Kidd, dis- tinguished in Greek, prize and certificate. Class 2, Brandrett, distinguished in Latin, prize and certificate; Down, distinguished in Latin, prize and certificate. Certi- ficates, Gandy ma., Healey, Jackson, ma., Wheeler, ma-. Williams. The HEAD MASTER also announced that he had received a telegram from Lord Winmarleigh expressing his lordship's regret at not being able to be present. He also announced that Lucius Carey, son of the late head master of the War- ringten Grammar School, had won a scholarship at Oriel College, Oxford, and that Edward Shonberg, son of the Rev. M. Shonberg, of Warrington, had been successful in obtain- ing an exhibition at Exeter College, Cambridge. (Ap- plause.) A latin essay, written by Hannah, ma, was then read by Its writer, and an English essay by Wheeler, ma (who was 'absent through illness), was read by Cutlet. Dr. GREENWOOD next addressed the assembly. He con- gratulated the governors, the head master, assistant masters, and the boys of the school on the very excellent results of their labours, which the proceedings of that day testified to. (Applause.) In looking over the constitution of the school, he was at once struck with this circumstance, that the go- vernor 3 and authorities when called upon, as most schools had been within the last 15 or 20 years, to submit their system of operations to the inspection and visitation of the Charity Commissioners, were able to steer a middle course between Scylla and Charybdis. (Applause.) While recognizing the demand on authorities of a school ins large town to make provision for the newly-developed wants of the modern community, they did not rush into the other extreme of doing away with those links which bound the school to the traditions of former generations. It would have been easy on the one hand to have insisted on the maintenance of the school on the old lines of purely classical and mathe- matical teaching, and still easier to have made a clean sweep of the older learning, and to throw the school into a purely modern system of modern languages and physical science. But it was very gratifying to know that the authorities of the school had avoided both of these extremes. While they had retained all those links which bound the school to the traditions of former times, be thought they had made ample .provision for the newly-developed wants of modern civiliza- tion, and the prizes which had been given that day showed that there hadebeen no incompatibility in binding the two teachings together; because not only did the school show well in the older and newer lines of teaching, but some of the boys had taken hononrs in the tem branches of learning, and this showed it was not difficult to combine the two branches in the same school. (Applause.) The Head Master had told them that after Christmas he expected to open an excellent chemical laboratory in connece tion with the school. Now, since Owens College was in the habit of receiving from that and other schools in the county some of their most promising scholars, it was always i satisfactory to know that the boys of schools n the county, and especially in that division of the county, were pre- paring to receive those branches of science with which they at Owen's College were concerned. And especially did he rejoice to know that the schools was in thorough and wholesome connection with the ancient Universities. He trusted the time would never come when the links which bound the school to those old Universities would become weaker. (Hear, hear) He trusted they would always send boys of fair ability te win honours for themselves in those great arenas. And he trusted that the school, in time to come, would not fail to become connected with a certain University nearer home—(applause)—whose chief merit was that it was a great, but humble follower of those Universities of which they were all so proud. Only within the last few weeks the Victoria University had added to its numbers the rising, though still very young, University Col- lege of Liverpool—(applause)—and DOW the University con- , sisted of Owen's College and Liverpool College, which, they hoped, would become the Trinity and St. John's of the future. He did not see why, with the wealth and liberality of the citizens of Warrington, which had already provided the , school with two scholarships for Oxford and Cambridge— why this wealth and liberality should not provide two more in order to send boys also th Manchester or Liverpool. (Ap- plause.) Far be it from him to under-rate for a moment the importance of the recently manifested system, especially in this part of England, of technical instruction. He be- lieved that the ability which their young men and boys possessed was only waiting for the same ample means of technical culture which Germany and France had provided for their youth to produce young chemists, physicists, and I
- _ - Mr. Henry Tate, a sugar refiner at Liverpool, is present- ing to that city a Homceopathic Hospital. Mr. Tate's gift will coat about £lO,OOO.

TRANSFERS OF LICENSES.—Bafore Messrs. F. W. Eirle and A. R Gladstone, at the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tues- day, the following licenses were transferred —Quarry Hotel, Whiston, from James Plant to Joseph Dingsdale ; Black Horse, Widnes, from Robert Moore to Selina Moore; Sun Inn, Widnes, from Win. Lomas to Sarah Lomax; and Farmers' Arms, Huyton, from William Buller' to Richard Powell.

A WHISTON LANDLADY FINED.—At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, before Messrs. F. W. Earle and A. R. Gladstone, Ellen Saunders, landlady of the Gecrge and Dragon, Whiston, was summoned for selling adulterated whiskey.—P.S. Ball stated that on Thursday, the 27th ult, in compliance with instructions from Superintendent Bar. ker he purchased whiskey from the defendant, for which he paid 2s. He told her that he intended to send a sample of it to the public analyst, and offered to leave her a portion of R.—Superintendent Barker stated that the certificate of the public analyst showed the whiskey to be 32 degrees under proof, or 7 per cent weaker than allowed by the Act. —Mrs. Saunders said she was sorry for the offence having been commitfod. and added that she was not aware that the whiskey was not of the requisite strength.—A flue of 20s and costs was imposed. ALLEGED BIGAMY AT PRESCOT.—Before Messrs F. W. Earle and A. R. Gladstone at the Prescot Courthouse on Tuesday, James Wainwright, a collier, was again charged on remand with cemmitting bigamy by inter.marrying Julia Melia, his first wife being then alive.—Superintendent Barker intimated that he would have to ask for another re- mand in that case as the witnesses to prove the first mar- riage were very difficult to find. He would, however, offer sufficient evidence to justify the remand.—Julia Melia was then called. She said she was a single woman up to the 27th April last year when, on that date, she went through the form of marriage with the prisoner at the Prescot Catholic Chapel. He had told herbs was a single man, and she believed him.—P.C. Middlebrook deposed that be had seen the certificate of marriage, produced, and had com- pared it with an entry in the register at St. Paul's Parish Church, Crewe. It was a certificate of the marriage of the prisoner with Mary Ann Griffin on the 31st July, 1876.— Superintendent Barker then remarked that on that evidence and on the admission of the prisoner that he had committed bigamy, he would be glad to have a remand for eight days. —The application was granted._

PRESCOT SCHOOL BOARD.—The monthly meeting of this Board was held on Mnday evening, when there were present—Messrs. T. P. Hewitt (in the chair), W. Golds. worth, H, Fogg, and H. Crum (clerk). The usual monthly return of the attendances at the schools was. read.—The Chairman's Generosity: Mr. W. L. Evans (chairman of the Board), who was unable to attend, forwarded a letter en- closing a cheque for £5 with which to buy prizes for distri- bution to the scholars when they broke up for the Christmas holidays. It was decided that the £5 should be expended in buying books, 20 of which should be given to each school, and that the holidays be from the 19th December to the 12th January. The Board passed a resolution that at the commencement of the holidays the scholars should be regaled with bum and oranges as on former occasions.—The Heating of the Schools : It was afterwards decided that six coke stoves should be purchased for use as follows: Girls School 2, boys' 3, infants 1, and at a cost of £3 each.—A Scholar's Dishonesty: Miss Harris, mistress of the Girls' School, reported that one of the girls had been guilty of theft by taking money from a drawer in her desk. It was decided that the mother of the accused girl should be re- quested to attend before the Board in reference to the matter.—This was the principal business.

MANSLAFGFITER OF A LANCASHIRE FUSILIER.—At Mun- ster Winter Assizes, on Monday, Jeremiah Murphy, who was charged with the wilful murder of Corgi. Ainsworth, of the Lancashire Fusiliers, was convicted of manslaughter, and sentenced to ten years' penal servitude. Mr. T. Bradshaw, County Court judge of Newctstle-on- Tyne, was taken 11l on Wednesday night whilst at a concert in the Town Hall, and died in a few minutes. The learned gentleman had held the judgeship since 1971, and was pre- viously secretary to the Judicature Commission.- SALE OF WORK AND CHRISTMAS TREE. A two-days' sale of wQrk and Christmas tree was formally opened in the Lecture Mall connected with the Brunswick Wesleyan Chapel, Cross-lane, Earlestown, on Thursday afternoon. The proceeds of the effort are in aid of a fund being raised for the purchase of an organ for that place of worship. The Wesleyans have laboured hard for some time past in order ' to secure the wherewithal to purchase a suitable musical in- strument, and up to the present about £2OO has been raised. , By the present effort they confidently hope to increase this sum considerably, and appearances indicate that these anti- cipations will be realised. The hall had been very tastefully bedecked with evergreens, tissue papers, &c., bv the ladies' sewing class and the elder scholars, and Mr 1' I Bell. of Haydock-street, kindly erected the stalls. They were two in number—one being well stocked with articles of a miscellaneous character, and under the charge of Mrs Fairboarne, Miss Oreenall, Miss Newman, Miss Watson, and Mrs Barr. The refreshment stall was entrusted to Mrs , Atkinson, Mrs Sothern, Mrs Stringer, Mrs Gosling, and Mrs Chandley. One of the principal features was the large Christmas tree, which proved a great attraction to the juveniles. It was in the care of Miss Annie Needham, Miss Annie Eckerslev, Miss Annie Marrow, Miss Ada Barr, Miss I Sothern, and Miss Millington. During the afternoon and evening a fair number of persons attended the "sale."

On Saturday, in the Loadon Cup competition, Upton Park beat Clapham Rovers by three goals to two ; Old Etonians played a drawn game with Dulwich, two goals each ; Old Foresters beat Union by three to two ; Notts. Forest, in Notts. Cup competition, beat United Amateurs by four to none; in the Birmingam Cup competition, Wednes- bury beat Aston Unity by four to two; Birmingham St. George's, in the Staffordshire Cup competition, beat Wed- nesbury Old Athletic by three to one, and Wolverhampton Wanderers beat Port Vale (Burslem) by two to one ; in the Dumbartonshire Cup competition, Vale of Leven beat Vale Wanderers by two to one; and Dumbarton beat Helenlonrg Athletics by ten to one; in the Edinburgh Shield competition, Hibernians beat Heart of Midlothian by three to sue, and University beat Glencairn by nine to two ; Aston Villa beat Cambridge University by three goals to one; Old West- minsters beat Royal Engineers by two to one ; Grimsby and Notts. played a drawn game at Grimsby, one goal each.

The gift of the Mayor of Liverpool of 1000 hotpots on Christmas Day to poor families is to be supplemented by 500, given by Mr. Ephraim Walker. A quarryman named John Jones was attempting to soften some dynamite in a tin before the fire at tiolywell, on Thursday morning, when it exploded, seriously injuring the man and his child.

SAD AccmErrr. Mrs. Mary Singleton, residing near the Sunbeam Inn, Wargrave, met with a serious acci- dent on Friday night. She was in the act of crossing Earle- street, when a horse and hansom driven by Mr. Richard Walton, of Cross-lane, Earlestown, suddenly turned from the road to Vitriol-square and the sugar works, and before Mrs. Singleton could get out of the way she was knocked down. She sustained injuries to her head, back, dic., in addition to the severe shock, which have necessitated the attendance of Dr. Patterson.

CORPORATION OF Sr. HELENS V. THE LONDON AND NORTK-WESTERN RAILWAY COBIPANY.—An arbitration was held at St. Helens Town Hall on the 9th inst to determine whether the railway company were entitled to any com- pensation by reason of the corporation haring laid a water main under the company's main line, and a siding adjacent thereto, at Gerard's Bridge. The company offered to accept a nominal cum if the corporation would undertake, at their own cost, to alter or relay the main in the event of the rail- way works rendering it necessary to do so. The corporhtion deeined to do this or to make any payment whatever, stating that the Act give them power to lay the pipe with- out paying compensation. The case thus became one of importance, as affecting all easements taken by local au- thorities under the Public Health Act, 1875. To settle the question the Local Government Board appointed Mr. Henry Robinson, C.E , of Westminster, as umpire, who has now awarded that the corporation shall pay the sum of £37 108 in respect of the easements, together with all the costs of the arbitration.

div.head: BRILFUL SURGICAL OPERATION.
div.p: A BRILFUL SURGICAL OPERATION.

The American Ambassador at Vienna, 111 r. Hasson, has lately forwarded to his Government an interesting account of a re- markable surgical operation lately performed by Professor Bill roth, of Vienna, which, wonderful to tell, consisted in the remo- val of a portion of the human stomach, involving nearly one- third of the organ—and, strange to say, the patient recovered— the only successful operation of the kind ever performed. The disease for which this operation was performed was cancer of the stomach, attended with the following syrniot cms :—The appetite is quite poor. There is a peculiar indescribable dis- tress in the stomach, a feeling that has been described as a faint all gone" sensation; a sticky slime collects about the teeth, especially in the morning, accompanied by an mtplea- sant taste. Food fails to satisfy this peculiar faint sensa- tion; but, on the contrary, it appears to aggravate the feeling. The eyes are sunken, tinged with yellow ; the hands and feet become cold and stleky—a cold perspiration. The sufferers feel tired all the time, and sleep doe 3 not seem to give rest. Af er a time the patient becomes nervous and irritable, gloomy, lals mind filled with evil forebodings. When rising suddenly from a recumbent position there is a direness, a whistling sen- sation, and he is obliged to grasp something firm to keep from falling. The bowels costive, the skin dry and lost at times; the blood becoming thick and stagnant, and does not circulate prr perly. After a time the patient spits up food soon after eating, sometimes in a sour and fermented condition, some- times sweetish to the taste. Often-times there is a palpitation of the heart, and. the patient fears he may have heart disease. Towards the last the patient is unable to retain any food what- ever, as the opening in the intestines becomes close, or nr any so. Although this disease Is indeed alarming, sufferers with the above-named symptoms should not feel nervous, for nine hundred and ninety-nine cases out of s thousand have no cancer, but simply dyspepsia, a disease easily removed If treated In a proper manner.
