O'Donnell. said of a certain lady, when she went to Dub- lin as lady-lieutena2t, that she had all the qualities of the kitchen-poker without its occasional warmth. The rich are able, bat not liberal; the poor are generous, bat lack ability. WHERE TRH RUB COMES.—" It is a beautiful thing to see a husband and wife of one mind," remarked Mrs. Blogg. "Yes," replied Blogg ; "but then it makes a good deal of difference who carries the mind."

PORTENTOUS COGITATION.—WheR a woman becomes so absent-minded as to forget to hold her hind so that the light will fall upon her diamond ring it is safest for her husband to give her a wide berth. She is doing some dangerous thinking,

"I wiali I were you for about two hours," she sail, with great tenderness. "And why, my dear," asked* the hus- band, with considerable interest. "Because," she said, toying affectionately with his watch chain—" because then I would buy my wife a new set of furs." SITE LET Hint HAVE H'. "You don't really love him, my dear." "Well, perhaps not; but it's my first chance, and I may never get another." "Never mind if you don't. Wait until you find a man after your own heart." "That's just what's the matter, mamma. Charlie has been after my heart for eighteen months, and I guess I'd better let him have it."

HER RELIGIOUS -TENEERABIENT —" Whit s3erns to be the matter ?" he asked, mildly, as they were returning from church; "didn't you enjoy the sermon?" "Enjoy the ser- mon ?" she repeated, shortly, "and that odious Mrs. Smith aitting directly in front of me with a new full wrap on that never cost a cent less than $125. You must think I hive a very warm religious temperament." DIDN'T GET MUCH PRACTICE. A young physician moved from an eastern town to Kansas, and hung out his shingle. One day a neighbour called on him, and during the conversation inquired if he had ever opened an office in the East. "Oh, yes, I had a very nice office, indeed," was the reply, with more or less prile in the tone. "Did you have much practice ?" "Well, no, not exactly." "That's strange, for you seem to be a well-posted man. What was the matter 1" "Really I don't know, but somehow my patients all seemed to die before I could practise on them very ranch."

THE WIDOW MC.CRAT'S CDT/RTSIDP.—" How did I come by my second husband ?" repeated a Mississippi steamboat- man's wife, "Why my first husband Tom, was mate on the ill-fated Red Fawn, and we were both blown up with her in the terrible explosion of '59. I saw poor Tom's head blown off, and the next thing I knew I was flying through the air higher than the smoke stacks. As I came down I passed Jack Hamer, the second cook, and he called out to me: 'Mrs. Mc.Cray, will you marry me?' I'm agreed to it when I land, Jack,' says I, for I knew straight enough that I was a widow. They fished me out of the water as sound as a dollar, and when Jack recovered from a broken rib we were aneeeied in the float town are landed at." Tem( WILL D IT.—They were two intelligent citizens —men who knew the affairs of the country like a 'peek, and could take the platform for a speech. One was warming his coat-tails at a grocery stove when the other came in. " Rainy morning!" " Yes—it really rains." "Rather damp! " Yea. Going to be wet." " Must be fall rain?' " Quite likely ; yes, I presume it is." " Rather disagreeable outside 2" -" Quite so. May rain for some time." "Didn't expect this, did you ? " " Well, hardly." "Think it will hold up? " Well—um—dunno." "May rain all day, eh? " "Quite probable—quite probable." "Muddy under foot, isn't it?" "Y-e-s, quite so." And then they rubbed their hands over the top of the stove and stared at each ether and mentally exclaimed: "What an infernal dolt that fellow is, anyhow!" The colonel of an Austrian regiment in garrison in Vianna, who seems to have been one of the class of persons popu- larly described as "more nice than wise," wrote, a little time before the recent manosuvres of the Austrian army, to a medical man in the little town ef Anzern, near which they took place, stating that he was about to start with his re- giment for Anzern, and that he would feel much obliged if the doctor would find a lodging of some sort for him, adding that he hoped it would be in a'Christian family, as he ob- jected to live with the Jews. A day or two afterwards he received the following reply from Doctor Neuwirth, the person to whom he had applied—" Honoured Colonel,—The contingency which you contemplate with so much dissatis- faction, of having to live with Jews during your stay here, is happily obviated by circumstances. There are only two Jewish families in the town. The Archduke Albert is staying with one of them, the Archduke William with the other, which is my own.—l have," &c. Actors and actresses have a good deal of fun amongst themselves on the stage, though " guying " is strongly dis- countenanced by good managers. Generally the fan is im- promptu; but sometimes a joke is carefully planned before. hand. In a performance of "The Lady of the Lake," one of the principal aetors—Rhoderick Dhu—was known to be in pecuniary difficulties. When Rhoderick Dhu gave the "I am Rhoderick Dhu," Fitz-James replied, " Yes, and your rent's due too." On the production of a piece called "The Spy," the early acts showed that it was going to prove a dead failure. Se, when at a certain point a eh .racter had to rush on and shout, "Fire hundred pounds for the spy!' the author who was concealed by a rock, arose and cried, "It's yours—copyright, manuscript, and parts!" That was the end of the performance. When eating takes place on the stage, the temptations to play tricks with the food are naturally great. In "Henry V." the leek which Pistol has to eat is usually made from an apple. But on one never-to-be-forgotten occasion the Fiuellen of the evening gave him a real onion, and he had no choice but to struggle through it, though the tears coursed down his fat cheeks.

BANKRUPT Tat DEALERS.—At the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court, on Monday, Win. Waddell and Win. Jones Evans, tea dealers, applied to pass their public examination. The debtors' it appeared, commenced business together in Liver- pool in 1882 under the style of "Caper and Green" and other titles at about five shops, and their mode of business was to " give away' presents of crockery, tea-trays, basket- work, and other articles to each purchaser. The debtors bad been bankrupts before—Waddell at Batley, Yorkshire, and Evans at Dodgelley. Evans bad also been in the advertising business, and the manager of a newspaper exchange in Lone don. They had £7O joint capital when they started to- gether, and their deficiency was now £2,380. Each admitted having falsely answered the questions put to debtera by the Official Receiver, and in the Case of Evans an Cement of scaadal was imported by the presence in court of a young woman, with whom it was admitted he had been living, whom it was suggested he 'had led into a false marriage, and who now claimed to be a creditor of his for a large sum. The Registrar stopped the examination as to the relations between the two, on the ground that they did not come within the province af the Bankruptcy Court. The es* amination was adjourned. CONDITION OF THE WORKING CLASSES.-31r. Hugh Mason, M.P., addressing a meeting of his workpeople at Ashton on Saturday evening, referred to a recent speech of Mr. Thomas Hughes, Q.O ,at Manchester. That learned gentleman had asserted that two-thirds of the people were underfed, badly clothed, and miserably housed ;" and that in commercial matters competition was so keen that" every man's hand had been against his neigh'amr, and the least scrupulous had got the control of almost every branch of industry and trade." In those remarks Mr. Hughes was totally wrong. Though a few persons put on for base pur- poses the garment of piety, he (Mr. Mason) felt assu-ecl that ' traders generally proceeded on the old maxim of honesty being the best policy. The position of working people had vastly improved within his recollection, and if the great body of waze earners could only be persuaded to abandon their pernicious habit of spendirg their meney on intoxicat- ing liquor—a source of misery and pauperism which ap- peared to have been overlooked by Mr. Hughes—be thought seven-eighths of the existing poverty would vanish like magic. An American Judge recently called at the village store, designing to make the purchase of a few mackerel. Several friends were in, who knew that the judge had become a temperance man, and were willing to run him a little. The storekeeper joined in the sport, and begged the Judge to take a little of something. "What will you have, Judge? Take anything you like." The Judge looked around, as if in doubt what to choose, and re- plied, "I believe I will take a mackerel !" Helping him- self, he gravely walked out of the store, and was not invited to take anything there again. How To Mese BREAD.—" Bread !" exclaimed a Vassar College girL " Bread ! TEETOTALISM AT EARLESTOWN. Sir,—Can any of your numerous readers point out as an historical fact that Christ was-not an abstainer; for cn Sun- day Dec. 14th a certain rev. gentleman at the Earlestown Wesleyan Chapel stated in his sermon that it was an historical fact that Christ was not an abstainer. Es ad- vocated the old exploded idea that moderation was the cure for the evils of the drink traffic, and recommended his con- gregation to try am, yours, A DISGUSTED TEETOTALLER.

A MISSION TO TETE POOR. Sir,—Are our clergy and preachers in Warrington going still to continue in the sing-song fashion of respectability in connection with our places of worship, pewed, appropria- ted, or free, having no regard to the poor amongst us? Is there never to be a mission to the mass of the people, the taking of the Gospel tO them in the lanes, streets, and high- ways? Is blood and fire, bringing war in its train only to go forth on the week day and Sabbath, instead of the banner of the Cross, bringing peace and good-will or glad tidings of great joy ? I have often thought all preachers should be disciples of our Lord, cot lords and masters, walking the streets as if they were something aloof from the people, or like gods amongst men. I charge them if they are the chosen teachers to come amongst thepeople, and fear nothing in these days of carelessness and infidelity; throw oil all disagreement and trust one another as fellow-sinners. There is none of us without failings; try to agree on some mode of a mission in each district, for it's a disgrace to the town and places of worship that" the poor should be so few in attendance. There bays been successfnl missions in London and other towns. Why should it not be so in War- rington, for it is to the poor the Gospel should be preached? —Yours, iSzc., ANXIOUS.

div.head: FAIR TRADE.
div.p: FAIR TRADE.

Sir,—Will you kinclli;floW-We-t-O reply to a few of the remarks made by your correspondent "Clifford Dix." In the first place, I cannot understand how a thing which AS fair can ba wrong. It is anfair for foreign nations to stop the acicles we manufacture from entering their markets, so long an we let their articles corns here, and nine men out of every dozen will admit this whether " Clifford Dix" does or not. Your correspondent writes of "the Carts of long ago" and before the introduction of steam power ; he might as well write about the days when labourers worked in the vineyards for one penny a day. Eighty years aFto sweet milk was sold at a pcnny per quart, and eggs three for a penny, but that 13 not to-day. We are face to face with two difficulties—the loss of our home orders by free impor- tations, and the lain of our export orders through low freights caused by foreign grants to steamship companies. Can "Clifford Dix " tell us a cure for these two evils ? Never mind talking about a dezen " sprats " ; we have to face the difficulty. These foreign nations subscribe 5 per tent. and get back 95 per cent. A reduction of wages is the only medicine Free Trade gives to care foreign competition, so those who catch the disease must swallow the medicine. Your correspondent says "you may take the horse to the water, but you can't make him drink " ; but I venture to say his horse would soon drink when he got thirsty and found no more water about, excPpt the water before him. "Clifford Dix" next beens to abuse the working-men— well, this is just what most Free Trade writers do at last for want of a better explanation. Your correspondent stye "the whole social system is rotten to the core, rich men get richer" and I suppose he means poor men get poorer. This is a beautiful picture to draw of a country such as ours ; perhaps, however, "Cliff erd Dix" refers to oar merchant princes; if so, he is getting nearer the truth. Warrington is, however, a manufacturing town, and its inhabitants are working-men, and they are not going to be charmed by the voice of the charmer whether be be one of Liverpool's princely merchants or one of the individuals who write Free Trade leading articles to order in the different news- papers, but who do not encounter foreign competition them- selves. Why has "Clifford Dix" ceased Writing about railway rates ? This matter will come to the front before long, when we shall want good men ta suop-ert it.—Yours truly, FAIR PRICE. Warrington, December 18, 1881.

div.head: • CHRISTMAS BEER AT THE WORKHOUSE.
div.p: • CHRISTMAS BEER AT THE WORKHOUSE.

Sir,—ln glancing over your last issne I happened to come across the report of the Board of Guardians, held on the previous Wednesday, and it was with something akin to contempt that I read the remarks of Mr. Darbyshire anent the paupers and their Christmas beer. Burns must have had such a one in his mind when he 'wrote :

Man's inhumanity to man Makes countless thousands mourn. Because, forsooth, Mr. Derbyshire is a teetotaller, therefore every inmate of the Workhouse must.be the same! I would like to bring the point home to him in this way: Suppose that, through misfortune, he should be brought to live in the house (which heaven forbid, if the rulers were all like him!) and suppose he ,as very fond of a cup of tea, with only the chance of having it on one day in the year, what would be his ftelings if debarred from it then through the the curmudgeony opposition of the Board ? "The bearin's on its in the application." Mr. Darbyehire is one of those who go mad over a miserable Murphyism; and who are so bliad that they can- not see the difference between the use of a thing and the abuse of it. And when he says "they (the paupers) would do much better bodily, and spirituilly they would be much better without beer," one wonders where his experience comes from. His assumption of medical knowledge is bumptious and grotesque; and his religious ethics are ridieubusly like " inspiration and -- water!"

Your professing moralists are always the most prcne to deal harshly with those in humbler circumstances than themselves; they pose as pietists, and assume to know so much that it is bard to discover why they were ever allowed to inhabit a sorry planet like ours. There is an incongruity in their Christian speech and Christian acts that cannot possibly be reconciled in any way. Mr. Jolley has my best thanks for resisting so successfully the " narrow-uncharit- ableness" of Mr. Darbyahire and Mr. Hunt; and I heartily commend to these two gentlemen Hood's pungent lines to Rae Wilson : A sorry sight it is to rest the eye on, To see a Christian creature gaze at Zion-; hen homeward, of the saiotly pasture full, Rush bellowing, and breathing fire and smoke, At crippled povery to butt and poke, Exactly as a skittish Scottish bull, //ants an old woman in a scarlet cloak —Yours fah hfully, Styx, 18th December, 1884.
PLUTO.

div.head: RAFFLES AT BAZAARS.
div.p: RAFFLES AT BAZAARS.

Sir,—At the risk of displeasing some of my good friends, I must say a word on this subject. Whet a pity it is the talent for philosophical argument should have been doomed for so long a period to lie dor- mant, as it seems to have, in the ctse of our respected tewnsaasn, Mr R B White. Really, when I read his short and pithy note in your last issue, I could but lament that it had not teen his good fortune to forestall the "Brummagem rads " in their efforts to teach Christian England how to be honest, and pat aside gambling. He has maniged to tack on a shrewd addendum "The end does not justify the mesas." Our friend, evidently, he no connection with the Jesuits. How the consciences of some of our goad Christian townsfolk must have been stirred up at reading this. I wonder how many churches have been re-built, new pulpits erected, and Bethesdas prepared for the reception of good easy folk, by the aid of "raffles at bazaars." Well may Mr Wog-n say "It is truly a cutting satire on the vaunted piety of a Christian Church,' when with all it wealth It is found reduced to such shifts to eke out the means necessary to build a place of worship. I wonder how many of the good Christian folk, who read the discourse recently given by the Dean of Manchester on gambling, struck the orthodox pharisaical attitude and were thankful teat they were not as other men are. The fact is, Mr Editor, not a church or chapel will in the future be erected without reference being made, and in no charit- able spirit, to the Watch Committee of Birmingham. Judge Talfourd tells us that "gambling changes enterprise to squalid greediness, makes heaven-born hope a shivering fever, and in vile collapse leaves the exhausted heart with- out oee fibre impelled by generous passion." And yet Mr Whits thinks "clergymen and ministers" should have notice against committing "such offences." Would it be presumption on my part to suggest to the Rev E. C: F. Carle- ton that before he goes to Liverpool again to talk about Atheism ia the back slams of Warrington he at once sees about putting his own house in order ? At a meeting held recently in London, one of the speakers , said the best argument in favour of Christianity would be that of showing it in their lives. Da they live it? Is it not a f tct that bazars and sales of work are merely means . .

to an end; that poor people are not wanted there. and that the well-to-do go with a full knowledge that they are going to be wheedled out of their money. What must be the feel- ings of an M.P. or a local baronet when invited to a baztar ? He knows full well that every article he purchases will be charged 109 per cent more than its value. At a hazier re- cently held in Birmingham one of the attractions was a grand ballot for five and ten poun l notes, and I aek the great champion and defender of the faith, the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, what difference there is between balloting for batik notes and playing at pitch and toss? But the worst of all this business is, that the " pot-house " is degraded to the level of a church or chapel bat tar, and we are to have no more raffles. Rather rich this, knowing as we do, that while we poor chaps may not be in a raffle for a Christmas goose or turkey, the whole of clubland may carry it on ad libitum. Now, I think I have a good suggestion to make. and I know that nine-tenth of the Virarringtonians will agree with it ; it is that we at once dispense with the bench of magistrates, and appoint the Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt) and the Magistrates' Clerk (Mr. White) sole custodians of the people's consciences. It would be treason, no doubt, to say this is at present the case, but a good many people think there is something in it. Well, for ages now the spiritual law has struggled with the temporal law for this great privilege ; and the odds (excuse this little touch of the g.iaiblirog spirit) seem to be with the temporal. CAPTAIN CUTTLE.

WARRINGTON SAVINGS-BANK.' The annual meeting of trustees and managers of this in- stitution was held at the Bank, Buttermarket-street, on Tuesday morning. Alderman Pickmere presided, and amongst those present were the Mayor (Alderman Harri- son), Aldermen Holmes, Davies, and Webster; the Rev. A. Kenworthy ; Messrs. Monks, Finney, Darbyshire, Dobson. J. Pierpoint, J. Cliffs, J. Morris, A. N. Houghton, J. R. Young, and J. E. Davies (actuary).—The Committee of Management presented the general statement of the bank for the year ending 20th November, 1884, and a summary of I the year's proceedings. The total funds now amounted to £285,989 Os 41, viz.: With the National Debt Commis- sioners—On general account, £281,802 13s sd; on separate surplus fund account, £700; and the balance with treasurer, £3,486 6s 11d; total, £285,989 N 4d. £7,430 14e 101 interest and £25 7s dividends on stock had been credited deposi- tors, and the total amount due to them was £284,075 7s 21, showing an increase for the year of £4,514 us 9d. 781 new accounts had been opened, and 553 accounts closed ; in- crease for the year, 228. The total number of depositors now was 9,286. Although the trade of the country had been depressed for some few years, the bank continued to show an increase in its funds and number of accounts. Ten years ETO the accounts numbered 6,910, and the amount deposited £237,074 Os 81, and now they number 9 286 and £284,075 7s 21 deposited. A new front entrance to the bank had been erected, and other additions and alterations made, which the committee considered desirable for the better accommoda- tion of the large number of depositors. The re?ort of the auditor, Mr. Vernon, certified the correctness of the books of the institution and the report.—The CHAIRMAN proposed the adoption of the statement of accounts. Having referred to the finances, he said that he should like the managers of the bank to interest theme:lees more in its behalf by advis- ing the working-classes and others who had money to invest to take it there, as such banks were principally int,nded for the working classes. He thought that the money expended in repairs—Zloo-liad been well spent, for more convenience was now afforded to depositors as well as to the officials.—Mr. F. MONKS seconded, and Mr. T. JOLLEY supported, the resolu- tion, which was carried.—Alderman WEBSTER moved the adoption of the report of the Committee of Management and an acknowledgment of the valuable services rendered lay that committee daring the past year.—Mr. D. W. FINNEY seconded the resolution. They were doing a great work in Warrington in trying to inculcate habits of thrift, aad were making great progress in that direction. He hoped none of their efforts would be relaxed. He then com- plimented Mr. G. E. Davies and his staff on their excellent services.—The resolution was carried.—Alderman Pickmere was re-elected chairman, and Mr. W. Long vice-chairman of thelnstitution: The following were appointed a com- mittee of management :—Trustees: The Chairman and Vice-chairman, and Messrs. F. Monks, C. Broadbent, J. Davies,T. Litton; managers: The Mayor. and Messrs. T. Jolley, W. Darbyshire, W. Owen. junr, , S. Lees, J. R. Young, J. Morris, and the Revs. J.Yonge. and A Kenworthy. Dodds (Penketh), J. Gandy (Enfield Hell), Wheeler, Fleming, R. Proud, E. Braids, D. Jones, J. Hartley, Warburton, T. Robinson, T. Eaude, R. Rowson, R. H. Kerr, J. Dewhurst, C. Twisq, W. Bennett, F. div.head: WYCLIFFE QUINCENTENARY.
div.p: WYCLIFFE QUINCENTENARY.

On Thursday evening, a public meeting was held in the Wycliffe Congregational Church, Warrington, in celebra- tion of the qaincentenarf of John Wycliffo, who died December 31st, 1331. There was a good attendance. The Rev. J. Yonge presided, and was supported by several local ministers. The Rev. W. It. Parry having offered up prayer, the CHAIRMAN explained that the character of the meeting was perfectly unsectarian. John Wycliffe, as some seemed to suppose, was by no means the exclusive property of Congregationalists; he was looked upon as being the pro- perty of all evangelical Christians, of those who believed in the rights of private judgment, in an open Bible, and in an entire freedom from tyranny and despotism such as had been exercised by Rome. They seemed now to be living in days of centeaary celebrations. It WAS said by some that the celebration of centenaries was being rather ran to seed, but he thought there must be usefulness in such a one as they were then met to celebrate ; they did not refer to such men as Wycliffe in simple laudation of them, but of the work that they did, the principles that they advocated, and the glorious results that accrued from their lives. It was good for Protestants of the present day to be reminded of the great principles that our forefathers strove for at great personal risk, and often at the cost of life itself. It might help them more to value the privileges that they enjoyed. Wycliffe was the precur- sor of the great Protestant Reformation, not only in Eng- land, but throughout Europe. He had been fitly styled the Morning Star of the Reformation. (Applause.) Of what. Wycliffe had done they would hear from succeeding speakers. The Rev. E. MOORE, of Golborne-street Baptist Chapel, then spoke of " Wycliffe's Times." He said that the work of Wycliffe had even a greater interest to them than the work of Luther, for Wycliffe was an Englishman. England was the scene ot his labours and his aim was to promote the happiness and well-being Of his own country. The condi- tien of things that existed in Wycliffe' time was to a large , extent the development of a long struggle that had taken ' place between the Papal Church and the King of England. It would be necessary to briefly glance at the history of that struggle to understand those times, which would necessi- tate their going back to somewhat early times. Pope Gregory conceived the idea of bringing our isles under the sway of the Church of Reme, and sent an expedition of monks to carry out the project. This took hold upon the ignorant heathenism of the British of that tines, and the Pope% sway became universal. But even in those days of darkness and and superstition there were a few sott,s who bore grand testimony for Christ. The first decisive step towards Protestantism in this country was the landing of William the Conqueror. Although he had come to England Linde :- the sanction ef Reme, William when he became king began to object to the domination of the Pope, and a controversy that lasted until William's death, was commenced. After his death the straggle between kings and popes was main- tained, but with less vigour. The pope's power again be- came almost absolute, and in the reign of the weak king John the pope made a successful attempt to re-cstablish his power. But the spirit of the nation was stirred and the barons forced John to sign the famous Magna Charts. The kings of England paid most attention to the political aspect of the question, and the whole ecclesiastical administration became a huge scandal, the priests and clergy plundering the people, and committing the most horrible crimes with- out interference. No one could wonder that there arose a I mistrust and hatred of the papal power. Nor were there wenting men to resist. It was not necessary te deal with the social and commercial aspects of the times of Wycl;ffe, whose efforts were directed against papal oppression. He was sure that as they listened to accounts of what Wycliffe had done they would be filled with gratitude. (Applause.) The Rey. J. HOWELL JONES. of Bold-street Wesleyan Chapel, addressed the meeting on " Wycliffe's Bible for the People." There were few men, he said, who had influenced English History as had Wycliffe, who took his place with those who had materially contributed to making Britain what it is to-day. Bat whatever his reatness it was derived from and founded upon a devout study of, and profound acquaint- ance with, the Word of God. Whatever he did for his country and his people, was the result of a resolve at which he ar- rived in his early life. In those days it was not accounted a high distinction to be a student of the word of God. Wycliffe was early imbued with the supreme purpose of de- voting himself to the study and exposition of that word. A young man starting in life with that purpose could not fail to come very speedily into contact with Rome. Mr. Moore had told them how the weakling John submitted to the Pope by consenting to hold his crown as the vassal of Rome. The claims of Rome, after being in abeyance for a time, were renewed in Ihe time of the third Edward. Edward's Parliament refused to pay the money claimed on the ground that they were not bound by the promises of John, and in the controversy that resulted Wycliffe bore a noble and pro- minent part. He came to the conclusion that the right of private judgment should be exercised, and that it was not right that the cemmon people shotild not be entrusted with the Bible in their own language. The outcome of that con- clusion was the first English Bible ever published. (Ap- plause.) Wycliffe set about the translation without any knowledge of Greek or Hebrew, taking it from the Latin vulgate. Wycliffe stated distinctly that what he did was through the conviction that the ills from which the country suffered resulted from ignorance of the Bible. Soon the land was flooded with Gospel light. All honour to the man who did so much for his country in its dark days. They knew not what might have happened but for his devotion and heroism. The priests of 'Rome, like wreckers on the coast, were seeking by false lights to allure the good ship to destruction, but Wycliffe saved it from breaking on the rocks. (Applause.) The Rev. G. E. CUTTING, of Bewsey-road Wesleyan Chapel, speaking on " Wycliffe's Evangelism," said that they must remember that Wycliffe was an evangelical pioneer. "He prepared the way." He did what the Sun- day school teacher did for the child, gave the elementary teaching so necessary for a work to be followed out. Wycliffe was an evangelistic hero;too, and a mighty power was meant by that. He believed that one reason why our blood was stirred by the mention of Wycliffe's name was because a fearless, noble, honest man, with God's name written upon him, could not live in vain. The night of the star of Wycliffe was not qnenched 500 years ago, but was glowing still, and filled that building that eight with the light of holy example. He wanted them to catch enthusi- asm from that example. They could learn by it to stand to their posts and gloriously to resist sin. Wycliffe Wee an emancipator in unlocking the truth from the keeping of a dead language. In combating the power of Rome, assert- tog be right of private judgment, he was an emancipator; be was free himself, and he tried to set others free. (Ap- plause.) The Rev. W. Mr LES, of Emmanuel Church, spoke on " Wycliffe's patriotism." There was no thoughtehe said, so calculated to stir up in the English heart feelings of in- tense enthusiasm as the thought of patriotism. In no nation was the love of country so strongly developed as in our own

div.head: IHE EXAMINPR, SATURDAY. DECEMBER 2O, 1834.
div.p: IHE EXAMINPR, SATURDAY. DECEMBER 2O, 1834.

land, and in the annals of no nation were there records of I nobler deeds or greater heroism than the history of England ' revealed, on the part of its sons. In the foremost rank of patriots stood the man whose name they had met to hon- our, and for whose work they so devoutly gave thanks Wycliffe did more for the freedom of our nation than any rcan who had lived before him or who bad lived since. His work was a national one, and his object was to deliver his country from the galling bondage of ecclesiasticism. They had had a vivid ske ch of the times in which Wycliff a lived and of the tyranny under which the nation groaned, and they had had a lucid exposition of the more remarkible phases of Wycliffe's work. He thought that it must be evident to al' that the prime motive of his life was the all absorbing desire to promote the country's highest good. That round which all his life seemed to revolve was that the nation's prosperity and honour were bound up with the nation's spiritual life ; that the former depended entirely on the latter. Charged with that conviction, it was impossible for him to look unmoved at the enormities perpetrated on Christianity. A man of his strength of principles only needed the conviction that a certain thing was an unen- durable curse in order to make the most strenuous efforts to

procure its removal. Hence Wycliffe set his face against ! the whole system of papal rule. He acted on the principle ' that the Lest way to expose and defeat error was to hold up the lamp of truth. As soon as England got the open Bible her proaperity incre.sed. The Bible was the foundation of England's greatness ; remove it and the whole fabric would come to the ground, and no complete would be their over- throw that in future ages their humiliation would be greater than their glory had been. The meeting was then brought to a conclusion.
Orr 3nnday the Rev. J. Warnock, 8.D., preached in St. John's Presbyterian Church, Winwick-street, on "John Wycliffe: The Morning Star of the Reformation," to a good congregation.

CHRISTMASTIDE AT WARRING roN. • The approach_ of Christmas is again beingleeafded by the extra display of -commodities which is usually made by tradesmen and shopkeepers when the season of " good cheer" comes round. As yet, however, the display is but partial, many of the shops and other places of business not having assumed their full Christmas garb. Especially is this the case with regard to the Market, which, as a rule, is the scene of the most effective display. But even here many of the stalls are already tastefully set out, while the piles of "mistletoe and evergreens lying about are altogether suggestive of ,the season. In the streets the usual amount of ornamentation seems to have taken, or lobe about to take place, and consequently they have assumed a more cheerful and varied aspect. In Bridge-street the tradesmen seem to have been laudably emulous to make their somewhat narrow thoroughfare as attractive as possible, and have, on the whole, been successful. The extensive frontage of the Grand Clothing Hall Company is particularly bright, being illuminated by numerous jets of gee, the rays of which are reflected by the rich, vari-celoured articles which are taste- fully displayed in the windows. What gives an additional attraction to the establishment is a remarkably faithful cork model of the Par'sh Church, designed by Mr. Rudd, of Latchford. The two windows of Mr. Hodgkinson, drap2r, are also dressed with taste, and affard a striking contrast of collar, one being displayed with light mate- rial, and the other with garments of a more sombre hue. Amongst the grocers' shops the large-siz3d window of Messrs. N. Gould and Company attracts a good deal of notice as it is stocked with a riph variety of seasonable commodities; and that of Mr. Brandreth while not so con- spicuous is so well replenished as to show that ample pre- paration has been made to meet all the demands of cus- tomers. The establishment of Mr. J. S. Garland has been neatly decorated, and the windows are set out with a variety of beautiful lamps and a quantity of the finer sorts of iron- mongery, which has been so arranged as to make a wonder- fully effective display considering :the somewhat intractable nature of the material. Among the bakers and confectioners the shops of Mr. Pierpoint, Mr. Carter, and Mr. Toft are most noticeable. In Horsemarket-street the Manchester Clothing Depot, and the shop of-Mr. F. Wright, draper, are conspicuous on account of their elaborate dressing. In the former shop there is a very .large assort- ment of ready-made clothing of all sirts and to suit all ages, a conspicuous feature in one of the windows being a handsome volunteer prize cup; while between Mr. Wright's two adjoining establishment an excellent contrast has been arranged, the window of one being set out with a variety of bright coloured articles, the other being filled with a tempting choice of more sober-coloured ladies' winter garments. The provision shop of Messrs. Milling and Co. is is usual amply replenished, and lower down the street the wide frontage of Messrs. T. and W. Woods on Horse- market-street and Scotland-road affords wide scope for an extensive display. Messrs. Hall and Son, hatters, make up by the exhaustless choice which they offer their customers for the artistic display which the colourless and unre3thetic nature of their commodity prevents them from making, and the same may be said of lessrs. Unsworth, Brothers, Lyme- street. Amongst the boot and shoe shops may be mentioned Messrs. Stead, Simpson, and Nephew, whose manager has ' displayed much taste in the setting out of the windows. From the daintiest slipper for a Cinderella and the bob-nai led boot for a Hodge, there is every gradation of fashion and configuration. In Buttermarket-street, Mr. Percival's grocery establishment is well stocked and tastefully dis- played. In the same street, Mr. Gleave, baker, has a nicely arranged window, and Mr. Craik, at his tailoring establishment, shows some stylish seasonable goods. Law- less Brothers have their shop in Market-street well supplied to equal any demand. The large establishment of Messrs. J. and W. Dutton, Sankey-stree, comes in for a considerable share of notice, a speciality being made of a Quantity of cheap-Christmas and New Year's presents. The establishments of Mr. W. J. Dann, clothier and out- fitter ; Mrs. Walsh, infants' outfitter ; and Mr. J. Buck, draper, all in Sankey-street, are also notice- able; whilst the Liverpool Supply Stores, in Win. wick-street, are replete with Christmas fare. The windows of the stationers are, of course, bright with Christmas and New Year's cards, the designs for which become year by year more artistic. Mr. J. S. Green, of Bridge-street, has laid in a large and choice stock which will be sure to tempt his cutomers. There is food, and plenty of it, both for mind and body, and, hoping all our readers will come in for a fair share, we wish them " A Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year.",

PADGATE WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY. —Last Thursday, Mr W Ambrose Lloyd read a paper en- titled "Why am I a Conservative ? " in which he sought at some length to justify his adherence to Conservative princi- ples, and to prove that the Conservative party were the truest friends of the working classes, and the best upholders of the honour and welfare of the country. The essay gave rise to an animated discussion, in which the following gen- tlemen took part :—Messrs Frederick Wright, W H J Jenkins, Arthur Bennett, Charles Plinston, J J Wild, Theo- dore C London, George Mather, and James Andrews..

it'VENILE iIIIEVES AT i'ENICETIL—At Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, two brothers named Elijah and John Fisher, the former 13 and the latter 11 years of age, pleaded guilty to a charge of breaking into a cabin on the Cheshire Lines Railway at Penketh, on the 3rd inst., and stealing a hedging hook, value 4s, the property of the Cheshire Lines Committee. The hook was left in the cabin on the evening of the day in question, and next morn- ing it was missed. Subsequently it was found at the house of the prisoners by the local constable. The magistrates committed the boys to prison for 14 days, to be followed by three years' residence in a reformatory. .

- WARRINGTON' LIBERAL CLUB —The annual meeting of the members of the Liberal Club took place on Thursday evening in the large Committee Room. Mr. McMinnies, M.P., presiied, and there was a large attendance of mem- bers. The following were elected officers and committee for the ensuing year :—President, J. G. McMinnies, E4g., M.P. ; vice-presidents, William Crosfield, Esq., J.P., C. Broadbent, Esq , J.P.; Cmncillors John Platt, Jas. Bar- ker, and William Pierpoint ; Messrs. J. H. Gornall, F. A. Roberts, Thomas Morris, Thomas Jones, Samuel Barlow ; hon. treas., Mr. John Crosfield, J.P.; committee of manage- ment, Messrs. Joseph Albinson' Arthur Browne, Peter Cald- well, jun., Robert Campbell, F. J. Dell, Joseph Garner, Samuel Gough, John W. Hall,Thos. Lowe, Thos. Mather, James Strange, Wm._,Unsworth.

TILE BIRTH AND DEATH RATE OF WARRINGTON.—For week ending Saturday, December 13th, 1884.—The mean temperature was 412 Fahrenheit, and therefore 58 degrees warmer than the preceding week. The maximum temperature, 54 Fahrenheit, was recorded on the oth inst., and the minimum temperature' 29 Fahrenheit, en the 10th inst. The rainfall measured .7 inches. The general direction of the wind was S.W. During the week, which was the 50th of the currc ,t year, 44 births and 19 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 221 per 1,000, against 341 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 180 the corresponding week of last year. The deaths included 5 from measles, 1 from typhoid fever' 1 from croup, 1 from old age, 5 from lung disease, 3 from brain disease, and 1 from debility.—Joms H. GORNALL, Medical Officer of Health.

ALLEGED THEFT OF A FIDDLE.— At the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday, before Messrs George McCorquodale, T. J. Gillespie, and A. C. McCorquodale, Mary Jane Towey, a girl, was charged with stealing a fiddle and a purse con- taining SI, together of the value of .£l. ss, at Poulton, on the 4th inst, the property of Joseph Enshaw, a travelling musician. The prisoner pleaded net guilty.—Superinten• dent Jackson stated that the girl lived with her mother, and the old man went to her and asked her to allow her daughter to go with him for the day. They started off to- gether, and rambled through some part of Cheshire Win. wick, Poulton, Sic., to Padgate Stocks. They called at various public-houses en the way, and when they got to Padgate the old man was drunk and was unable to go fur- ther. He fell down on the floor, and the girl took the purse and fiddle to her own home. From inquiries he (Superin- tendent Jackson) had made he did not think there was any appearance cif theft, or that the girl had the slightest notion of stealing. When the old man fell down she simply took the fiddle and purse to her own house and took care of , them. She had been brought up on the charge at Warring- , toa ar.lel remanded to that court—Mr. Gillespie asked if the money in the purse was intact. —Superintendent Jackson replied that it was and he did not think it wise to offer evi- dence in the matter.—The girl said she did not intend to steal the fiddle or the purse ; and the Bench ultimately discharged her.

WARRINGTON AND THE • SHIP CANAL. SPECIAL MEETING OF THE TOWN COUNCIL. A special meeting of this Council was held in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall yesterday afternoon for the pur- pose of passing a resolution with respect to the Manchester Ship Canal Bill. The Mayor (Alderman Harrison, • J.P.I presided, and there were also present: Aldermen Burgess' Davies, and Holmes, and Councillors Broadbent, MackiL9 Litton. Brown, Bolton, Roberts, Taylor, W. Pierpoint, Marsh, J. Pierpoint, Ashton, and Wright; Mess-s. Brook (town clerk), Whittle (deputy town clerk), and Longdin (borough surveyor.) Alderman DAVIES said that seeing how serious and Im- portant the discussion of that meeting would be he would suggest that the discussion be taken down verbatim. The MAYOR : That is rather an ominous note of warning. What power have we to require that our discussion should be taken down verbatim. Alderman DAVIES said that the Council had power if they paid for it; he moved that that course be adopted. Alderman Hoeeres secoeled the propoaal, as he did not I think it would have been made by Alderman Davies with- out due cause. Councillor MACKIE thought it was not necessary to take such a course without special reason. Alderman DAVIES said that he had good reason for the request, and that their proceedings of that night with res- pect to the Ship Canal were looked upon with great jealousy. He should not be at all surprised if very sevcre action were taken by some of the ratepayers as to whether the course taken was or was not strictly legal. His reason was that they should protect themselves as far as possible in what they did. Alderman BURGESS asked if the proceedings they were asked to take part in had the concurrence of their legal adviser ? Would he say that the Council were acting right in what they proposed to do. If the Town Clerk did so be should take no notice of anything that might take plac?, ou.side, and should not allow his position in the Council chamber to be influenced by an idle threat from outside. If those outside were prepared to take severe action let them do it.

--The TOWN CLERIC: In my opinion there is nothing illegal in what we are going to do to night. lam backed up by the opinion of counsel on the subject. Alderman DAVIES decided to withdraw his resolution that a verbatim note of the proceedings should be taken. The MAyOR then moved "That the common seal of the borough be affixed to a petition to the House of Commons for leave to bring in the Manchester Ship Canal Bill, and to the agreement between the promoters of the bill and the ' Corporation." Alderman BURGESS seconded the resolution, and the Council went into committee to discuss it, the proposed agreement being read by the Town Clerk, In answer to Councillor J. Pierpoint, the TOWN CLERK said that the same privileges were inserted in the present bill as were in the previous one. The MAYOR : What is the distinction between the pro- moters of the bill and the members of the company ?--The Towle CLERK: The members of the company are those re- ferred to in the bill. You become promoters, but not mem- bers of the company. Alderman DAVIES said he should like to ask the Town IClerk whether that private agreement—for virtually it was la private agreement—would save them from any proceedings from third parties in the first instance ?-The TOWN CLERK: I think that the third parties would be able to take pro- ceedings against you, but with the present conditions you could relieve yourselves from liability and substitute those parties who give the guarantee. Alderman DAVIES: I want to make it known that it is not a proper agreement, and does not hold us harmless; if we were entirely free there would be no necessity for a guarantee at all. I should like to ask the Town Clerk whether those guarantors would extend the guarantee to the individual members of the Council? It is quite possible In law that an action might not lie against the Corporation, but against individual members of the Council who have taken an active part in these proceedings, and I want to know if it is not desirable to ask the guarantors to let the guarantee be extended P—The Tower CLERK: I have ex- pressed the opinion already that there is no personal liabil- ity, so I do not see the necessity of forming a personal guarantee; of course it could be extended. Alderman DAVIES: Are we still to have a meeting of rate- payers to approve of the action of the Council at the first meeting? It has already been beld.—ls the confirmatory meeting of the Council to confirm that first meeting still to be held? Yes it is.—ls the meeting of to-night to be car- ried by a simple majority of the Council now present, or will it be necessary to carry it by a majority of the whole members of the Council ? Only by an ordinary majority. —Unless you carry it at the confirmatory meeting what will be the position of the Council? The whole thing will fall through, notwithstanding our having signed the petition.— I want to know what the position of the Council will be if we do not confirm the first resolution of the Council by a second meeting, at which it is necessary to have more than 18 members voting for it? Ido not apprehend such a thing can happen. 'This agreement is entered into with the sanction of the Secretary of State, and if you pass a resolu- tion refusing to confirm what has been previously done, it is clear that the Secretary of State will not allow it, and the thing will fall to the ground.—! feel AI should be in a serious dilemma if, baying lodged a bill in conjunction with others who have it in their power as to how that bill should go en, what is our position if our action is not confirmed by ;the confirmatory meeting? The only way would be to petition for leave to withdraw.—l want to know bow far we should be compromised, for it would be a fatal thing for the Council to be put in a false position. I was going to sug- gest whether, even if we sign the petition to night, we could not delay the deposit. When should it be deposited? To-morrow.—l urn sorry. I should like the Council to think that we should be safe. Councillor MAcKIE said that few of them had antici- pated any opposition now. He would appeal to Alderman Davies whether it was not a very unsuitable time to bring ' forward what was evidently intended to be a stab at the Ship Canal, given through the medium of the poor, humble town of Warrington, which expected to gain so much by it (the canal.) Some time ago the Alderman eulogised the scheme, and there was no change in it from that day to the present that should CRISS any of them to at their words, but, had there been such a change he thought that it was only due to the Council that Alderman Davies should have spoken before. At none of the great meetings that had been held bad Alderman Davies raised a finger or suogested that anything illegal was being done, and he appealed to him whether it was becoming the antecedents of a gentleman who had been twice mayor of Warrington, and who was likely to be so again, to come in at the last gasp and ctuse the town to be looked at with contempt ,throughout the whole of Lancashire. To come at the twelfth hoar, when the friends of the canal were almost helpless to take further steps, and when the petition must be presented next day, was unkindly, ungenerous, unwise, and totally un- worthy the antecedents of Alderman Davies. The Tows' CLERK thought that the objection of Alder. man Davies might be met by the insertion in the agree- ment of the words "Subject also to the resolution being confirmed at the confirmatory meeting necessary to be held under the Municipal Corporations Act." Alderman DAVIES said that he only discovered these matters late the previous night when reading the bill itself. i He had rather sacrifice popularity on the alter of duty than I duty on the altar of popularity. He then proceeded to criticise the bill at length. Councillor MACKIE said that it would be a painful fact if Ithey threw out the bill as far as Warrington was concerned, when their twenty-two acred dock and its connections, and an outlay of £200,000 at least, would be lost as the result of a sudden and unexpected opposition from a most unex- pected quarter. Mr. Davies had been so quiet, whilst some others hod been so loud in their protestations, that he cer- tainly did not expect this from him. Councillor BROADBENT thought the time spent in listen- ing to Alderman Davies had been profitably occupied, and that it would be well if the members of the Council had had the ability to examine the question as carefully as he had done. He (Councillor Broadbent) believed that nothing had incited Alderman Davies to the work except a strong sense of public duty, and he for one thanked him for the great attention he had bestowed On the question and the in- formation he bad that night given them Aldermen BURGESS remarked that the jurisdiction of the Council did not extend to places beyond the borough, men- tioned by Alderman Davies. He thought they might safely lea-e the places outside the borough in the hands of those with whom they were entrusted. Alderman DeviEs said that he should no doubt be in an un- favourable position, but he did not think that should weigh with him. He felt that he had a duty to perform, and no desire for the popular voice would deter him. It was a pain- ful thing for him to do, and he should not 'Mittel:lce a single member of the Council to take the same course. Although he had not consulted counsel professionally he had done so indirectly, and one was thoroughly under the impression that the course the Council was taking was ultra olive. In another case counsel told him that it was very open question, and could only be determined in a court of law. If he could be sure the question would rest at 21 in the .E he would vote with them, but it was their being forced into the position of promoters of the canal to which he objected. He believed that the action by the coming promoters was outside the intentions of the muni- cipal Acts, and that the liability would extend beyond the I Corporation to individual members. Be would not vote against the resolution, but holding the convictions that he did he could not vote for it. Councillor BROADI3ENT said that it was not the question whether or no the scheme was desirable. It might both be desirable and beneficial and still be an undesirable, impropers and rash thing to vote corporate money for its promotion. They were acting irregularly, and in order to protect them- selves from the consequences of their rashness they had to get a guarantee from several Lancashire men. Alderman CRANDLEY said he should vote in favour of the agreement being signed, as he thought that the Council, having put its band to the plough; should honourably carry out the werk. Councillor ROBERTS said that the guarantee was either worth having as it was or it was worth nothing, and would not be improved by being extended to individual members. I He should vote for the resolution. The MAYOR did not think that they should incur any liability such as Alderman Davies seemed to fear. The resolution was then put, and carried without any hands being held up to the contrary, and the meeting con- cluded.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
Her Majesty's ship Rambler left Ireerness yesterday for Horz Kong to reinforce the British fleet on the China station.
The third tiial of James Ellis French commenced in Dublin yesterday, but excited remarkably little public in- terest.
A special telegram to the Debats (Paris) says that the doctors have ordered Prince Bismarck cntire repose and change of air:

- Wil!cock and Richard Thomas were killed, and Wm. Richards injurcd by the fall of a mineral bucket in the Gregory Mine, Penzance, on Friday. The steamer Oxenholme, from New York to Liverpool, put into Queenstown yesterday, lying on her beam ends, and with loss oi forty-five head of cattle. The annual return of vessels launched at Sunderland during the present year shows that the aggregate tonnage amounted to only 98,521, as against 212,360 tons last year. The prospects of trade for the coming year me, however, brighter.

_ „ SINGULAR CASE OF BLOOD POISONING.— Early on Fri- day morning James Howarth (20), son of Mr. John Howarth, brush manufacturer, Market-place, Heywood, died from blood poisoning under singular circumstances. The deceased had a pimple on his face which he pricked on Friday and Saturday last with a needle. Erysipelus set in immediately. Three medical men have since attended the deceased, whose body is awfully swollen, and they say that the cause of death is blood poisoning. ATTEMPTING TO MURDER A SWEETHEART.—At Bury, on Friday, Hugh Kennedy, engine tenter, was chaaged with wounding Rose Stevens. The prisoner lodged with the prosecutrix's mother, and kept company with the prosecu- trix. On Thursday morning he charged her with being too familiar with a man named Reader, and a quarrel ensued. He left the house, but returned in the afternoon and attempted to cut her throat with a razor. He, however, missed her throat, but cut her foreheaC. He was remanded. THE DYNAMITE SCARE.—Colonel Majendie's presence was not required at Bayer on 'Thursday night, the local authorities who have been trained of late to distinguish be- tween various explosive agents having been able to deter- mine very quickly that the stuff seized at Dover was not

dynamite, bat gunpowder prepared for manufacture into fireworks. Colonel Majendie was therefore again enabled to devote his attention to the more important investigations at London Bridge. He embarked on the police cutter from the Surrey pier chant half-past eight, and was at once rowed to the damaged buttress. It has already been stated that the granite blocks bear the appearance of having been scraped, but it was noticed yesterday that the surface is here and there smeared or dyed with peculiar shades of pink and purple. Colonel Majendie very carefully traced the direc- tion and extent of the iissures, especially a very plain one running in.an upward direction. He ascertained that one of the blocks of granite at the top was badly damaged and displaced, whilst outside a large niece at the bottom of the eastern corner was wrenched bodily trona its place, and had fallen in the water.

AN ORPHAN ASYLLTNI ,DESTROYED BY FIRE. A Central News New York telegram sips that St. John's Catholic Orphan Asylum, Brooklyn, was destroyed by lire on Thursdey. One of the nuns in charge and one boy were killed by jumping from a window. The rest of the children and the nuns were saved. The loss is estimated at half a milliou dollars.

EXTRAORDINARY CHARGE OF CONSPIRACY. A most remarkable case came before the Chester magis- trates on Friday morning, when Thomas Adams Stevens, ac- countant, of Chester, and Thomas Pugh, farm labourer, of Carndon, near Chester, were charged that in October last they did falsely and maliciously conspire fraudulently to le • present to Mary Emma Harris, of Sholach, that she was law- fully married to the prisoner, Thomas Pugh, and that he did therefore procure Miss Harris, who was then a woman , under the age of 21 years, to live with him as his wife, whereas, in truth, and in fact no lawful marriage service had been performed. Mr. Cartwight appeared on behalf of the public prosecutor, whose attention had been directed to the else by Mr. G. L. Fenwick, chief-constable of Chester. In consequence of the absence of several witnesses the de- tails were not gone into, but the allegation of the prosecu- tion is that in order to induce Miss Harris to live with Pugh, the prisoner took her to Steven's office, where, it is said, he induced Stevens to perform a mock marriage. Miss Harris, believing she was Pugh's wife, remained with him in Chester the same night. Mr. Cartwright said he was not quite prepared to go on with the case, and asked for an adk.urnment, which was granted, both prisoners being ad- mitted to bail,

div.head: AFRICAN ASSOCIATION.
div.p: THE AFRICAN ASSOCIATION.
BERLIN, FRIDAY AFTERNOON.—ItaIy to•day signed the treaty recognising the International African Association as a friendly State. THE GRAND DUKE OF HESSE'S DIVORCE.

LEIPSIC, FRIDAY.—The Imperial Supreme Court has to- day given judgment, rejecting the appeal of Madame de Kolemine against the decree of divorce granted to the Grand Duke of Hesse on July 9th last. THE AUSTBIAN BANK FRAUDS: SUICIDE OF A DIRECTOR.

VIENNA, FRIDAY AFIERNOON.—Herr Janner, the ab- sconding director of the Lower Austrian Discount Bank, committed suicide with a revolver. It is confirmed that his defalcations amount to over two million marks. The Go- vernment is assisting the bank to meet the heavy run.

div.head: LYMAL
div.p: LYMAL

WARIIIMOTON Gent, 111 TneenLE.—At the Lynarn Pollee Court on Toes lay, b3fore Mr. G. C. Dewhurst, Kate O'Brien and Bridget Toon, of Vi'arriegton, were charged with being on the premises of Mr. John Winstanlev, Lymm, for an unlawful purpose on the 15th inst. They were both sent to gaol for seven days with hard labour. PROPOSED CLOSING OF A FOOTPATH.—On Friday, Mr. T. J. Ridgway, clerk to the Lymm Local Board, appeared on behalf of the Local Board before the Lymm bench of magistrates to ask that they would inspect a footpath run- ning from Higher-lane to Long Butt, which, on the applica- tion of Mr. Dewhuret, it was proposed to close. In lieu of this footpath it was proposed to make a new road to run past the Grammar School.—The Chairman asked if there was any opposition to the project ?—Mr. Ridgway said there would be no objection at that stage. If there was any opposition it would be made at the Quarter Sessions.—lt was agreed that Mr. Stanton and Mr. Long should inspect the footpath. BILLIARDS AND WIIIST.—TtIO members of the Earles- town Conservative club spent a very enjoyable evening on Tuesday, when several visitors from Lymm contested games of billiards and whist with their Earlestown friends. In the billiard matches there were eight games played in the presence of a large number of other members, the room being nicely filled. The Lymm players won five games to three by their opponents, the aggregate scores being : Lymm 744, Earlestown 707, majortti, for Lymm 37. In the whist contest there were four sets of players, and the Earlestown representatives won three rubbers out of the four played. The visitors were subsequently entertained to refreshments by their Earlestown friends in one of the rooms of the club, the proceedings being interspersed with songs by Messrs G. Wright, R. Wright (Earlestown), Thomason (Lymm), Sec.

FRlDAY.—Before Messrs P. Stabs (in the chair), W. Long, E. Collins, IL Stanton, and T. P. Norris..

ALLEGED ASSIIILTS.—John Shaw, a young men, was charged with assaulting Richard Winrstanley on the Bth December in Peter Winstanley's beerhouse, at Lymm. The complainant said that be had been a witness in a former case against a relative of Shaw's and since then the latter had assaulted him twice, the assault in question consisting in his being dragged out of the beerhouse by Shaw. It was stated, however, on the other side that Winstanley had been noisy, and bad been ordered out of the house by the land- lord. The case was dismissed.—William Dewharst was also charged with assaulting Winstanley on the same occa- sion, and was bound over to keep the peace for six months.

ILL•TREATING A Housn.—Edward Dean, a young cab driver, was charged with ill-treating a horse at Altrincham, on the 13th November.—He was seen on that day by P.C.'s Buchanaa and Chatterton beating the horse, which was in a cab, in a very severe manner, and on the constables examin- ing the animal it was found to have a large number of weals on its body, evidently cause' by the blows.—Defen- dant having been convicted for drunkenness on the same day, was now fined the costs, 10s 6d. ASSAULTING A WIFE.—John Johnson, an elderly man, was charged with haying assaulted his wife, Mary Johnson, on the night of the 13th inst., at Peppery-street, Lymm. Mr. Jenkins, Warrington, appeared for the complainant, and Mr. P. Davies for the defendant. John Lea and James Holt were also charged with baying assaulted John Johnson, and in this cise the complainant was represented by Mr. Davies, and the defendants by Mr. Jenkins.—Mr. Jenkins said that was one of those unfortunate cases too common in the present day. If the charge brought by the wife against her husband for a very brutal assault was borne out by the facts the Bench would have no difficulty in finding that this assault was one of such a character as would justify them in making an order for a judicial separation, which he was instructed to apply for. The facts were that on the night of the 13th inst. the complainant went to a shop in Lymm, and when she returned she found the door of the house locked, and on inquiry she learned that her husband was in the house. She asked him several times to let her into the house, but he refused. Be (Mr. Jenkins) might say that what in all probability had given rise to that case was that owing to the prevalence of fever in Lymm Mrs. Johnson had taken three children belonging to a family with which she was connected in order that they might be out of the way of the disease. When the defendant persistently refused to open the door complainant's son, James Holt, who had come up in the meantime, broke a :Ample of panes and opened the window to get in, and as he was getting in he was assaulted by the defendant. Holt opened the door, and Mrs. Johnson was just going in, when the defendant struck her on the eye and knocked her down. Defendant threatened to throttle her, and Holt and complainant's son- in-law, John Lea, preyented him, end a scuffle ensued, in which the alleged assaults were committed on defendant.— After a protracted hearing the Bench decided that John Johnson should be fined 20s and costs for the assault on his wife, and be bound over to keep the peace for 12 months in his own security of £2O; the other charges of assault were dismissed.

CHRISTMAS AND NEVI, YEAR'S CARDS. For beauty, artistic design, and charming variety no cards in town sur- pass those shown by Mr. John S. Green, 34, Bridge-street, Warrington, whose collection includes all the latest novel- ties in photos,, watercolours, screens, drc., and is well worth inspection.—Advt. AN AFFRAY WILII SOLDIERS —Four privates of the South Lancashire Regimht, stationed at Orford, were brought up at the Borough Court, on Thursday, under serious circum- stances. One, Michael Ktllane, was charged with being drunk and disorderly, and the other three—Patrick Gavan, John Gragan, and Thomas Green—with assaulting several of the borough constables. It appeared that Kallane was fighting, stripped to the waist, when he was surprised by the police, who proceeded to take him into custody. The other prisoners interfered and became violent, whereupon a severe struggle ensued, belts and staffs being need in the row. One of the soldiers escaped and ran away, but he was afterwards arrested. With difficulty prisoners were got to the police station. Kallane was sent to prison for 14 days, and his comrades were sentenced to two months each. IMPUDENT THEFT IN A PUBLIC-HOUSE —At the Borough Court, on Monday, Ellen Connor, fustian cutter, was charged with stealir,g. a basket containing 41bs. of beef, value is. 9d., the property of Patrick Garritty, on Saturday evening, and with assaulting Robert Arguy.—Mr. Hunt (chief-constable) said that the prosecutor and his wife on Saturday evening went to the Curriers Arms to have a glass of beer. The wife put her basket on a form near where the prisoner was sitting. Prisoner removed the basket, and then took it out of the house, followed by Mrs. Garritty, who, however, could not discover where he had gone. In about a quarter of an hour prisoner returned to the public-house without the basket, and when asked about it she used foul language and asked what she had to do with the basket. P.C. Corcoran was called in, and she was taken into custody. On the way to the police station she kicked Arm,, a militiaman, who was assisting. She afterwards told In- spector Spinks where the basket would be found.—Sentenced to two months' hard labour. WARRINGTON TRAINING COLLEGE.—The first annual prize distribution took place at this college yesterday after- noon week. There was a good gathering of friends of the college, amongst those present being the Bishop of Man- chester and Mrs. Fraser, Canon Penrhyn, Rev. S. Wilkin- son, Rev. E. C. E. and Mrs. Carleton, Rev. B. Prescott, Rev. J. Phillips, Rev. F Slater, Rev. M. Schonberg, Rev. R. W. Montgomery, Rev. J. Weller, Mr. N. Waterhouse, Dr. Wat- kins (hon. sec.), Mrs. Beamont, Mrs, Stevenson, Major and Mrs. Hamilton, Mrs. J. Jones, Mrs. and Miss Appleton, Mrs. Willcecks, Mrs. McFall, Mr. Charles and Miss White, Mrs. and Miss Buckton, Mrs. Dodd, Miss Smith, dm., besides the Principal (Rev. Morley Stevenson), and the members of the college staff. The Principal read a short sum- mary of the work of the college during the past year. The Bishop of Manchester next proceeded to distribute the following prizes to the successful students :-2nd year, Holy Scripture, Bertha Hodgson ; English literature. Margaretta Timewell ; school maoaeetnent, Margaret Rogers and Jane Aiken; geography, Lizzie Chambers; domestic economy, Lizzie Chambers; arithmetic, Mary Mellor mid Sarah Rigby; history. Margaret Timewell ; French, Mary Mellor; music, Amers Salter; needlework, result not yet received from Miss Hopwood. let year, Holy Scripture, Elizabeth Airey ; English literature, Louisa Gamon ; school manage- ment, Hannah Gee; geography, Mary Bibby; domestic economy, Mary Bibby; arithmetic, Mary Marguison ; his- tory, Ada Morley; French, Mary Marguison ; needle- work, Mary Dawson, Helen Little, Ada Lloyd, Elizabeth Airey. The prizes were from various sources— the Committee, many kind friends of the college, the Principal, and the members of the college staff.— The Bishop, having given away the prizes, made a few remarks. He said he was very pleased that, at this their first annual gathering, it had fallen to him, 119 senior bishop of the three dioceses for which the college was founded, to be present and distribute the prizes. He thought that, when all things were considered, the Principal's report of the year's work might be considered eminently satisfactory. Mr. and Mrs. Baker might feel that they left the college in an effi- cient state, and he was confident that the success would be continued and increased.—Dr. Watkins (hon. sec.) proposed, and the Rev. S. Wilkinson seconded, a vote of thanks to the Bishop.—ln another room some exceedingly good speci- mens of needlework were laid out. Most of the visitors inspected them with much pleasure, and after tea asd coffee had been served the company separated.

IN PAIILIAMENT. SESSION 1855. THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. WHERW, a Meeting of the Owners and Ratepayers of tbe Borough of Warrington, in the Counties of Lancaster and Chester. was held on Thursday, the Twenty-third day of Octo- ber, 1854, in the Public Hall. Rylands-street, in the said Borough, in pursuance of the Act of the 35th and 36th Vic., cap, 91, intituled "An Act to authorize the application of Funds of Municipal Corporations and other governing bodies in certain cases." And whereas at the said Meeting, held at the time and place aforesaid. 1, as Chairman of such Meeting, and in compliance with the statute, proposed the following resolution:— . That this meeting eonsents to the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses of the Borough of Warrington promoting, in con- junction with others, a local and personal Bill in Parliament for the purpose of incorporating a Company and empowering such Company to construct a canal from the River Mersey to the City of Manchester, navigable for Ocean Steamers and Ships of largo burthen, and to the contribution ant of the Borough Rate to the cost of such promotion of a sum not ex- ceeding twopence in the pound upon the annual rateable value of the Borough for one year." And whereas the said resolution, on being put to the Meeting, was carried, whereupon demand was made that such question should be decided by a Poll of the Owners and Rate- payers. And whereas a Poll was accordingly taken in manner pro- vided by the Public Health Act, 1875, and the schedules thereto, and the votes recorded thereat were as follows In favour of the above resolution Against -- Majority in favour of resolution 5,840 Dated this 3rd ?ay of December, 1584. JOSEPH HARRISON. Mayor and Returning Officer.

- Soft was the violet's vernal hue, Fresh was the rose's morning red, • Full-robed and stately dahlia grew— x..ar.ure. , All gone! Their short-lived beauty shed; The shadows lengthening stretch at noon, The fields are stripped, the groves are dumb, The frost flowers greet the icy moon— Still blooms the bright Chrysanthemum. TM The stiffening turf is white with snow; _ Undimmed its radiant disks are seen, Where soon the hallowed morn will show The wreath and cross of Christmas green, "4- As if in Autumn's dying days It heard the heavenly song afar, And opened all its living rays, , The herald-lamp of Bethlehem's star. Orphan of Summer, kindly sent To cheer the waning year's decline, Of all that pitying heaven has lent, No fairer pledge of hope than thine; Yes! June lies hid beneath the snow, And Winter's unborn heir shall claim In every seed that sleeps below A spark that kindles into flame. Thy smile the scowling storm-cloud braves, Last of the bright-robed flowery train, Soft sighing o'er their garden graves "Farewell! farewell! we meet again;" So may life's chill November bring Hope's golden flower, the last of all Before we hear the angels sing Where blossoms never fade and fall. —Oliver Wendell Holmes.
