AIKOri has disappeared. He had, when last seen, a large sum of - ! money. Mr. Jacob Bright, M.P., delivered an address on Conti. nental travel before the members of the Manchester arts , Club, on Wednesday evening. Messrs John Brinsmead and Sons, through their agents at Aberdeen have supplied two pianos to her Majesty the Queen and to the Duchess of Edinburgh. Mr. P. J. Smyth, M.P., has been appointed 5,:.•."( t tiy to the Irish Loan Fund Board. There will consequ,n'Av be a vacancy is the repeesentation of Tipperary. The Queen, accompanied by Princess Beatrice and the Royal suite, left Windsor on Wednesday morning for Osborne, where Her Majesty will spend Christmas. At the Burnley police court, on Wednesday, John Berry and Henry Baxter, butchers, were each fined £lO and costs for being in possession of diseased meat intended for sale. A plan is in preparation for sending Dutch milk to Lon- don daily. Four steamers will ply between Amsterdem and Harwich. The necessary capital is estimated at 1,700,000 florins. At the Syston Park Library, Sale, on Saturday, a cele- brated Mazarin Bible was put up for competition, and after some spirited bidding was knocked down to Mr. Quaritch for £3900. A fire broke out on Wednesday morning in a spinning room at. Messrs Hawkins and Sons' mill, Gordon-street, Preston, doing damage to the amount of several thousand pounds. The match between Shaw's team and Murdoch's eleven concluded on Tuesday at Adelaide. The Australian, were all out for 191, leaving the Englishmen with 63 to win, which they scored with the loss of two wickets. At Axbridge, on Wednesday, John Day, farmer, was com- mitted for trial on a charge of having, at Lympsham, near Weston-super-Mare, murdered his wife's aunt by the ad- ministration of poison under circumstances previously re- corded. A CONSIDERATE LANDLORD.—The Earl of Aberdeen pro- poses to devote £350 to be applied to a redaction of the pre- sent half-year's rent of those tenants who were the principal sufferers by the hail storm of the 4th September last about Quilquox and the adjacent district. PIRACY.—The Treasury have directed a prosecution against three Yarmouth smacksmen for an alleged act of piracy on the high seas. It is alleged that these men, with eight other English smacksmen, boarded a German cooper named Diedrich, in July, while off the Dutch coast and took away tobacco, spirits, Sic. The trial at Carrick-on-Shannon Assizes of a man named Fogarty, charged with being concerned in the murder of Peter Doherty, ended at a late hour on Wednesday night, in the disagreement of the jury. The jury were in consulta- tion for nearly two hours before they announced their in- ability to find a verdict. PROFESSOR FAWCETT'S SUCCESSOR.—Mr. Alfred Marshall, of St. John's College, was on Saturday appointed professor of political economy at Cambridge, in succession to the late Professor Fawcett. Mr. Marshall will have to resign the appointment as political economy lecturer at Balliol College, Oxford, which he has held since 1881. TEE REPRESENTATION OF LIVERPOOL.—It is IDMOUred that Mr. Charles Russell, Q.C., who now sits for Dundalk, will probably contest one of the divisions of Liverpool in which the Roman Catholic population predominates. Mr. Russell is not a Home Ruler, but he has frequently acted with the Parnellite party in Parliament. ALLEGED MURDER OF A HUSBAND.—Elizabeth Gibbons was indicted at the Central Criminal Court on Thursday for the murder of her husband at Uxbridge, by shooting him with a revolver. The defence is to the effect that the fatal wound was inflicted in a struggle for the possession of the revolver. The trial is not concluded. SAD END OF AN AMERICAN BIOLOGIST.—OOIODeI VV. R. Newton, the celebrated American biologist, was riding a tricycle in Aldersgate•street, London' on Tuesday, when 'the machine collided with a cab. Colonel Newton was thrown violently to the ground, sustaining a fracture of the skull, from which he died two hours afterwards. VacceNerron.—The supplementary report of the Medi• cal Officer of the Local Government Board for 1883-4, Issued on Wednesday as a parliamentary paper, sets forth that the returns of the vaccination officers show a fairly steady advance in obedience to the law. The precautions taken against the possible importation of cholera are de- tailed. FATAL COLLIERY ExPLosrow.—An explosion occurred early on Thursday morning at Pwllcarn Colliery, Garw Valley, Glamorganshire. Three men were descending the pit at the time. One of them was blown off the " bowk " by the force of the explosion, and falling 100 yards was The other two were rescued, but were much injured, all their clothes having been burned off. FATAL ACCIDENT AT NEWTON MOOR. A young man named Samuel Hadfield died on Thursday at Ashton-under- Lyne Infirmary from the effects of a fall at Mr. Daniel Adamsou's works at Newton Moor, where he was employed. It appears that the deceased was on a crane in the fitting shop superintending the removal of a casting weighing 15 or 20 tons. The casting had been raised, and the deceased was moving the crane when some chain broke, and the de- ceased fell to the ground on his head. ELECTION OF AN AecnersnoP.—An event of the first importance to the Irish Church and of great interest to Episcopalian Churchmen everywhere took place on Thurs- day. It was the election of an Archbishop of Dublin in the place of the Most Rev. Dr. Trench, whom age and declining health have compelled to retire from his high office. Votes were recorded for about a dozen bishops and clerics of lower ' degree, but the choice really lay between the Bishop of Meath and the Bishop of Ossory. The result of the final voting was the election of the Bishop of Meath (the Right Rev. Lord Plunket) to the Archiepiscopal See of Dublin. A STRUGGLE FOR POSIESSION.—There has been another ' scene in connection with the dispute for possession of Dundee (Ramsbottom) Chapel, the keys of which were re- turned to the governing body of the chapel on Monday ' morning in accordance with the decision of the High Court of Justice. This time the struggle was for the house for- merly occupied by the minister, which had been barricaded to prevent a forcible entrance. Notwithstanding this, the Rev. W. H. Elliott and his friends succeeded in getting into the house and ejecting the man in possession. They were, however, in turn forced out of the house, and the rev. gen- tleman and his friends had to retire under the protection of the police. PROPORTIONAL REPRESENTATION.—At a meeting of the I Proportional Representation Society, held in London, on Monday evening—at which Sir J. Lubbock presided—Mr. Courtney explained the principles of the society's scheme. He said they proposed that all the electors of the kingdom should have a chance of being represented according to their strength. They would secure the representation of all classes and interests, and bring all forms of thought and of I national aspiration within the National Assembly. Under the new Bill the agricultural labourer would get the vote, but there was no security that he would also secure a re- presentative. The Government scheme failed as a repre- sentative scheme. Whatever else it did, it did not secure the representation of classes. At the City Council meeting on Thursday, the Chairman of the Bridge House Committee said that directly the ex- I plosion took place instructions were given to the architect to make an examination. Fortunately the drain hole in which the miscreants intended to place the charge had been protected by a grating, which was placed there in August atlhe suggestion of the Government; but for this the bridge would have suffered severe injury. The disturbance of several stones showed the violence of the explosion. A report from Major Majendie was read, saying that the curb. stone at the bottom of the river had been more or less pul- verized, but the strength of the bridge was not affected. Subsequently, a motion was carried to offer a reward of £5,000 for the discovery of the miscreants. Mierram. DAVITT ON Home RULE. Speaking at Cork, on Saturday, Mr. Michael Davitt expressed his dissent from the proposal to establish a parliament of Lords and Com- mons in Dublin, as he considered such a project wholly im- practicable. What he advocated was the election of a national assembly on the vote of every adult male citizen in Ireland to legislate in all matters appertaining to that coun- try. This he considered a more feasible proposal than the constitution of a Republic, which would not work with a powerful nation like England so near at hand.—Mr. Deasy, M.P., proposed, and Alderman Madden, Mayor•elect, secon- ded a vote of thanks to Mr. Davitt, explaining that how- ever they differed with his nationalisation scheme they could not help admiring him as an earnest and patriotic Irishman. A SUNDAY LECTURE BY PROFESSOR BLACKlZ.—Professor Blackie delivered, on Sunday, at Glasgow, a lecture on Scottish love songs, to an audience oi 4,000 persons. In the course of his lecture the professor said some people thought it profane to deliver such a lecture on Sunday, but he thought that what was harmless or good on week-days could not be bad on Sunday. Ministers opposed his speak- ing on love songs and beautiful women, but clergymen usually sought for beautiful wives, especially if they pos- sessed the added advantage of a well-filled purse. For his own part he liked to see a woman's beautiful face. At the conclusion of the lecture, which provoked much cheering and laughter, Professor Blackle sang, to the intense delight of his auditors, the old Scotch ballad, "Will ye gang to Kelvingrove,bonnie lassie, 0" MRS. WELDON IN TUE APPEAL CCIORT.—Mrs. Weldon on Wednesday appealed from the decision of Justices Stephen, Mathew, and Smith, staving execution in her libel action against Mr. Johnson, London correspondent of the Paris Figaro, in which she got £5OO damages. The Court dismissed the appeal, costs to abide the final result of the appeal by Mr. Johnson. The appeal cage of Weldon v. De Bathe was also heard on Wednesday, Mrs. Weldon appealing against the decision of Justices Mathew and Day in her action against Sir Henry De Bathe for trespass, slander, and libel. The Divisional Court ordered the causes of action alleging trespass and slander to be struck out of the state- ment of claim, and this was the order appealed against. Mrs. Weldon appeared in person and argued against the decision. Their lordships decided that the order of the Divisional Court, as regards the slander, must be confirmed. As re- garded the trespass they intimated that they would give judgment next morning. In the Court of Appeal, on Thurs- day, the Master of the Rolls gave judgment, with Lord Justices Cotton and Lindley, in the appeal of Mrs. Weldon from the decision of the Divisional Court in the case of Weldon v. de Bathe. The Court granted the appeal on tie point of trespass, but not on that of slander, and gave her the costs of the appeal. KAY'S TIC Friss, a specific In Neuralgia, Face ache. Ac. 94d. ANOTHER NARROW ESCAPE ON THE RAILWAY.—On Wed- nesday a man named Patrick Butler, generally known a " Patsy," who is employed as guard on a local goods train by the Cheshire Lines Committee, and who resides at Stockport, had a narrow escape when on the line near Pad. gate. A train from Manchester, running at a speed of about 40 miles an hour, came upon him, and, striking hinn on the left arm, knocked him out of the way. He was not seriously injured, but is under medical care. A Pinnaces HEAVILY FINED.—At the Borough Court on Monday, two men named Alfred Walker and Alexander Flanagan, were charged with having, on the 11th inst., been . drunk on the licensed premises of John Wood, the Old Ball, Town's.end.—lnspector Spinks stated that on the evening of the date named he, in company with P.S. Bawsn, went tO the premises of Mr. Wood. Outside the counter he saw Flanagan, who was the worse for liquor, and inside the bar • sat the landlord, drunk, with Walker, who was also drunk, beside him. A man "put in" the house by the sheriff of ' the county was acting as barman, and the defendant Walker was his assistant. When he served the summonses the fol. lowing morning the landlord was then drunk.—Walker was " fined 103 and costs, or 14 days', and Flanigan 5s and costs, or 7 days.--The landlord, John Wood, was then charged with permitting drunkenness, and the evidence was repeated. —Mr. Robert Davies, who appeared for the owners of the house, said that the defendant ssemed to be quite losing hint. self.—Chief Constable Hunt said that the defendant had occupied the house since 1805, but of late he seemed to have taken to drink and to have become thoroughly reckless— The magistrates fined the defendant £5 and costs, or a month, and he was also told that the license would • be endorsed if he did nut leave the house as soon as possible.
